key_obligations: Member states should conduct readiness assessments
AI must respect human dignity and rights
Gender equality and non-discrimination must be ensured
Environmental impact of AI must be assessed
Moratorium on high-risk AI applications recommended pending robust safeguards

impact_assessment.detail: Recommends AI ethics impact assessments before deployment; includes Readiness Assessment Methodology for states.

prohibited_categories.detail: Recommends moratorium on high-risk applications (e.g., real-time biometric surveillance) but does not formally prohibit.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals should have the right to contest significant AI decisions affecting them.

private_right_of_action.detail: Non-binding recommendation; no enforcement or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not specifically address synthetic media or deepfakes.

biometric_data.detail: Recommends moratorium on real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces pending adequate safeguards.

training_data_transparency.detail: Transparency principle covers outputs but not training data specifically.

anti_discrimination.detail: Requires impact assessments to identify and mitigate discriminatory outcomes; impact-based standard.

risk_classification.detail: Recommends risk-based approach; states to develop own classification schemes aligned with Recommendation principles.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding; implementation through national AI strategies and RAM assessments; no penalty mechanism.

short_name: G7 Hiroshima AI Code of Conduct
full_name: G7 Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
max_penalty: None — Voluntary industry code of conduct; no penalty mechanism.
preemption_notes: Voluntary industry code of conduct agreed by G7 leaders (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, UK, US, EU). Directly influenced Japanese AI Promotion Act and EU GPAI Code of Practice.
summary: The G7 Hiroshima Process Code of Conduct, agreed by G7 leaders in October 2023 under Japan's G7 presidency, establishes 11 voluntary principles for advanced AI developers. It covers transparency, safety, security, content authentication, reporting incidents, cybersecurity, and trustworthy AI. It was the first major international agreement specifically targeting frontier AI systems.
notable: First G7 agreement specifically targeting frontier AI; directly shaped the EU GPAI Code of Practice and Japan's AI Promotion Act.
legal_citation: G7 Hiroshima AI Process (2023)
key_obligations: Identify and mitigate risks throughout AI lifecycle
Report AI incidents to governments
Implement content authentication (watermarking)
Prioritise safety and security in AI development
Publish transparency reports

impact_assessment.detail: Principle 1 requires developers to identify and mitigate risks; safety evaluations required before and after deployment of frontier models.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary code; no prohibited categories defined.

human_review_rights.detail: Code targets developers; no individual human review rights created.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary code; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Principle 8 requires implementation of technical mechanisms (watermarking) to enable identification of AI-generated content.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions in the Code.

training_data_transparency.detail: Principle 5 requires sharing information with governments on AI capabilities, training data sources, and risk evaluations.

content_labeling.detail: Watermarking and content provenance mechanisms required; disclosure to users of AI-generated content.

anti_discrimination.detail: No explicit anti-discrimination provisions; fairness addressed through general risk mitigation principle.

risk_classification.detail: Applies to 'advanced AI systems'; no formal risk tier classification scheme.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary code; no penalty regime. G7 tasked OECD with monitoring adoption.

short_name: UN General Assembly AI Resolution (2024)
full_name: UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/265: Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development
max_penalty: None — Non-binding UN GA resolution; no enforcement mechanism.
preemption_notes: Non-binding UN General Assembly resolution adopted by consensus of 193 member states. Politically significant as first UN-level consensus on AI governance.
summary: The first UN General Assembly resolution on AI governance, adopted by consensus in March 2024. It calls on member states to develop safe, secure, and trustworthy AI; emphasises the need to bridge the digital divide; highlights AI risks to human rights; and requests the Secretary-General to establish a High-Level Advisory Body on AI.
notable: First UN General Assembly consensus on AI; US co-sponsored with 120+ co-sponsors; establishes the High-Level AI Advisory Body (AIAB).
key_obligations: States to promote safe, secure, trustworthy AI for SDGs
Bridge the AI divide between developed and developing nations
Respect human rights in AI development and use
Support the UN Secretary-General's AI governance initiatives

impact_assessment.detail: Resolution encourages responsible AI; does not mandate specific impact assessment procedures.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not define prohibited AI uses.

human_review_rights.detail: References human rights generally; no specific human review right created.

private_right_of_action.detail: UN resolution; no enforcement mechanism or private right.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media specifically.

anti_discrimination.detail: Resolution emphasises human rights and non-discrimination; defers to existing international human rights framework.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding political resolution; no penalty mechanism.

short_name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
full_name: NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
max_penalty: None — Voluntary framework; compliance is self-assessed. No penalty.
preemption_notes: Voluntary framework for private sector; referenced as standard in federal procurement. Some agencies and states cite NIST AI RMF compliance as a safe harbour factor.
summary: Published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the AI RMF provides a structured approach to managing AI risks through four core functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. It is voluntary for private industry but referenced in federal contracting requirements and cited in state AI bills. It is accompanied by the AI RMF Playbook with specific recommended actions.
notable: The dominant US private-sector AI risk management standard; referenced in Colorado SB 205, Texas TRAIGA, and over 30 state AI bills as a compliance benchmark.
legal_citation: NIST AI 100-1
key_obligations: Establish AI governance policies (GOVERN)
Identify AI risks in context (MAP)
Analyse and prioritise AI risks (MEASURE)
Address and monitor AI risks (MANAGE)
Document AI system capabilities and limitations

impact_assessment.detail: MEASURE function requires systematic risk assessment; MAP function identifies context-specific harms before deployment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary framework; no prohibited categories — risk management approach instead.

human_review_rights.detail: Framework is organisational; does not create individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary framework; no enforcement mechanism or private right.

synthetic_media.detail: Generative AI profile (NIST AI 600-1) addresses deepfake risks but does not mandate labeling.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions in core framework.

training_data_transparency.detail: Documentation requirements in GOVERN function include training data quality, lineage, and bias assessment.

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling requirements; content authenticity addressed in Generative AI Profile.

anti_discrimination.detail: Bias and fairness assessment required in MEASURE function; impact-based approach aligned with disparate impact analysis.

risk_classification.detail: MAP function requires classification of AI use cases by risk level; higher risk applications require more rigorous treatment.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary framework; compliance is self-assessed. Federal procurement increasingly references alignment as evaluation criterion.

operative_dates: Published Jan 2023. Living document; Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) released Jul 2024 as supplementary guidance.

short_name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI Management System
full_name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)
max_penalty: None — Voluntary standard; certification is optional. No regulatory penalty.
preemption_notes: Voluntary international standard. EU AI Act references harmonised standards as a compliance pathway; ISO 42001 certification is expected to serve as a conformity route for some EU AI Act obligations.
summary: ISO/IEC 42001 is the first international management system standard for AI, modelled on ISO 9001 (quality) and ISO 27001 (information security). It provides a certifiable framework for organisations to establish, implement, maintain, and continuously improve an AI management system. It is designed to align with the EU AI Act's conformity assessment requirements.
notable: First certifiable international AI management standard; expected to serve as a conformity pathway under EU AI Act harmonised standards mandate.
key_obligations: Establish AI policy and objectives
Conduct AI impact assessments
Implement risk treatment controls
Maintain records of AI system inventory
Conduct management reviews and continual improvement

impact_assessment.detail: Clause 6.1.2 requires AI impact assessments; Annex A provides controls including data quality and bias assessment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Management system standard; does not define prohibited AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Standard is organisational; does not create individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary standard; no enforcement or private right of action.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific controls; general data governance applies.

training_data_transparency.detail: Annex A Control A.7 addresses data quality; training data documentation required in management system records.

anti_discrimination.detail: Fairness objectives addressed generally through impact assessment controls; no explicit discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: Clause 6.1.2 requires context-specific risk assessment; higher-risk applications require more extensive controls.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary; certification is third-party verified but no regulatory penalty for non-certification.

short_name: ISO/IEC 23894:2023 AI Risk Management
full_name: ISO/IEC 23894:2023 — Information Technology: Artificial Intelligence — Guidance on Risk Management
max_penalty: None — Voluntary guidance standard; no penalty mechanism.
preemption_notes: Technical guidance standard aligned with ISO 31000 (general risk management). Designed to be used alongside ISO 42001.
summary: ISO/IEC 23894 provides technical guidance on integrating AI risk management into organisational risk management processes, aligned with ISO 31000. It identifies AI-specific risk sources (bias, opacity, data quality, adversarial inputs) and provides a structured process for risk identification, analysis, evaluation, and treatment.
notable: Companion standard to ISO 42001; provides technical risk methodology that 42001 management system standard implements organisationally.
key_obligations: Identify AI-specific risk sources
Analyse and evaluate AI risks in context
Implement risk treatment measures
Monitor AI risks continuously

impact_assessment.detail: Provides structured methodology for pre-deployment AI risk assessment aligned with ISO 31000 process.

prohibited_categories.detail: Technical guidance; no prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Does not create individual rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary standard; no enforcement.

training_data_transparency.detail: Data quality as a risk source identified; no disclosure requirement.

anti_discrimination.detail: Bias identified as risk source; no formal discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: Risk level determines treatment intensity; higher-risk AI requires more comprehensive treatment measures.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary guidance; no penalty mechanism.

short_name: EU AI Office Guidelines on Prohibited Practices
full_name: EU AI Office Guidelines on Prohibited AI Practices (Article 5 EU AI Act)
preemption_notes: Authoritative interpretation of EU AI Act Article 5 prohibited practices. Directly applicable guidance; member state authorities must apply it from 2 February 2025.
summary: Published by the EU AI Office on 4 February 2025, these guidelines provide authoritative interpretation of the eight categories of prohibited AI practices under Article 5 of the EU AI Act. They cover: subliminal manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring by public authorities, real-time biometric surveillance in public, emotion recognition in workplace/education, biometric categorisation from scraping, and AI-enabled manipulation of criminal risk.
notable: First binding interpretive guidance under the EU AI Act; effective from 2 February 2025 alongside the prohibited practices provisions.
legal_citation: EU AI Office Guidelines (Art. 5 EU AI Act)
key_obligations: Ban on subliminal manipulation causing harm
Ban on exploitation of vulnerabilities
Ban on public authority social scoring
Ban on real-time biometric surveillance with limited exceptions
Ban on emotion recognition in workplace and education
Ban on biometric categorisation from internet scraping

impact_assessment.detail: Guidelines interpret prohibitions, not impact assessment requirements (addressed in separate EU AI Act provisions).

prohibited_categories.detail: Authoritatively interprets all 8 prohibited practice categories in EU AI Act Art. 5, including subliminal manipulation, social scoring, and biometric surveillance.

human_review_rights.detail: Guidelines focus on prohibited practices; human oversight addressed in high-risk AI provisions separately.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement is administrative by national market surveillance authorities; private action follows national procedural law.

synthetic_media.detail: Prohibited practices guidelines do not specifically address synthetic media (covered in GPAI and transparency provisions).

biometric_data.detail: Guidelines interpret the prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces, including the narrow law enforcement exceptions.

training_data_transparency.detail: Not addressed in prohibited practices context.

content_labeling.detail: Content labeling is a transparency provision, not a prohibition.

anti_discrimination.detail: Guidelines explicitly link prohibited practices to fundamental rights; biometric categorisation prohibition grounded in anti-discrimination principle.

risk_classification.detail: These are the unacceptable risk (prohibited) tier of the EU AI Act four-tier system; guidelines do not address the broader classification framework.

enforcement_model.detail: Violations of prohibited practices carry the highest EU AI Act penalties: €35M or 7% global turnover. EU AI Office and national market surveillance authorities enforce.

operative_dates: Guidelines issued Feb 2025 on the prohibited AI practices provisions of the EU AI Act, which became applicable 2 Feb 2025.

short_name: EU GPAI Code of Practice (2025)
full_name: EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice — First Draft (EU AI Act Articles 53–55)
preemption_notes: Developed under EU AI Act Art. 56 multi-stakeholder process. Compliance creates a presumption of conformity with GPAI obligations. Final version expected mid-2025.
summary: Developed through a multi-stakeholder process convened by the EU AI Office under Article 56 of the EU AI Act, this Code of Practice sets out the specific obligations for General-Purpose AI (GPAI) model providers. It covers transparency, training data copyright compliance, systemic risk assessment, cybersecurity, and content watermarking for frontier models. Compliance creates a presumption of conformity with the EU AI Act's GPAI provisions.
notable: First international compliance code specifically for frontier AI model providers; creates a presumption of conformity with EU AI Act GPAI chapter — effectively a safe harbour.
legal_citation: EU AI Act Art. 53–56
key_obligations: Publish technical documentation and model card
Copyright compliance policy for training data
Systemic risk assessment for high-capability models
Implement adversarial testing (red-teaming)
Watermark AI-generated content
Report serious incidents to EU AI Office

impact_assessment.detail: Systematic risk assessment and adversarial testing required before deployment of GPAI models above capability thresholds.

prohibited_categories.detail: Code addresses GPAI obligations; prohibited practices are covered in separate EU AI Act provisions.

human_review_rights.detail: GPAI Code does not create individual human review rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Code creates presumption of conformity; enforcement is by EU AI Office and national authorities.

synthetic_media.detail: GPAI providers must implement technical solutions to mark AI-generated content; watermarking standards to be specified by EU AI Office.

biometric_data.detail: GPAI Code does not address biometric data specifically.

training_data_transparency.detail: Training data summary (including copyright compliance policy) must be published; detailed documentation provided to EU AI Office on request.

content_labeling.detail: AI-generated content from GPAI models must be marked to enable detection; technical specifications issued by EU AI Office.

anti_discrimination.detail: GPAI Code focuses on systemic risks; anti-discrimination for applications is addressed under high-risk provisions.

risk_classification.detail: GPAI models classified by capability threshold (training compute ≥ 10²⁵ FLOPs = systemic risk); higher tier faces additional requirements.

enforcement_model.detail: EU AI Office enforces GPAI obligations directly; penalties up to €15M or 3% global turnover; Code compliance creates safe harbour presumption.

implementation_phases.description: GPAI model transparency obligations under EU AI Act begin applying
First draft of GPAI Code of Practice published
GPAI systemic risk provisions and Code of Practice expected to be finalised

short_name: Argentina AI National Plan Decree 1182/2024
full_name: Argentine Artificial Intelligence National Plan — Decree 1182/2024
enforcement_body: Secretariat of Innovation, Science and Technology
max_penalty: None — Executive decree for government internal use; no penalty for private sector.
preemption_notes: Federal executive decree; applies to national public administration. Provincial AI rules may coexist under Argentina's federal system.
summary: Decree 1182/2024 establishes Argentina's National AI Plan and creates an AI Ethics Committee within the national public administration. It requires impact assessments for AI systems used in government decisions, adopts a risk-based approach aligned with OECD principles, and mandates transparency for AI systems affecting citizens. The decree applies to national executive branch agencies and sets principles for future legislation.
notable: First Latin American executive decree establishing a mandatory AI ethics framework for government; creates a precedent before any national AI legislation is enacted.
legal_citation: Decreto 1182/2024 — Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial
key_obligations: Impact assessment for AI in government decisions
AI Ethics Committee review of high-risk applications
Transparency to citizens of AI use in public services
Adherence to OECD AI Principles in government procurement

impact_assessment.detail: Mandatory algorithmic impact assessment required for AI systems used in government decisions affecting citizens.

prohibited_categories.detail: Framework decree; does not define prohibited AI uses beyond general human rights constraints.

human_review_rights.detail: Citizens have right to request human review of significant government AI decisions under the decree.

private_right_of_action.detail: Government internal decree; no private right of action.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under Argentina's Personal Data Protection Law separately.

anti_discrimination.detail: Requires compliance with constitutional equality principles; defers to existing anti-discrimination framework.

risk_classification.detail: High-risk government AI uses require Ethics Committee review; binary classification applied within government context.

enforcement_model.detail: Internal government oversight by AI Ethics Committee; no penalty mechanism for private sector.

short_name: Canada Voluntary Code of Conduct on GenAI
full_name: Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems
enforcement_body: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
max_penalty: None — Voluntary industry code; signatories self-report. No penalty.
preemption_notes: Voluntary industry code; Canada's AIDA (Artificial Intelligence and Data Act) Bill C-27 failed to pass before 2025 election call. This code is the operative federal AI governance instrument for the private sector pending legislation.
summary: Canada's Voluntary Code of Conduct on Generative AI was published by ISED in September 2023 as an interim governance instrument following the failure of Bill C-27 (AIDA). It applies to organisations developing and deploying advanced generative AI systems and covers: safety testing, fairness and bias assessment, transparency to users, content labeling, human oversight, and reporting of significant harms. Major Canadian tech companies and multinational AI labs signed the code.
notable: Operative federal AI governance instrument for Canada following AIDA's failure; signed by major AI companies including Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and major Canadian banks.
legal_citation: ISED Voluntary Code of Conduct on GenAI (2023)
key_obligations: Safety testing before deployment
Bias and fairness assessment
Transparency disclosures to users about AI use
Content labeling of AI-generated material
Human oversight mechanisms for high-stakes decisions
Reporting significant AI harms to ISED

impact_assessment.detail: Safety testing and bias/fairness assessment required before deploying advanced generative AI systems.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary code; no prohibited categories defined.

human_review_rights.detail: Human oversight required for high-stakes decisions but no individual right to request review created.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary code; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Content labeling of AI-generated material required; technical implementation left to signatories.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions in the voluntary code.

training_data_transparency.detail: Signatories must maintain information on training data sources; sharing with ISED on request.

content_labeling.detail: Explicit requirement to label AI-generated content to users; technical standard not prescribed.

anti_discrimination.detail: Bias assessment required; reasonable care to prevent discriminatory outcomes standard applied.

risk_classification.detail: No formal risk classification framework; applies to 'advanced' generative AI without defining threshold.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary; signatories self-report to ISED; no penalty mechanism.

short_name: Switzerland FADP (Revised Federal Act on Data Protection)
full_name: Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (revDSG / nFADP) — AI Applicability
enforcement_body: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
preemption_notes: Switzerland is not an EU member state; FADP is an independent sovereign framework not subject to EU AI Act directly. Switzerland and EU have a data adequacy arrangement; FADP was substantially revised to align with GDPR to maintain adequacy.
summary: Switzerland's revised Federal Act on Data Protection (revDSG/nFADP), in force since September 2023, substantially aligns Swiss data protection with the GDPR. It is relevant to AI through: mandatory data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects, opt-out from automated profiling, transparency obligations for automated processing, and special category protections for biometric and genetic data.
notable: Non-EU European country with GDPR-equivalent framework; the only significant European AI-applicable law outside EU, UK, and Council of Europe frameworks.
key_obligations: Data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing
Right to opt out of automated profiling decisions
Transparency about automated decision-making
Explicit consent for sensitive data including biometrics
Data subject rights to access, rectification, and deletion

impact_assessment.detail: Art. 22 requires data protection impact assessment for high-risk automated processing; FDPIC must be consulted if risks cannot be mitigated.

prohibited_categories.detail: No AI-specific prohibited categories; general data protection principles constrain high-risk processing.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 21 provides right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects; controller must enable human review on request.

private_right_of_action.detail: Criminal sanctions apply to serious violations; civil remedies under Swiss civil law; no statutory private right of action equivalent to GDPR damages.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not specifically address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data classified as sensitive personal data requiring explicit consent or other lawful basis under Art. 5.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; focuses on processing of existing personal data.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory automated profiling restricted; defers to Swiss constitutional equality provisions.

risk_classification.detail: No formal AI risk classification; risk assessed through DPIA process on case-by-case basis.

enforcement_model.detail: Maximum CHF 250,000 (~USD 280,000) criminal fine for intentional violations; significantly lower than GDPR. FDPIC has investigatory but limited enforcement powers.

short_name: Ukraine Draft AI Law (2024)
full_name: Ukraine Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (No. 11175)
max_penalty: None — Draft law not yet enacted; no penalty schedule finalised.
preemption_notes: Pending draft legislation; Ukraine is an EU candidate country and draft closely mirrors EU AI Act framework as part of EU accession alignment obligations.
summary: Ukraine's Draft Law No. 11175 on Artificial Intelligence, registered in the Verkhovna Rada in March 2024, closely mirrors the EU AI Act framework as part of Ukraine's EU accession obligations. It establishes a risk-based classification system, impact assessment requirements for high-risk AI, prohibited AI practices, content labeling, and human oversight rights. Legislative progress has been slow due to the ongoing war.
notable: EU candidate country AI law closely tracking EU AI Act; unique context of wartime AI use (drone targeting, surveillance) creating pressure for both adoption and carve-outs.
legal_citation: Draft Law No. 11175 (Verkhovna Rada)
key_obligations: Risk-based AI classification aligned with EU AI Act
Impact assessments for high-risk AI systems
Prohibited AI practices (social scoring, subliminal manipulation)
Content labeling and transparency requirements
Human oversight for consequential AI decisions

impact_assessment.detail: Draft requires impact assessments for high-risk AI systems; assessment framework closely mirrors EU AI Act Annex VI.

prohibited_categories.detail: Draft prohibits social scoring, subliminal manipulation, real-time biometric surveillance in public — EU AI Act prohibited practices adopted wholesale.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have right to human review of significant AI decisions; mirrors EU AI Act Art. 14 human oversight requirement.

private_right_of_action.detail: Draft provides for administrative enforcement; private action under general civil law.

synthetic_media.detail: Content labeling of AI-generated material required; similar to EU AI Act transparency provisions for synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Draft prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces (with national security exceptions — broader than EU given wartime context).

training_data_transparency.detail: Technical documentation including training data information to be filed with national supervisory authority.

content_labeling.detail: AI-generated content must be labeled; applies to text, images, audio, and video.

anti_discrimination.detail: Impact assessment must identify discriminatory risks; reasonable care to prevent disparate impact required.

risk_classification.detail: Four-tier risk framework (prohibited/high-risk/limited-risk/minimal-risk) mirroring EU AI Act adopted in draft.

enforcement_model.detail: Administrative penalties for violations; enforcement authority TBD pending final passage; levels not yet specified in draft.

implementation_phases.description: Draft Law No. 11175 registered in Verkhovna Rada
Expected first reading (delayed due to wartime priorities)

short_name: Serbia Personal Data Protection Law (AI Applicability)
full_name: Serbia Law on Personal Data Protection — Provisions Applicable to AI (Law No. 87/2018, updated 2023)
enforcement_body: Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection (Serbia)
max_penalty: RSD 2,000,000 (~USD 18,000) for legal entities
preemption_notes: Serbia is an EU candidate country; PDPL substantially mirrors GDPR as part of EU accession Chapter 10 obligations. Serbia is also a Council of Europe member and has ratified Convention 108+.
summary: Serbia's Law on Personal Data Protection (Law No. 87/2018), modelled closely on GDPR, provides the operative AI governance framework for Serbia pending specific AI legislation. It covers: data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, right not to be subject to solely automated decisions, explicit consent for biometric data, and data subject access and rectification rights applicable to AI-processed data.
notable: Western Balkans EU accession candidate — GDPR-mirroring law provides interim AI governance; Serbia is on CoE Convention 108+ implementation path.
legal_citation: Zakon o zaštiti podataka o ličnosti, Sl. glasnik RS, br. 87/2018
key_obligations: Data protection impact assessment for high-risk automated processing
Right to opt out of solely automated decisions
Explicit consent for biometric data processing
Data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure)

impact_assessment.detail: Art. 54 requires DPIA for high-risk processing including systematic evaluation of individuals using automated means.

prohibited_categories.detail: No AI-specific prohibited categories; general data protection principles apply.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 38 provides right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects; right to human review on request.

private_right_of_action.detail: Complaints to Commissioner; civil damages under Serbian tort law; no specific private AI right of action.

biometric_data.detail: Art. 17 classifies biometric data as special category requiring explicit consent.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; focuses on processing of existing personal data.

anti_discrimination.detail: Non-discrimination in data processing required; defers to Serbia's Law on Prohibition of Discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: No AI risk classification; DPIA triggered by processing risk, not AI risk level.

enforcement_model.detail: Maximum RSD 2M (~USD 18,000) fine for legal entities; significantly lower than GDPR. Commissioner has investigatory powers.

short_name: Tunisia National AI Strategy 2023–2025
full_name: Tunisia National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2023–2025 and Digital Economy Framework
enforcement_body: Instance Nationale de Protection des Données Personnelles (INPDP)
max_penalty: None — National strategy document; no penalty mechanism.
preemption_notes: National strategy document; Tunisia's data protection authority (INPDP) applies the 2004 personal data protection law to AI processing. New AI-specific legislation under development.
summary: Tunisia's National AI Strategy 2023–2025 focuses on four pillars: AI for economic competitiveness, AI infrastructure development, AI skills and talent, and regulatory and ethical framework. The strategy commits Tunisia to developing AI-specific legislation by 2025, adopting the UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation, and strengthening the INPDP's capacity to regulate AI data processing.
notable: First Maghreb country with a formal national AI strategy; INPDP (data protection authority) is one of the most active African AI regulators.
legal_citation: Tunisia National AI Strategy 2023–2025
key_obligations: Develop AI-specific legislation by 2025
Implement UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation
Build AI regulatory capacity at INPDP
Invest in AI infrastructure and skills

impact_assessment.detail: Strategy document; mandatory impact assessments not yet established.

prohibited_categories.detail: Strategy does not define prohibited AI uses.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights established by the strategy document.

private_right_of_action.detail: Strategy only; no enforcement mechanism.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under 2004 data protection law separately.

anti_discrimination.detail: Strategy references fairness principles but creates no binding standard.

enforcement_model.detail: Strategy document only; enforcement through INPDP's existing data protection mandate.

short_name: Morocco CNDP AI Data Protection Guidance
full_name: Morocco Commission Nationale de Contrôle de la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel — AI and Personal Data Guidelines
enforcement_body: CNDP (Commission Nationale de contrôle de la Protection des Données à caractère Personnel)
preemption_notes: Guidance issued under Morocco's Law 09-08 on Personal Data Protection (2009). Morocco is developing comprehensive AI legislation separately.
summary: Morocco's CNDP issued guidelines in 2024 on the application of Law 09-08 to AI systems processing personal data. The guidelines address: lawful basis for AI training data collection, transparency obligations for automated processing, DPIA requirements for high-risk AI, right to human review of algorithmic decisions, and restrictions on biometric AI use. Morocco's CNDP is one of the most active data protection authorities in Africa and Francophone world.
notable: Morocco's CNDP is among the most active African AI regulators; guidance adopted as a model by several Francophone African nations.
legal_citation: CNDP Recommandations sur l'IA et la Protection des Données (2024)
key_obligations: Lawful basis required for AI training data collection
DPIA for high-risk automated processing
Transparency to individuals about automated decisions
Right to contest automated decisions affecting individual rights
Prior authorisation for biometric AI systems

impact_assessment.detail: CNDP guidance requires DPIA under Law 09-08 for high-risk AI processing; CNDP consultation required for certain applications.

prohibited_categories.detail: Guidance does not define prohibited AI applications; general data protection principles constrain high-risk uses.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have right to contest significant automated decisions under Law 09-08 as interpreted by CNDP guidance.

private_right_of_action.detail: Complaints to CNDP; civil remedies under Moroccan civil law.

synthetic_media.detail: CNDP guidance does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric AI systems require prior CNDP authorisation; special category requiring explicit consent under Law 09-08.

training_data_transparency.detail: Guidance addresses lawful collection of training data but not public disclosure of training datasets.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory AI processing restricted; defers to Morocco's equality and civil rights framework.

risk_classification.detail: No formal AI risk classification; risk assessed through DPIA process.

enforcement_model.detail: Maximum MAD 300,000 (~USD 30,000) under Law 09-08; CNDP issues warnings, injunctions, and can refer to courts.

short_name: Shanghai AI Industry Development Ordinance
full_name: Shanghai Municipality Regulations on the Promotion and Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry
enforcement_body: Shanghai Municipal Commission of Economy and Information Technology (SMECIT)
max_penalty: None — Promotion ordinance; violations referred to national regulatory framework.
preemption_notes: Municipal ordinance; must conform to national AI regulations (CAC GenAI, Algorithm Recommendations). Shanghai uses AI promotion ordinance to attract investment; does not contradict national rules.
summary: China's first city-level comprehensive AI ordinance, Shanghai's AI Industry Development Regulations promote AI innovation while establishing governance requirements. Key provisions: regulatory sandbox for AI products, mandatory disclosure for AI-enabled public services, training data governance requirements, risk classification for AI applications in public services, safe harbour for compliant AI products, and support for international AI cooperation.
notable: First city-level comprehensive AI ordinance in China — a legislative model subsequently adopted by Beijing and other major municipalities.
legal_citation: 上海市促进人工智能产业发展条例
key_obligations: AI products must register in municipal AI registry for public services
Training data governance policy required
Disclosure when AI used in public-facing government services
Risk assessment for high-impact AI in critical sectors
Safe harbour for AI products certified under national standards

impact_assessment.detail: Risk assessments required for AI applications in public services and critical sectors before deployment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Promotion-focused ordinance; prohibited categories deferred to national regulations.

human_review_rights.detail: Does not create individual human review rights; aligned with national framework.

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative enforcement by SMECIT; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Synthetic media addressed under national Deep Synthesis regulation; ordinance does not add requirements.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under national PIPL and Facial Recognition Measures.

training_data_transparency.detail: AI enterprises must establish training data governance policies; data quality and content compliance required.

content_labeling.detail: Content labeling requirements deferred to national regulations.

anti_discrimination.detail: No explicit anti-discrimination standard; fairness implied in general governance requirements.

risk_classification.detail: AI applications in public services classified by risk; higher-risk applications subject to additional assessment and approval requirements.

enforcement_model.detail: SMECIT enforces; administrative penalties for non-compliance; amounts specified for specific violations under ordinance.

short_name: Beijing GenAI Services Implementing Rules
full_name: Beijing Measures for the Administration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (Trial)
max_penalty: RMB 500,000 (~USD 70,000) for serious violations
preemption_notes: Municipal implementing rules for national GenAI Measures (2023); Beijing rules add city-specific requirements for registration and security assessment of GenAI services operating in Beijing.
summary: Beijing's Measures for Administering Generative AI Services implement the national GenAI Interim Measures at the municipal level, adding Beijing-specific requirements. Key additions: mandatory security assessment filing with Beijing Cyberspace Administration for GenAI services, content labeling requirements stricter than national standard, AI product registration for public-facing services, and prohibited content categories aligned with national CAC regulations but with additional local restrictions.
notable: China's most active AI regulation city; Beijing rules are followed by AI companies as de facto national standard given concentration of major AI labs in Beijing.
legal_citation: 北京市生成式人工智能服务管理暂行办法
key_obligations: Security assessment filing with Beijing Cyberspace Administration
Content labeling of all AI-generated content
Training data compliance with national content standards
Prohibited content detection and filtering system
Real-name registration of users for high-risk GenAI services

impact_assessment.detail: Security assessment filing required before operating GenAI service in Beijing; more stringent than national standard.

prohibited_categories.detail: GenAI services must not produce content subversive to state power, undermining national unity, or spreading false information — aligned with national CAC prohibited content categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Does not create individual human review rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative enforcement; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: All AI-generated content must be labeled; stricter than national GenAI Measures requirement.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under national PIPL and Facial Recognition Measures.

training_data_transparency.detail: Training data must comply with national content standards; providers must maintain records of training data sources.

content_labeling.detail: Comprehensive content labeling requirement for all GenAI output; technical labeling standards specified by Beijing Cyberspace Administration.

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination standard; content regulation focused on political/national security content.

risk_classification.detail: GenAI services classified by risk; public-facing services face highest scrutiny including real-name user registration.

enforcement_model.detail: RMB 500,000 (~USD 70,000) for serious violations; Beijing Cyberspace Administration and Public Security Bureau enforce jointly.

short_name: Guangdong AI Industry Development Regulations
full_name: Guangdong Province Artificial Intelligence Industry Development Regulations
enforcement_body: Guangdong Provincial Department of Industry and Information Technology
max_penalty: None — Promotion ordinance; penalties deferred to national CAC/MIIT framework.
preemption_notes: Provincial ordinance complementary to national AI regulations. Guangdong (home to Tencent, Huawei, DJI) uses the ordinance to attract AI investment while aligning with national governance requirements.
summary: Guangdong's AI Industry Development Regulations, building on Shanghai's 2022 model, establish a provincial framework for AI development and governance. Key provisions include: provincial AI innovation corridors (Shenzhen-Hong Kong, Guangzhou), safe harbour certification for compliant AI products, training data governance requirements, risk assessment for AI in critical applications, and provincial AI standard-setting in manufacturing and industrial AI.
notable: Largest provincial GDP in China; Guangdong ordinance shapes AI regulation for Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and the Greater Bay Area tech ecosystem.
legal_citation: 广东省人工智能产业发展条例
key_obligations: Risk assessment for AI in critical manufacturing and public safety applications
Training data governance policy required for AI enterprises
Provincial AI product certification for safe harbour
Disclosure for AI used in government public services
AI product registration for cross-border Greater Bay Area deployment

impact_assessment.detail: Risk assessment required for AI applications in critical sectors including manufacturing, transportation, and public safety.

prohibited_categories.detail: Promotion ordinance; prohibited categories deferred to national CAC regulations.

human_review_rights.detail: Does not create individual rights; aligned with national framework.

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative enforcement by provincial authorities; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Content requirements deferred to national regulations.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under national PIPL and Facial Recognition Measures.

training_data_transparency.detail: AI enterprises must establish training data governance policies including content compliance and quality standards.

content_labeling.detail: Content labeling deferred to national GenAI and Deep Synthesis regulations.

risk_classification.detail: Critical-sector AI applications classified by risk; provincial standards supplement national framework.

enforcement_model.detail: Provincial Department of Industry and Cyberspace Administration enforce; penalty amounts per national framework.

short_name: ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2023)
full_name: ASEAN Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics (2nd Edition, 2023)
max_penalty: None — Voluntary regional guide; no enforcement mechanism.
preemption_notes: Non-binding voluntary guide; developed by ASEAN Digital Ministers (ADGMIN). Directly influenced Singapore's voluntary AI frameworks and Indonesia's and Thailand's national AI strategies.
summary: The ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2nd edition, 2023) provides a voluntary framework for AI governance across the 10 ASEAN member states. It is organised around seven principles: transparency and explainability; fairness and equity; security and safety; human-centricity; privacy and data governance; accountability and integrity; and robustness and reliability. The 2nd edition adds a chapter on generative AI and updates guidance on foundation models. It is accompanied by case studies from Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand.
notable: The primary AI governance reference for all 10 ASEAN member states; directly shaped Thailand AI Act, Vietnam AI Law, and Indonesia AI policy discussions.
legal_citation: ASEAN AI Governance Guide (2nd ed., 2023)
key_obligations: Transparency and explainability for significant AI decisions
Fairness and non-discrimination assessment
Human oversight mechanisms for high-stakes AI
Privacy and data governance aligned with national frameworks
Safety and security testing before deployment

impact_assessment.detail: Guide recommends impact assessment before deployment of significant AI systems; methodology provided in Annex.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary guide; no prohibited categories defined — left to member states.

human_review_rights.detail: Human oversight required for consequential AI decisions; individuals should be able to request explanation and review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary framework; no enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: 2nd edition mentions generative AI risks but does not specifically address deepfakes or synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions; privacy principles apply generally.

training_data_transparency.detail: Data governance chapter covers quality and provenance; no public disclosure requirement.

anti_discrimination.detail: Fairness and equity principle requires non-discrimination; defers to member states' existing equality frameworks.

risk_classification.detail: Risk-based approach recommended; member states to develop own classification consistent with guide principles.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary framework; no enforcement model. Member states implement through national legislation.

short_name: African Union AI Continental Strategy (2024)
full_name: African Union Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy
max_penalty: None — Continental strategy document; no enforcement mechanism.
preemption_notes: Continental strategy adopted by AU heads of state; non-binding but politically significant. Implementation through national strategies and African Digital Compact.
summary: The AU Continental AI Strategy, adopted by the African Union Assembly in February 2024, sets a continent-wide framework for AI development and governance across 55 member states. It is structured around five strategic objectives: developing African AI capabilities; ensuring responsible and trustworthy AI; creating AI-enabling infrastructure; building human capacity; and establishing an African AI governance architecture. The strategy mandates development of an AU AI Policy Framework by 2025.
notable: First continent-level AI governance framework for Africa; represents 55 countries and 1.4 billion people; focuses explicitly on avoiding 'AI colonialism' and ensuring African data sovereignty.
legal_citation: AU Continental AI Strategy (2024)
key_obligations: Member states to develop national AI strategies aligned with AU framework
Establish AU AI governance architecture and regulatory coordination
Promote African AI research and data centres
Ensure AI benefits reach marginalised and rural populations
Develop AU AI Policy Framework by 2025

impact_assessment.detail: Strategy document; no mandatory impact assessment requirements established.

prohibited_categories.detail: Strategy does not define prohibited AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights created by the continental strategy.

private_right_of_action.detail: No enforcement mechanism; political commitment only.

training_data_transparency.detail: Addresses African data sovereignty but no specific training data disclosure requirement.

anti_discrimination.detail: Strategy explicitly addresses AI fairness and non-discrimination; defers to member states' legal frameworks.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework; to be developed through AU AI Policy Framework process.

enforcement_model.detail: Continental strategy; implementation through member states. AU Commission monitors progress.

short_name: FTC AI Policy Statement (2023)
full_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making
max_penalty: $50,120 per violation per day (FTC Act Section 5)
preemption_notes: FTC Act Section 5 applies nationally; FTC AI enforcement supplements state consumer protection law. FTC has brought multiple AI-related enforcement actions targeting deceptive claims, biased algorithms, and unfair data practices.
summary: The FTC's 2023 Policy Statement on AI articulates the Commission's approach to AI enforcement under existing FTC Act authority. It asserts that unfair or deceptive AI practices, discriminatory algorithmic decisions, unfair data collection for AI training, and deceptive AI claims all fall within the FTC's existing Section 5 jurisdiction. The statement covers generative AI, algorithmic pricing, biometric data, and synthetic media.
notable: Most significant US federal AI enforcement signal; FTC has brought multiple AI-related actions (Amazon Alexa, Rite Aid, and others) under existing FTC Act authority without new AI-specific legislation.
legal_citation: FTC Policy Statement (Nov. 2023)
key_obligations: Truthful claims about AI capabilities required
Discriminatory algorithmic outcomes may violate FTC Act Section 5
Unfair data collection for AI training prohibited
Algorithmic pricing coordination subject to antitrust scrutiny

impact_assessment.detail: FTC policy statement does not mandate impact assessments; enforcement is reactive to unfair/deceptive practices.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited categories; FTC uses case-by-case unfairness analysis.

human_review_rights.detail: FTC policy does not create individual rights; remedies through enforcement actions.

private_right_of_action.detail: FTC Act does not include a private right of action; consumers cannot sue directly.

synthetic_media.detail: Statement addresses deceptive AI claims broadly; synthetic media covered through deception analysis.

biometric_data.detail: FTC has taken action against biometric data misuse; opt-out and consent requirements inferred from unfairness analysis.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure requirement; unfair training data practices (scraping without consent) subject to Section 5.

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling mandate; deceptive unlabeled AI content subject to FTC deception analysis.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory algorithmic outcomes may constitute unfair practices under Section 5; impact-based analysis applied in enforcement.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; FTC uses context-specific unfairness/deception analysis.

enforcement_model.detail: FTC civil penalties up to $50,120/day/violation; injunctions; consent orders. Landmark AI enforcement actions include Amazon Alexa children's privacy and Rite Aid facial recognition.

short_name: CFPB Circular on AI in Credit Decisions
full_name: CFPB Circular 2023-03: Adverse Action Notification Requirements and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act in the Context of Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: $50,000 per day for pattern-or-practice violations (ECOA)
preemption_notes: Federal circular; ECOA and Regulation B apply nationally and preempt less protective state credit rules. CFPB enforcement supplements OCC, Fed, and FDIC examination for regulated entities.
summary: CFPB Circular 2023-03 clarifies that lenders using AI or complex machine learning models in credit decisions must comply with ECOA adverse action notice requirements regardless of model complexity. Lenders cannot use model opacity as an excuse to avoid providing specific reasons for credit denials. Circular addresses "black box" AI and requires explanations that are meaningful to applicants.
notable: First US federal agency guidance prohibiting 'black box' credit AI; effectively mandates explainability for AI in lending regardless of model complexity.
legal_citation: CFPB Circular 2023-03; 15 U.S.C. 1691e (ECOA)
key_obligations: Specific adverse action reasons required for all AI credit denials
Model complexity is not an excuse for inadequate explanation
Explanations must be meaningful and specific to the applicant
Discriminatory AI credit decisions violate ECOA

impact_assessment.detail: Circular addresses adverse action explanation; no impact assessment requirement created.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI categories; existing ECOA protected class prohibitions apply.

human_review_rights.detail: Applicants have right to specific explanation for AI credit denial; human review not mandated but explanation requirement effectively requires review capacity.

private_right_of_action.detail: ECOA provides private right of action; actual damages, punitive damages up to $10,000, and attorney fees available.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric provisions; credit context only.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; focuses on output explainability.

anti_discrimination.detail: ECOA disparate impact standard applies to AI credit models; lenders liable for discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; ECOA obligations apply to all credit AI regardless of model type.

enforcement_model.detail: CFPB civil penalties up to $50K/day; ECOA private right of action; state AGs may also enforce under Dodd-Frank.

short_name: EEOC Technical Assistance on AI in Employment
full_name: EEOC Technical Assistance: Selecting Employees and Applicants Using Artificial Intelligence and Other Automated Systems
preemption_notes: Federal employment discrimination law; EEOC guidance applies nationally. State employment discrimination laws may provide additional protections. NYC LL144 (annual bias audit) operates alongside federal EEOC framework.
summary: The EEOC's Technical Assistance document clarified that employers who use AI, algorithmic decision-making, or automated systems in employment decisions remain fully liable under Title VII, ADA, ADEA, and other employment discrimination statutes. The guidance confirmed disparate impact liability for AI hiring tools, employer responsibility for vendor AI tools, ADA reasonable accommodation requirements for AI assessment formats, and application of the 4/5ths adverse impact rule to AI screening. The EEOC removed this document from its website in January 2025 pursuant to EO 14179.
notable: EEOC removed this technical assistance document from its website in January 2025 pursuant to EO 14179.
legal_citation: EEOC Technical Assistance (May 2023); 42 U.S.C. 2000e (Title VII)
key_obligations: Employers liable for AI hiring tool discrimination regardless of vendor responsibility
4/5ths adverse impact rule applies to AI screening tools
ADA reasonable accommodation must extend to AI assessment formats
Disparate impact analysis required for AI selection procedures

impact_assessment.detail: No mandatory impact assessment; EEOC recommended but did not require pre-deployment adverse impact analysis.

prohibited_categories.detail: Existing Title VII prohibited classifications (race, sex, religion, national origin) applied to AI; no new AI-specific prohibitions.

human_review_rights.detail: No right to human review of AI employment decisions; EEOC focused on outcome liability.

private_right_of_action.detail: Title VII, ADA, ADEA all provide private rights of action; compensatory and punitive damages up to $300,000; injunctive relief available.

synthetic_media.detail: Employment context only; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions beyond ADA accommodation for biometric assessments.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; emphasis on employment outcome compliance.

anti_discrimination.detail: Disparate impact liability under Title VII applied to AI selection procedures; 4/5ths rule was the operative standard.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; all employment AI subject to same Title VII framework.

enforcement_model.detail: EEOC investigates, conciliates, and litigates; private right of action after EEOC charge; compensatory + punitive damages up to $300K.

short_name: FDA AI/ML Action Plan for Software as Medical Device
full_name: FDA Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan
enforcement_body: FDA Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH)
max_penalty: Per 21 U.S.C. 333 — up to $15,000 per violation for device violations
preemption_notes: Federal medical device regulation preempts state SaMD requirements. FDA regulatory jurisdiction over AI/ML Software as Medical Device is exclusive federal domain; state laws cannot impose additional premarket requirements.
summary: The FDA's AI/ML Action Plan for Software as Medical Device (SaMD) establishes the agency's regulatory approach to AI-enabled medical devices. It outlines five action areas: tailored regulatory framework for AI/ML-based SaMD, good machine learning practice standards, patient-centred approaches, algorithm transparency, and real-world performance monitoring. The Action Plan underpins FDA's pre-submission program for AI medical devices and is being updated through the Predetermined Change Control Plan (PCCP) pathway.
notable: Governs all AI in FDA-regulated medical devices; the primary reason AI diagnostic tools, surgical robots, and clinical decision support require FDA clearance or approval.
legal_citation: FDA AI/ML SaMD Action Plan (2021); 21 U.S.C. 360 (FDCA)
key_obligations: Premarket submission (510(k) or PMA) for AI/ML-based SaMD
Good Machine Learning Practice standards compliance
Algorithm transparency for clinical users
Post-market performance monitoring and adverse event reporting
Predetermined Change Control Plan for continuously learning algorithms

impact_assessment.detail: Premarket review is a mandatory assessment before marketing; FDA evaluates clinical validation, training data, and performance across subgroups.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited categories; risk classification determines pathway (exempt/510(k)/De Novo/PMA).

human_review_rights.detail: FDA requires human oversight for high-risk clinical decisions; purely autonomous AI diagnosis in life-threatening contexts requires PMA and human review safeguards.

private_right_of_action.detail: FDCA enforcement is FDA/DOJ; no private right of action under FDCA; medical malpractice claims available separately.

synthetic_media.detail: Medical device context; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data used in medical AI devices subject to device-specific FDA requirements; not general biometric regulation.

training_data_transparency.detail: Training and validation data characteristics must be submitted in premarket applications; subgroup performance across demographics required.

content_labeling.detail: Device labeling (instructions for use) must disclose AI nature; not content labeling in the generative AI sense.

anti_discrimination.detail: FDA requires subgroup performance analysis to identify demographic disparities in AI device performance; impact-based standard.

risk_classification.detail: Three-class device risk framework applies to AI SaMD: Class I (exempt), II (510(k)), III (PMA); higher risk = more rigorous review.

enforcement_model.detail: FDA Warning Letters, consent decrees, injunctions, and criminal referrals for device violations; civil penalties up to $15K/violation.

short_name: SEC Proposed Rule on Conflicts of Interest in AI (2023)
full_name: SEC Proposed Rule: Conflicts of Interest Associated with the Use of Predictive Data Analytics by Broker-Dealers and Investment Advisers
max_penalty: Per Exchange Act — civil penalties, disgorgement, injunctions
preemption_notes: Federal securities regulation; SEC rules preempt state securities laws for broker-dealers and registered investment advisers. Rule proposed under Exchange Act Section 15(l) and Advisers Act Section 211.
summary: The SEC's proposed rule would have required broker-dealers and investment advisers to evaluate and eliminate or neutralise conflicts of interest when using predictive data analytics (including AI and ML) in investor interactions. The rule targeted AI systems that optimise for firm interests at investors' expense, requiring conflict identification through testing, documented conflict elimination or neutralisation, disclosure to investors, and compliance program requirements. The SEC formally withdrew the rule in June 2025.
notable: SEC formally withdrew the predictive data analytics rule in June 2025.
legal_citation: Release Nos. 34-97990; IA-6383 (proposed 2023; withdrawn 2025)
key_obligations: Test AI/ML tools for conflicts of interest
Eliminate or neutralise identified conflicts
Disclose use of predictive analytics to investors
Maintain compliance programs for AI investment tools

impact_assessment.detail: Proposed rule required pre-deployment testing of AI tools for conflicts of interest; documented assessment must be maintained.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI categories; rule required conflict neutralisation rather than prohibition.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual human review rights; compliance focus was on firm obligations.

private_right_of_action.detail: SEC enforcement only; no private right of action under the proposed rule.

synthetic_media.detail: Financial services context; does not address synthetic media.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; compliance focus was on conflict identification.

content_labeling.detail: Disclosure to investors of AI use required; not content labeling.

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination provisions; conflict of interest focus was on investor harm, not protected class discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework; conflict identification applies to all covered AI tools.

enforcement_model.detail: SEC enforcement through civil penalties, disgorgement, and injunctions; criminal referral to DOJ for wilful violations.

short_name: Russia AI Foundations Law
full_name: Federal Law on the Foundations of State Regulation of Areas of Application of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in the Russian Federation
enforcement_body: Authorized body in the field of artificial intelligence
max_penalty: Administrative and criminal liability under existing legislation
preemption_notes: Federal law; preempts inconsistent regional regulations
summary: Russia's draft comprehensive AI governance framework law, submitted by the Government. Establishes foundational principles for AI development and deployment including risk-based regulation, disclosure obligations, data localisation requirements for trusted AI models, a register of certified trusted AI models for use in state systems, and liability provisions. Emphasises technological sovereignty and Russian value alignment. A sovereign AI model development programme supports domestic large foundation models. Mandatory human-in-the-loop rights for autonomous decisions affecting citizens. Watermarking/labelling requirements for AI-generated content. Enters into force 1 September 2027.
notable: Russia's first comprehensive horizontal AI law, replacing the 2020 Moscow sandbox as the primary AI governance framework. Introduces a 'trusted AI models' register for state procurement, sovereignty requirements for state-adjacent AI systems, and an explicit 'traditional values' compliance criterion — a globally distinctive feature. Draft status: submitted by government, not yet enacted.
legal_citation: Draft Federal Law submitted by the Government of the Russian Federation (2025/2026)
key_obligations: Disclose to users when AI is used in service delivery (Article 9)
Notify citizens when autonomous AI decisions affect their rights (Article 9)
Provide opt-out from AI for service delivery where feasible (Article 9)
Allow pre-trial appeal of AI-assisted government decisions (Article 9)
Developers must document model architecture and conduct risk modelling (Article 10)
Operators must appoint AI safety officers and record incidents (Article 10)
Service owners must label all AI-generated content in human- and machine-readable formats (Article 12)
Only certified trusted AI models permitted in state information systems (Article 8)
Data processing for trusted AI models must remain within Russian territory (Article 8)
Training data text/data mining permitted without IP rights holder consent if lawfully acquired (Article 13)

impact_assessment.detail: Risk-oriented approach; risk assessment required prior to deployment, scaled to probability and scale of potential harm (Articles 5, 10)

prohibited_categories.detail: No explicit prohibited AI application categories in this framework law; sector-specific prohibitions may be established by subordinate legislation

human_review_rights.detail: Citizens have right to pre-trial appeal of AI-assisted government decisions; opt-out from AI service delivery in certain cases (Article 9)

private_right_of_action.detail: Citizens have right to compensation for harm from unlawful AI use under civil legislation (Article 9); fault-based liability for developers/operators/service owners (Article 11)

synthetic_media.detail: Mandatory human- and machine-readable watermark/label on all AI-generated audio, visual, and other content; platforms with >100k daily users must verify presence or remove (Article 12)

biometric_data.detail: Not specifically addressed in this framework law

training_data_transparency.detail: Service owners must inform users of lawfulness of training data origins; developers must guarantee no IP rights violations in training data (Article 13)

content_labeling.detail: All AI-generated content must carry perceptible-to-humans and machine-readable warning; removal of labels is a specific administrative offense (Article 12)

anti_discrimination.detail: Developers must eliminate model features capable of leading to discrimination based on behaviour or personal characteristics (Article 10)

risk_classification.detail: Risk-oriented approach mandated by Article 5; specific risk tiers to be established by subordinate legislation based on autonomy, legal significance, and information sensitivity

enforcement_model.detail: Authorized federal AI body can initiate inspections and issue mandatory corrective instructions; admin and criminal liability under existing codes; recourse claims available between operators and developers (Articles 11, 14)

short_name: NIST AI 600-1 (GenAI Profile)
full_name: NIST Artificial Intelligence 600-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
preemption_notes: Voluntary guidance document; no enforcement or preemptive legal effect
summary: NIST AI 600-1 is a companion profile to the AI RMF 1.0, developed pursuant to the Biden EO 14110 mandate, that identifies 12 unique risk categories for generative AI systems — including hallucination, CBRN uplift, data poisoning, and information integrity — and maps over 200 suggested mitigations to the AI RMF's GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions. It is a voluntary document but serves as the primary federal technical benchmark for GenAI risk management by federal agencies and the private sector.
notable: Published per Biden EO 14110 mandate; used as voluntary compliance benchmark by federal agencies under OMB M-24-10. Covers all GenAI modalities: text, image, video, audio, code, and multimodal systems.
legal_citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024)
key_obligations: Framework for GenAI risk management organized around 12 GenAI-specific risk categories
Identifies 12 unique GenAI risk categories including confabulation, CBRN uplift, data poisoning, and information integrity
Provides 200+ suggested mitigations mapped to AI RMF GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions
Addresses responsibilities of AI developers, deployers, operators, and users separately
Federal agencies directed by OMB M-24-10 to apply framework in GenAI governance

impact_assessment.detail: Recommends rigorous pre-deployment and ongoing risk assessment for all 12 GenAI risk categories; maps specific MEASURE actions to each risk. Not legally binding.

prohibited_categories.detail: Guidance document does not prohibit specific AI applications; instead identifies risks and suggests mitigations.

human_review_rights.detail: Recommends human oversight configurations (GOVERN 3.2) but does not establish individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary guidance; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Identifies information integrity and ODAC as distinct risk categories for GenAI; recommends content authentication and output monitoring mitigations but does not mandate specific technical controls.

biometric_data.detail: Does not specifically address biometric data protection; covered indirectly under data privacy risk category.

training_data_transparency.detail: Identifies training data privacy and data poisoning as GenAI-specific risks; recommends documentation and disclosure practices but does not mandate specific disclosures.

content_labeling.detail: Does not require content labeling; information integrity risk category includes recommendations for authentication but no mandatory labeling.

anti_discrimination.detail: Identifies harmful bias and homogenization as a GenAI-specific risk category; recommends bias testing and diverse team composition but does not establish enforceable anti-discrimination standards.

risk_classification.detail: Organizes GenAI risks into 12 named categories mapped to AI RMF functions; does not use a tiered high/limited risk classification system like the EU AI Act.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary guidance; no enforcement body, penalty structure, or compliance mandate beyond OMB direction to federal agencies.

operative_dates: Published July 26, 2024. Voluntary guidance effective immediately upon publication. No sunset date.

short_name: FTC Fake Reviews Final Rule (2024)
full_name: FTC Final Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials — Prohibition on Fake or False Consumer Reviews
max_penalty: Up to $51,744 per violation
preemption_notes: Federal agency rule; preempts conflicting state law under Supremacy Clause to the extent of direct conflict
summary: The FTC's Final Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465), effective October 2024, is the first binding federal rule to explicitly prohibit AI-generated fake consumer reviews. It bans buying, creating, or distributing fake reviews including AI-generated ones, prohibits review suppression and insider reviews without disclosure, and imposes civil penalties of up to $51,744 per violation.
notable: First binding federal rule to explicitly prohibit AI-generated fake consumer reviews. Published 89 Fed. Reg. 60064 (Aug. 14, 2024).
key_obligations: Ban on creating, buying, or disseminating AI-generated or otherwise fake consumer reviews
Prohibition on review suppression using legal threats or selective display
Required clear and conspicuous disclosure for compensated reviews and insider reviews
Prohibition on fake social media followers, likes, and engagement indicators
Civil penalty liability up to $51,744 per violation

impact_assessment.detail: Rule does not require impact assessments; it is a specific conduct prohibition.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits AI-generated fake reviews, review gating, review suppression, and fake social media indicators — specific deceptive uses of AI in consumer marketing.

human_review_rights.detail: Rule does not address individual rights to human review of AI decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action; enforcement exclusively by FTC. Competitors may file complaints with FTC.

synthetic_media.detail: AI-generated fake reviews are explicitly prohibited as a form of synthetic deceptive content; rule is the first binding federal prohibition on AI-generated synthetic consumer deception.

biometric_data.detail: Rule does not address biometric data.

training_data_transparency.detail: Rule does not address AI training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Requires clear and conspicuous disclosure of material connections (compensation, employment) in reviews and testimonials; does not require AI-generated content labeling per se, but AI-generated fake reviews are prohibited outright.

anti_discrimination.detail: Rule does not address algorithmic discrimination or protected-class bias.

risk_classification.detail: Rule does not use a risk classification system; it is a specific conduct prohibition.

enforcement_model.detail: FTC civil penalty enforcement at up to $51,744 per violation; each day of violation is a separate violation. No criminal penalties under the rule itself.

operative_dates: Published August 14, 2024. Effective October 21, 2024.

short_name: EO 14365 (National AI Policy Framework)
full_name: Executive Order on Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence
preemption_notes: EO explicitly seeks to establish federal preemption of conflicting state AI laws; directs FTC to issue preemption statement and DOJ to litigate against conflicting state laws. Legal effectiveness of preemption subject to judicial review.
summary: Executive Order 14365, signed December 2025, directs the FTC to assert federal preemption of conflicting state AI laws, creates a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to challenge such laws in court, directs the FCC to consider a federal AI content disclosure standard, and conditions certain federal funding on states not enacting laws that conflict with national AI development priorities. The order reflects the Trump administration's strategy of using federal authority to prevent a patchwork of state AI regulations from impeding AI development.
notable: Trump administration's primary vehicle for federal preemption of state AI regulations. Creates DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to actively challenge state AI laws. Narrow carve-outs for children's safety laws and state AI procurement.
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,365 (Dec. 11, 2025)
topics: federal preemption of state AI law
key_obligations: FTC directed to issue preemption policy statement on conflicting state AI laws within 120 days
DOJ directed to create AI Litigation Task Force to challenge conflicting state AI laws
FCC directed to initiate rulemaking on federal AI content disclosure standard within 90 days
OMB directed to issue updated federal AI governance framework within 180 days
Federal funding in certain categories conditioned on states not enacting conflicting AI laws

impact_assessment.detail: EO does not require impact assessments; it is a federal coordination and preemption directive.

prohibited_categories.detail: EO does not prohibit specific AI applications; it seeks to limit state-level AI prohibitions.

human_review_rights.detail: EO does not address individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Executive order; no private enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: EO does not address synthetic media specifically, though FCC rulemaking may eventually address AI content disclosure in broadcasting.

biometric_data.detail: EO does not address biometric data protection.

training_data_transparency.detail: EO does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Directs FCC to initiate rulemaking on a federal AI content disclosure standard — intended to supersede conflicting state-level AI content labeling laws.

anti_discrimination.detail: EO does not address algorithmic discrimination or anti-discrimination standards.

risk_classification.detail: EO does not establish a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Primary enforcement mechanism is DOJ litigation against conflicting state AI laws, supplemented by federal funding conditions. No private enforcement or civil penalties.

operative_dates: Signed December 11, 2025. Agency deadlines: FCC rulemaking initiation within 90 days; FTC preemption statement within 120 days; OMB framework within 180 days.

short_name: Alabama HB 172 (AI Election Deepfakes)
full_name: Alabama House Bill 172 — Prohibition on Materially Deceptive AI-Generated Media in Elections
max_penalty: First offense: Class A misdemeanor (up to 1 year jail, $6,000 fine); subsequent offense within 5 years: Class C felony (1–10 years prison)
preemption_notes: No express preemption clause; operates alongside federal election and campaign finance laws
summary: Alabama HB 172 makes it a criminal offense to knowingly distribute materially deceptive AI-generated media intended to influence an election within 90 days before that election, and requires a prominent disclaimer for any AI-generated content used in political advertising. First violations are Class A misdemeanors; repeat violations within five years are Class C felonies. Satire and parody are exempted.
legal_citation: Alabama HB 172 (2024 Regular Session); Ala. Code § [TBD]
