key_obligations: Criminal prohibition on distributing materially deceptive AI-generated media within 90 days of an election with intent to influence
Required prominent disclaimer for AI-generated content in political advertising
First violation: Class A misdemeanor; subsequent violation within 5 years: Class C felony

impact_assessment.detail: Law does not require impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated media in election campaigns within 90 days of an election with intent to influence.

human_review_rights.detail: Law does not address individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Criminal prosecution only by Attorney General or District Attorneys; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Prohibits materially deceptive AI-generated media in elections; requires disclosure for non-deceptive AI-generated political content.

biometric_data.detail: Law does not specifically address biometric data.

training_data_transparency.detail: Law does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Requires prominent disclosure that political advertising content is AI-generated.

anti_discrimination.detail: Law does not address algorithmic discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: Law does not use a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal enforcement by AG and District Attorneys. Class A misdemeanor for first offense; Class C felony for repeat offense within 5 years.

operative_dates: Enacted April 24, 2024. Effective October 1, 2024.

short_name: Alabama HB 161 (AI NCII)
full_name: Alabama House Bill 161 — Prohibition on Nonconsensual AI-Generated Intimate Images
max_penalty: Class A misdemeanor (criminal); civil liability to victim including actual damages, statutory damages, and punitive damages
preemption_notes: No express preemption clause; operates alongside federal law including potential Section 230 questions for platforms
summary: Alabama HB 161 prohibits the creation and distribution of nonconsensual AI-generated sexually explicit images of identifiable real persons, including both fully AI-generated images and AI-manipulated real photographs, providing criminal penalties (Class A misdemeanor) and a private civil cause of action for victims including actual, statutory, and punitive damages.
legal_citation: Alabama HB 161 (2024 Regular Session); Ala. Code § [TBD]
key_obligations: Prohibition on creating AI-generated sexually explicit images of identifiable persons without consent
Prohibition on distributing such images without consent
Criminal penalty: Class A misdemeanor for first offense
Civil cause of action for victims including actual damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees

impact_assessment.detail: Law does not require impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits creation and distribution of nonconsensual AI-generated sexually explicit depictions of identifiable persons.

human_review_rights.detail: Law does not address rights to human review of AI decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Victims have an explicit private civil cause of action for actual damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees against creators and distributors of nonconsensual AI-generated intimate images.

synthetic_media.detail: Prohibits AI-generated and AI-manipulated sexually explicit depictions of identifiable persons absent explicit consent. Covers both fully synthetic images and real-image manipulation.

biometric_data.detail: Law does not address biometric data protection directly; identity protection in intimate context addressed through NCII prohibition.

training_data_transparency.detail: Law does not address training data transparency.

content_labeling.detail: Law does not require content labeling; it prohibits the covered content outright.

anti_discrimination.detail: Law does not address algorithmic discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: Law does not use a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal enforcement by AG and District Attorneys (Class A misdemeanor); private civil action by victims. Both tracks available independently.

operative_dates: Enacted April 24, 2024. Effective October 1, 2024.

short_name: Delaware AI Commission Act (HB 333)
full_name: Delaware House Bill 333 — Delaware Artificial Intelligence Commission Act
preemption_notes: Study and advisory body only; no preemption implications
summary: Delaware HB 333 establishes the Delaware Artificial Intelligence Commission within the Office of the State Auditor, charged with assessing AI risks and benefits across all three branches of state government, recommending AI governance and procurement standards, and reporting annually to the legislature. The Commission has no enforcement powers and imposes no obligations on private industry, and is scheduled to automatically terminate after 10 years.

key_obligations: Establishes Delaware AI Commission within Office of State Auditor
Commission to assess AI risks and benefits across all three branches of state government
Commission to recommend AI governance and procurement standards
Annual reporting to Governor and General Assembly
Commission auto-terminates after 10 years

Civil and criminal enforcement by Hawaii AG (enjoined)

enforcement_model.detail: Enforcement through civil litigation by estate or authorized representatives; injunctive relief, actual damages, and disgorgement of profits.

operative_dates: Enacted and effective December 11, 2025

short_name: Texas SB 1188 (Healthcare AI Disclosure)
full_name: Texas Senate Bill 1188 — Healthcare AI Disclosure Act
max_penalty: Medical Board disciplinary action; potential license suspension or revocation
summary: Requires Texas healthcare practitioners who use AI for diagnostic purposes to disclose that use to patients verbally or in writing before or at the time of the clinical encounter, covering AI-assisted diagnosis, AI-generated treatment recommendations, and AI interpretation of medical imaging. Also prohibits offshoring of electronic medical records outside the United States.
legal_citation: SB 1188, 89th Tex. Leg. Sess. (2025).
key_obligations: Healthcare practitioners using AI for diagnostic purposes must disclose to patients verbally or in writing before or at the clinical encounter
Covers AI-assisted diagnosis, AI-generated treatment recommendations, and AI interpretation of medical imaging
Prohibition on offshoring electronic medical records outside the United States

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed; disclosure is required but human review is not mandated by this bill.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action; enforcement is by the Texas Medical Board.

enforcement_model.detail: Texas Medical Board may impose disciplinary sanctions including license suspension or revocation for non-compliant practitioners.

operative_dates: Enacted June 20, 2025; effective September 1, 2025

short_name: Texas SB 441 (Intimate Deepfake Criminalization)
full_name: Texas Senate Bill 441 — Unlawful Production or Distribution of Intimate Deepfake Images
max_penalty: Class A misdemeanor (up to 1 year, $4,000 fine); state jail felony if depicted person is a minor
summary: Criminalizes the production or distribution of AI-generated or AI-manipulated intimate images without the depicted person's consent (Class A misdemeanor), elevated to a state jail felony when the depicted person is a minor. Also separately criminalizes threatening to produce or distribute such imagery as a form of sexual coercion.
legal_citation: SB 441, 89th Tex. Leg. Sess. (2025); Tex. Penal Code (as amended).
key_obligations: Prohibition on production or distribution of nonconsensual AI-generated or AI-manipulated intimate imagery (Class A misdemeanor)
Enhanced penalty (state jail felony) if depicted person is a minor
Criminalization of threats to produce or distribute nonconsensual intimate deepfakes as sexual coercion

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action; criminal prosecution only.

synthetic_media.detail: Covers wholly AI-generated and AI-manipulated intimate images; criminal offense with enhanced penalty for minor victims.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal prosecution by Texas state prosecutors; Class A misdemeanor or state jail felony depending on victim's age.

operative_dates: Enacted June 20, 2025; effective September 1, 2025

short_name: Utah SB 332 (UAIPA 2025 Amendments)
full_name: Utah Senate Bill 332 — Utah Artificial Intelligence Policy Act Amendments 2025
max_penalty: Civil penalties under UAIPA framework
summary: Amends the Utah Artificial Intelligence Policy Act (UAIPA) to further refine mental health chatbot regulation and generative AI disclosure requirements for consumer transactions, and extends the UAIPA's sunset date by two years to allow time for development of a permanent governance framework. Includes updated definitions and scope clarifications addressing interpretive ambiguities from the law's first year.
notable: Utah has been an early and iterative mover on AI regulation, with UAIPA now amended twice since its 2024 enactment.
legal_citation: Utah Code Ann. §§ 13-72-101 et seq. (as amended by SB 332, 2025 Utah Gen. Sess.).
key_obligations: Further refines mental health chatbot regulation provisions in UAIPA
Revises generative AI disclosure requirements for consumer transactions
Extends UAIPA sunset/repeal date by two additional years
Updates definitions and scope clarifications for key UAIPA terms

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action under UAIPA framework.

enforcement_model.detail: Enforcement by Utah Division of Consumer Protection with civil penalty authority under the UAIPA framework.

operative_dates: Enacted March 25, 2025; effective May 7, 2025

short_name: EU GPAI Guidelines (Art. 53)
full_name: European Commission Guidelines on the Scope of Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models (Article 53 EU AI Act)
preemption_notes: Commission Guidelines under Article 96 EU AI Act; bind national competent authorities in enforcement interpretation; GPAI Code of Practice compliance creates rebuttable presumption of conformity
summary: Binding interpretive guidelines published by the European Commission on 18 July 2025 under Article 96 of the EU AI Act, clarifying which AI models qualify as General-Purpose AI Models and the specific compliance obligations for GPAI model providers under Article 53. Establishes the 10²³ FLOPs compute threshold for GPAI model classification and the 10²⁵ FLOPs threshold for systemic risk designation. Covers technical documentation, training data summaries, copyright compliance policies, and incident reporting requirements. Legally distinct from the non-binding GPAI Code of Practice.
notable: Hard-law interpretive instrument — distinct from the voluntary GPAI Code of Practice. Compliance with the Code creates a rebuttable presumption of conformity with these Guidelines.
legal_citation: EU AI Act Art. 53, Art. 55, Art. 96; Annex XI, XIII
key_obligations: Maintain and publish technical documentation (Annex XI)
Publish sufficiently detailed training data summary
Implement and publish copyright compliance policy with opt-out mechanism
Provide technical documentation to downstream providers
Report serious incidents to EU AI Office
Systemic-risk models: adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures, 24-hour incident reporting

impact_assessment.detail: Systemic-risk GPAI models (≥10²⁵ FLOPs) must conduct model evaluation including adversarial testing; all GPAI providers must assess risks documented in technical documentation.

prohibited_categories.detail: Guidelines focus on GPAI model obligations; prohibited AI practices are addressed in EU AI Act Article 5 and separate instruments.

human_review_rights.detail: GPAI Guidelines do not create individual human review rights; those are addressed under deployer-level AI Act obligations.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement is by EU AI Office and national competent authorities; no private right of action created.

synthetic_media.detail: Content labelling for synthetic media is addressed in EU AI Act transparency obligations; these Guidelines focus on GPAI model provider obligations upstream.

training_data_transparency.detail: Providers must publish training data summary covering major data categories, geographical and temporal coverage, and language composition; detailed documentation provided to EU AI Office on request.

content_labeling.detail: Content labelling is a downstream deployer obligation; GPAI Guidelines address upstream model provider obligations.

anti_discrimination.detail: Not directly addressed in GPAI Guidelines.

risk_classification.detail: 10²³ FLOPs threshold for GPAI model classification; 10²⁵ FLOPs for systemic risk designation; systemic risk also determinable by Commission on other criteria including user reach and capability evaluations.

enforcement_model.detail: EU AI Office as primary enforcer for GPAI obligations; national competent authorities for downstream; penalties up to 3% global turnover for Article 53/55 violations.

operative_dates: In force 2 August 2025

short_name: EU Digital Omnibus — AI Act Amendments
full_name: European Commission Proposal — Digital Omnibus Regulation Amending the AI Act (COM/2025)
preemption_notes: Amending regulation; if adopted, modifies EU AI Act Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 directly
summary: European Commission legislative proposal (November 2025) to amend the EU AI Act as part of the Digital Omnibus package. Key changes: defer Annex III high-risk AI system obligations from August 2026 to December 2027; narrow AI literacy obligations for deployers; expand SME and research exemptions; add legitimate interest legal basis for personal data use in AI training. In trilogue as of May 2026 — second trilogue failed to reach agreement; third trilogue scheduled 13 May 2026.
notable: Second and third trilogues failed to reach agreement; final text uncertain as of May 2026.
key_obligations: Defers Annex III high-risk AI compliance to December 2027
Narrows AI literacy requirements to staff directly interacting with high-risk AI
Expands SME and micro-enterprise exemptions from conformity assessment obligations
Adds legitimate interest legal basis for AI training data use

impact_assessment.detail: Proposal does not modify impact assessment requirements; defers when they must be completed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Proposed amendments do not alter prohibited AI practices under Article 5.

human_review_rights.detail: No changes to human review rights proposed.

private_right_of_action.detail: No changes to enforcement model proposed.

synthetic_media.detail: No changes to transparency/labelling obligations proposed.

biometric_data.detail: No changes to biometric AI provisions proposed.

training_data_transparency.detail: Proposes legitimate interest legal basis for training data use; does not modify transparency obligations.

content_labeling.detail: No changes to content labelling obligations proposed.

anti_discrimination.detail: No changes to anti-discrimination provisions proposed.

risk_classification.detail: Risk classification tiers unchanged; proposal only adjusts compliance timelines.

enforcement_model.detail: Enforcement model unchanged; proposal adjusts deadlines and exemptions.

operative_dates: Proposed 19 November 2025; in trilogue May 2026; adoption timeline uncertain

short_name: EU Digital Omnibus — Digital Law Amendments
full_name: European Commission Proposal — Digital Omnibus Regulation Amending GDPR, NIS2, Data Act, DORA and Related Instruments
preemption_notes: Amending regulation modifying GDPR, NIS2, Data Act, DORA, CER Directive, and eIDAS 2.0; does not create independent preemption
summary: European Commission proposal (November 2025) amending six EU digital regulations simultaneously: narrows GDPR personal data identifiability standard; extends breach notification from 72 to 96 hours; integrates cookie consent into GDPR framework; clarifies legitimate interest basis for AI training data; amends NIS2, Data Act, DORA, CER, and eIDAS 2.0. Part of the Digital Omnibus package alongside the AI Act amendment proposal.
key_obligations: Narrows personal data definition identifiability standard (GDPR amendment)
Extends breach notification window to 96 hours (GDPR Art. 33 amendment)
Moves cookie consent framework into GDPR (ePrivacy simplification)
Clarifies legitimate interest for AI training data (GDPR Recital)
Harmonizes NIS2 significant incident definition across member states
Clarifies DORA application to AI-based financial tools

impact_assessment.detail: Does not introduce AI-specific impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not an AI-specific instrument; no prohibited category provisions.

human_review_rights.detail: No changes to automated decision-making human review rights under GDPR.

private_right_of_action.detail: GDPR private right of action framework unchanged.

biometric_data.detail: GDPR special category protections for biometric data unchanged.

training_data_transparency.detail: Proposes legitimate interest clarification for AI training; does not impose training data disclosure obligations.

risk_classification.detail: Not an AI risk classification instrument.

enforcement_model.detail: Enforcement models of amended instruments unchanged in structure; procedural modifications only.

operative_dates: Proposed 19 November 2025; pending adoption

short_name: Latvia AI Centre Law
full_name: Law on the Latvian Artificial Intelligence Centre (Mākslīgā intelekta centra likums)
summary: Establishes the Latvian Artificial Intelligence Centre as a public-private-academic foundation by statute, making Latvia the first EU member state to create a dedicated national AI institution through legislation. Creates a statutory AI regulatory sandbox with limited liability waivers for participants. The Centre coordinates AI policy, research, international cooperation, and AI literacy programs. Funded by state budget, private sector contributions, and EU structural funds.
notable: First EU member state to establish a dedicated AI Centre by statute.
legal_citation: Mākslīgā intelekta centra likums (2025)
key_obligations: AI Centre coordinates Latvia's national AI strategy implementation
AI Centre operates national regulatory sandbox with limited liability waivers
AI Centre provides regulatory guidance to sandbox participants
AI Centre represents Latvia in EU and international AI governance forums
AI Centre delivers public sector AI literacy programs

impact_assessment.detail: Institutional law; does not impose AI impact assessment obligations.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI category provisions.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed; EU AI Act risk classification applies directly.

enforcement_model.detail: Institutional law creating AI Centre; enforcement of AI Act handled by separate market surveillance authority designation.

operative_dates: In force 20 March 2025

short_name: Lithuania AI Supervisory Authority Designation
full_name: Lithuania — Amendments to the Law on Communications Designating AI Act Supervisory Authorities
summary: Amends Lithuania's Law on Electronic Communications to designate supervisory authorities for the EU AI Act: Innovation Agency as notifying authority for conformity assessment bodies; Communications Regulatory Authority (RRT) as primary market surveillance authority. Lithuania also launched the EU's first national AI regulatory sandbox pilot program (€3 million allocated). Among the first EU member states to formally designate AI Act authorities.
notable: Lithuania launched the first EU national AI regulatory sandbox pilot (€3 million); among first EU member states to formally designate AI Act authorities.
legal_citation: Amendments to Law on Electronic Communications of the Republic of Lithuania (2025)
key_obligations: Innovation Agency designated as notifying authority for conformity assessment bodies
RRT designated as primary market surveillance authority for EU AI Act
Inter-agency coordination mechanism established
National AI regulatory sandbox operated by Innovation Agency and RRT

impact_assessment.detail: Designation law; EU AI Act impact assessment obligations apply directly.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed; EU AI Act prohibited practices apply directly.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: EU AI Act risk classification applies directly.

enforcement_model.detail: Designates national authorities; substantive enforcement powers derive from EU AI Act.

operative_dates: In force 14 January 2025

short_name: Germany KI-MIG
full_name: Germany — Gesetz zur Durchführung der europäischen KI-Verordnung (KI-Marktüberwachungs- und Innovationsgesetz — KI-MIG)
enforcement_body: Federal Office for Artificial Intelligence Safety (BAIS - proposed)
max_penalty: Up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover (AI Act maximums)
preemption_notes: Implementing legislation for directly applicable EU AI Act; national rules on enforcement procedures and authority designation only
summary: German implementing legislation for the EU AI Act; designates the Federal Network Agency (BNetzA) as primary market surveillance authority and BaFin for financial sector AI. Establishes national enforcement procedures, a penalty scale mirroring AI Act maximums (up to €35M / 7% turnover), and an AI regulatory sandbox program. Provides for future establishment of a Federal Office for Artificial Intelligence Safety (BAIS). Cabinet adopted February 2026; before Bundestag as of May 2026.
notable: Cabinet adopted February 2026; legislative passage through Bundestag expected 2026.
legal_citation: KI-Marktüberwachungs- und Innovationsgesetz (KI-MIG)
key_obligations: BNetzA designated as primary market surveillance authority for EU AI Act
BaFin designated for financial sector AI oversight
National enforcement procedures and appeals processes established
Penalty scale mirrors EU AI Act maximums with differentiation criteria
National AI regulatory sandbox program funded for three years
GPAI model enforcement coordination powers granted to BNetzA

impact_assessment.detail: National implementing law; EU AI Act impact assessment obligations apply directly.

prohibited_categories.detail: EU AI Act prohibited practices apply directly; KI-MIG provides enforcement procedures.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed independently; EU AI Act human oversight obligations apply.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action created; enforcement through BNetzA and BaFin.

risk_classification.detail: EU AI Act risk classification applies directly; KI-MIG provides national enforcement framework.

enforcement_model.detail: BNetzA as cross-sectoral lead authority; BaFin for financial sector; sectoral coordination mechanism; penalties up to €35M / 7% global turnover; AI regulatory sandbox.

operative_dates: Cabinet adopted 11 February 2026; Bundestag passage expected 2026; effective date TBD

short_name: UK ADM Code of Practice SI 2026
full_name: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on AI and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425)
summary: Statutory instrument mandating the ICO to draft, consult on, and issue a statutory Code of Practice on AI and automated decision-making (ADM) under the Data Protection Act 2018. Implements a commitment in the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The code, once finalized, will carry statutory weight governing AI/ADM practices under UK GDPR and must be taken into account by courts and the ICO in compliance assessments. ICO launched public consultation on draft ADM guidance on 31 March 2026.
legal_citation: SI 2026/425; Data Protection Act 2018, s. 121
key_obligations: ICO mandated to issue statutory ADM Code of Practice within 18 months
Minimum 12-week public consultation on draft code required
Code must cover UK GDPR Chapter III rights, human review rights, transparency, and documentation
Secretary of State approval required before code issuance
Code to be laid before Parliament
Courts and ICO must take code into account in ADM compliance determinations

impact_assessment.detail: SI mandates code development; code may address impact assessment requirements for ADM.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: SI mandates code to cover human review rights for significant automated decisions under Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action; enforcement through ICO.

anti_discrimination.detail: Code may address ADM fairness; SI itself does not specify anti-discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed; code may introduce risk-based ADM guidance.

enforcement_model.detail: ICO enforces DPA 2018; code compliance creates presumption of UK GDPR conformity; no new enforcement powers created by SI.

operative_dates: In force 12 May 2026; Code to be issued within 18 months

short_name: Norway KI-loven (AI Act EEA)
full_name: Norway — KI-loven (Artificial Intelligence Act — EEA Implementation)
preemption_notes: EEA EFTA implementation of EU AI Act via EEA Agreement; EFTA Surveillance Authority (ESA) plays analogous role to European Commission for Norway-specific enforcement
summary: Norwegian implementing legislation to incorporate the EU AI Act into Norwegian law via the EEA Agreement. Consultation package published 30 June 2025; consultation closed 30 September 2025; formal Storting introduction expected 2026. Designates Nkom as coordinating national AI supervisory authority. Provides national enforcement procedures, language localization requirements, and NOK-denominated penalty thresholds. Requires parallel EEA Joint Committee decision to incorporate EU AI Act into EEA Agreement Annex XX.
notable: Norway participates in EU AI Act as EEA EFTA state; must incorporate AI Act via EEA Agreement amendment; EFTA Surveillance Authority takes Commission-equivalent role.
key_obligations: Nkom designated as coordinating national AI supervisory authority
Sector-specific authorities retain jurisdiction in their domains
Technical documentation and user instructions to be available in Norwegian
Penalty thresholds converted to NOK
National AI regulatory sandbox aligned with EU AI Act Article 57

impact_assessment.detail: Pending legislation; EU AI Act obligations will apply via EEA incorporation.

prohibited_categories.detail: EU AI Act prohibited practices will apply directly via EEA incorporation.

human_review_rights.detail: EU AI Act human oversight provisions will apply via EEA incorporation.

private_right_of_action.detail: Not addressed.

synthetic_media.detail: EU AI Act transparency obligations will apply via EEA incorporation.

biometric_data.detail: EU AI Act biometric provisions will apply via EEA incorporation.

training_data_transparency.detail: EU AI Act GPAI training data obligations will apply via EEA incorporation.

content_labeling.detail: EU AI Act content labelling obligations will apply via EEA incorporation.

anti_discrimination.detail: EU AI Act anti-discrimination provisions will apply via EEA incorporation.

risk_classification.detail: EU AI Act risk classification will apply directly via EEA incorporation.

enforcement_model.detail: Nkom as coordinating authority; EFTA Surveillance Authority for Commission-equivalent monitoring; sector-specific authorities retain domain jurisdiction.

operative_dates: Consultation closed September 2025; Storting introduction expected 2026; EEA entry into force pending Joint Committee decision

short_name: Russia Federal Law 169-FZ (AI Sandbox Amendment)
full_name: Federal Law No. 169-FZ on Amendments to Federal Law on Experimental Legal Regimes in the Field of Digital Innovations
enforcement_body: Ministry of Digital Development, Communications and Mass Media
max_penalty: Civil liability; insurance requirements
summary: Extends and updates Russia's experimental legal regime (regulatory sandbox) framework for AI development under Federal Law No. 258-FZ. Introduces mandatory civil liability insurance for AI developers operating within regulatory sandboxes. Expands the ELR framework to cover generative AI systems, adding content moderation and user disclosure requirements during testing. Updates governance procedures for sandbox applications. Builds on the original 2020 framework that created the Moscow AI digital sandbox.
legal_citation: Федеральный закон № 169-ФЗ от 4 января 2025 г.
key_obligations: Mandatory civil liability insurance for AI developers in regulatory sandboxes
Generative AI ELR participants must implement content moderation during testing
Generative AI ELR participants must disclose ELR status to users
Generative AI ELR participants must report content-related incidents
Extended statutory authority for ELRs for five additional years

impact_assessment.detail: No mandatory impact assessment; ELR framework provides controlled testing environment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed in this amendment.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Civil liability framework applies; specific private right of action not created.

synthetic_media.detail: Generative AI systems covered by ELR framework but no specific synthetic media labelling requirements.

content_labeling.detail: Disclosure of ELR status required to users; not a general content labelling mandate.

risk_classification.detail: No formal risk classification; ELR eligibility criteria serve gating function.

enforcement_model.detail: Ministry of Digital Development coordinates ELR authorization; civil liability insurance provides compensation mechanism; Bank of Russia for financial sector ELRs.

operative_dates: In force 4 January 2025

short_name: Turkey AI Amendment Bill (2/3358)
full_name: Turkey — Kanun Teklifi Esas No. 2/3358 — Bill on Amendments to Certain Laws Regarding Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: Administrative fines; content blocking; criminal penalties under amended Penal Code provisions
summary: Turkish omnibus bill amending multiple laws to address AI: introduces statutory AI definition; mandates deepfake content labelling; creates 6-hour takedown obligation for AI-generated content violating personal rights; grants BTK emergency blocking powers for harmful AI-generated content; establishes joint liability for AI developers and platform operators; amends Internet Law (No. 5651), Turkish Penal Code, KVKK (Law 6698), Electronic Commerce Law, and Cybersecurity Law. Submitted to Grand National Assembly November 2025; passage timeline uncertain.
notable: Submitted to Grand National Assembly November 7, 2025; passage timeline uncertain. 6-hour takedown obligation is shorter than EU DSA timeframes.
legal_citation: Kanun Teklifi Esas No. 2/3358
key_obligations: AI-generated content depicting real persons must be labelled
Platform operators must remove personal-rights-violating AI content within 6 hours
BTK empowered to issue emergency access blocking orders without prior judicial authorization
Joint liability for AI developers and content providers for harmful AI-generated content
Criminal penalties for deliberate deepfake creation to harm reputation
Critical AI system operators must conduct periodic cybersecurity assessments

impact_assessment.detail: Cybersecurity assessments required for critical AI systems; no general AI impact assessment mandate.

prohibited_categories.detail: BTK emergency blocking authority effectively prohibits certain AI-generated content categories (election disinformation, non-consensual intimate imagery, impersonation of officials).

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Joint liability framework applies; specific private right of action structure not detailed in bill.

synthetic_media.detail: AI-generated content depicting real persons must be labelled; 6-hour takedown obligation for personal-rights-violating AI content; criminal penalties for harmful deepfake creation.

content_labeling.detail: AI-generated content depicting real persons must carry 'yapay zeka ile üretilmiştir' (produced with AI) disclosure; BTK to issue technical labelling standards.

risk_classification.detail: No formal risk classification system; critical AI systems identified in cybersecurity provisions.

enforcement_model.detail: BTK administrative enforcement with emergency blocking powers; KVKK for data protection aspects; criminal penalties via amended Penal Code; joint civil liability.

operative_dates: Pending; submitted to Grand National Assembly 7 November 2025

short_name: Japan APPI (2022 Amendments)
full_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)
max_penalty: Up to JPY 100 million (~$650K) for organizations; JPY 1 million for individuals
summary: Japan's 2022 APPI amendments represent the most expansive revision of Japan's primary personal data protection law, introducing mandatory breach notification, a strengthened opt-out regime for third-party data transfers requiring PPC registration, new data subject rights including cessation of third-party provision, tightened cross-border transfer rules with explicit consent requirements, and a new pseudonymously processed information category enabling AI development use cases. Corporate penalties increased tenfold to JPY 100 million.
notable: Introduced the 'pseudonymously processed information' category relevant to AI model training — organizations can use pseudonymized data internally for analytics and AI development with fewer restrictions than fully identifiable data.
legal_citation: Act No. 57 of 2003 (as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021)
key_obligations: Mandatory breach notification to PPC and affected individuals for qualifying incidents
Registration with PPC required before third-party data transfers via opt-out mechanism
Explicit consent required for cross-border transfers with full destination country disclosure
Data subjects may request cessation of third-party provision of their personal data
Sensitive personal information (health, criminal, biometric) requires explicit consent for any transfer

impact_assessment.detail: APPI does not require formal privacy impact assessments, though the PPC issues guidance encouraging risk assessments for new technologies.

prohibited_categories.detail: APPI does not prohibit specific AI applications; it restricts processing of certain sensitive data categories.

human_review_rights.detail: APPI does not provide rights specific to automated decision-making; no right to human review of algorithmic decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: APPI does not provide a private right of action; enforcement is through the PPC.

synthetic_media.detail: APPI does not address synthetic media or AI-generated content specifically.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is classified as sensitive personal information requiring explicit consent for collection and prohibiting opt-out transfers to third parties.

training_data_transparency.detail: APPI does not require disclosure of AI training data sources or practices.

content_labeling.detail: APPI does not address labeling of AI-generated content.

anti_discrimination.detail: APPI does not contain anti-discrimination provisions; Japan's anti-discrimination framework is addressed in separate legislation.

risk_classification.detail: APPI does not establish a risk classification system for AI or data processing activities.

enforcement_model.detail: Enforcement through PPC with powers to issue corrective orders, conduct inspections, and impose administrative fines up to JPY 100 million; criminal penalties for serious violations.

operative_dates: Enacted June 4, 2021 (Act No. 77 of 2021). Fully effective April 1, 2022.

short_name: Japan METI/MIC AI Business Guidelines 2024
full_name: AI Business Guidelines (AI事業者ガイドライン) — Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications
enforcement_body: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC)
summary: Japan's joint METI/MIC AI Business Guidelines are the country's primary operational governance document for AI, establishing ten guiding principles (human-centric AI, safety, security, fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, education, innovation, social contribution) and tier-specific guidance for AI developers, providers, and users. Voluntary compliance with sector-specific appendices covering healthcare, financial services, legal services, and employment.
notable: Structured around three tiers of the AI supply chain (developers, providers/operators, users) — a governance model distinct from the EU's approach and reflective of Japan's Hiroshima Process leadership. Voluntary but expected to inform future mandatory regulation.
key_obligations: AI developers should conduct safety testing and provide documentation (model cards) for foundation models
AI providers should disclose to users when interacting with AI systems and implement human oversight for high-stakes decisions
AI users should conduct risk assessments before deploying AI in business operations
All actors should implement privacy protections consistent with the APPI
AI actors should promote AI literacy among employees and users

impact_assessment.detail: Guidelines recommend risk assessments proportionate to AI system risk levels, but do not mandate formal impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Guidelines do not prohibit specific AI applications; they recommend safeguards against misuse for weapons, cyberattacks, or illegal content.

human_review_rights.detail: Guidelines recommend human oversight mechanisms for high-stakes AI decisions (medical, legal, financial, employment) but do not create individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary guidelines; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Guidelines do not specifically address synthetic media or AI-generated content labeling requirements.

biometric_data.detail: Guidelines reference privacy protections under APPI but do not specifically address biometric data in AI systems.

training_data_transparency.detail: Guidelines encourage AI developers to disclose training data scope to the extent feasible without compromising proprietary interests, but this is non-binding.

content_labeling.detail: Guidelines encourage transparency about AI-generated content but do not mandate labeling.

anti_discrimination.detail: Fairness principle requires avoiding inappropriate discrimination, but no enforcement mechanism or specific standard.

risk_classification.detail: Guidelines do not establish a formal risk classification system for AI applications.

enforcement_model.detail: Entirely voluntary; no enforcement mechanism. METI and MIC may reference guidelines in procurement and public recognition programs.

operative_dates: Published April 19, 2024. Voluntary; no mandatory effective date.

short_name: South Korea PIPA (2023 Amendments)
full_name: Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) — 2023 Amendments (Act No. 19234)
max_penalty: Up to KRW 30 billion or 3% of global revenue (~$22M USD)
summary: South Korea's landmark 2023 PIPA amendments introduce Asia-Pacific's strongest statutory right to explanation for automated AI decisions and the right to object to and demand human review of purely automated decisions that legally or significantly affect individuals. The amendments also modernize cross-border transfer mechanisms (SCCs, BCRs, adequacy decisions), introduce 72-hour breach notification aligned with GDPR, expand PIPC enforcement powers, and clarify extraterritorial scope covering foreign online service providers processing Korean residents' data.
notable: Among the first statutes in Asia-Pacific to grant individuals an explicit right to explanation of automated decisions and a right to request human review — directly applicable to AI systems in hiring, credit, healthcare, and other high-stakes domains.
legal_citation: Act No. 19234 (Personal Information Protection Act, as amended 2023)
key_obligations: Controllers using automated decision-making must notify individuals of their right to explanation and to request human review
Provide explanation of automated decision logic, significance, and consequences upon individual request
Pause automated decision effects pending human review when objection is filed
Notify PIPC of data breaches within 72 hours
Foreign online service providers processing Korean residents' data must designate a domestic representative

impact_assessment.detail: PIPA does not mandate formal AI impact assessments, though data protection impact assessments are encouraged for high-risk processing.

prohibited_categories.detail: PIPA does not prohibit specific AI applications; it restricts processing of sensitive data categories and requires safeguards for automated decisions.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have a statutory right to object to purely automated decisions with legal or significant effects and to demand human review; controllers must suspend decision effects pending review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Data subjects may seek civil damages for violations of PIPA rights, including violations of automated decision rights.

synthetic_media.detail: PIPA does not address synthetic media or AI-generated content labeling.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is a special category requiring explicit consent; processing without consent or legal basis is prohibited.

training_data_transparency.detail: PIPA does not require disclosure of AI training data sources or practices.

content_labeling.detail: PIPA does not address labeling of AI-generated content.

anti_discrimination.detail: PIPA does not contain anti-discrimination provisions; Korea's anti-discrimination framework is addressed in separate legislation.

risk_classification.detail: PIPA does not establish a risk classification system for AI applications.

enforcement_model.detail: PIPC enforcement with powers to issue corrective orders, impose fines up to KRW 30 billion or 3% of global revenue, and publish decisions; data subjects may bring civil damages claims.

operative_dates: Enacted March 14, 2023 (Act No. 19234). Effective September 15, 2023.

short_name: Hong Kong PCPD AI Framework 2024
full_name: Artificial Intelligence: Model Personal Data Protection Framework (Hong Kong Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data)
summary: The PCPD's Model Personal Data Protection Framework for AI is Hong Kong's primary practical governance tool for organizations using AI systems that process personal data. Organized around four lifecycle phases — procurement, development, deployment, and monitoring — it provides checklists and guidance for applying the PDPO's six Data Protection Principles to AI contexts, addresses generative AI risks, and recommends AI interaction disclosure, human oversight for significant decisions, regular bias testing, and AI-specific incident response planning.
notable: Non-binding framework under the PDPO that bridges Hong Kong's existing privacy law and emerging AI governance needs; particularly relevant to multinational financial and technology firms operating across Hong Kong, mainland China, and other Asia-Pacific jurisdictions.
key_obligations: Conduct due diligence on AI vendors' data practices before procurement
Implement privacy by design in AI development including data minimization in training datasets
Disclose to users when they are interacting with an AI system
Implement human oversight mechanisms for significant decisions affecting individuals
Conduct ongoing bias assessments and maintain AI-specific incident response plans

impact_assessment.detail: Framework recommends privacy impact assessments for AI systems involving significant personal data processing, but these are non-binding.

prohibited_categories.detail: Framework does not prohibit specific AI applications; it provides guidance on applying PDPO protections to AI contexts.

human_review_rights.detail: Framework recommends human oversight mechanisms for significant decisions but does not create a statutory individual right to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary framework; enforcement only through PDPO mechanisms. No additional private right of action created.

synthetic_media.detail: Framework does not specifically address synthetic media or deepfakes.

biometric_data.detail: Framework does not specifically address biometric data beyond general PDPO protections for sensitive data.

training_data_transparency.detail: Framework recommends organizations assess whether AI vendors' training data includes personal data of Hong Kong residents and whether appropriate consents were obtained.

content_labeling.detail: Framework recommends AI interaction disclosure (chatbot identification) but does not address labeling of AI-generated content.

anti_discrimination.detail: Framework recommends bias testing and fairness assessments but does not establish anti-discrimination standards or enforcement.

risk_classification.detail: Framework does not establish a risk classification system for AI applications.

enforcement_model.detail: Framework is non-binding. PCPD may reference adherence or deviation in PDPO enforcement proceedings. Underlying PDPO provides maximum penalties of HKD 1 million and 5 years imprisonment for serious violations.

operative_dates: Published June 2024. Voluntary; no mandatory effective date.

short_name: Brunei PDPO 2021
full_name: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (Brunei Darussalam)
max_penalty: Up to BND 100,000 (~$75,000) and 3 years imprisonment for serious violations
summary: Brunei's first comprehensive personal data protection law, the PDPO establishes nine data protection principles (purpose limitation, consent, accuracy, retention, transfer, access, correction, openness, security) governing all private-sector organizations processing personal data. Administered by AITI, the PDPO provides data subjects with access and correction rights, restricts cross-border transfers, and classifies biometric and health data as sensitive categories requiring explicit consent. Implementation was phased through 2024.
notable: Brunei is one of the last ASEAN member states to enact comprehensive data protection legislation; the PDPO aligns Brunei with ASEAN's Model Framework and positions it for cross-border data flow agreements with regional partners.
legal_citation: Personal Data Protection Order 2021 (S 96/2021)
key_obligations: Obtain consent before collecting personal data unless a specific exception applies
Limit data collection and use to the stated purpose (purpose limitation)
Implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data
Respond to data subject access and correction requests within 30 days
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with equivalent protection or under contractual safeguards

impact_assessment.detail: PDPO does not require formal privacy impact assessments; AITI may issue guidance on risk assessment.

prohibited_categories.detail: PDPO does not prohibit specific AI applications; sensitive data categories require heightened protection.

human_review_rights.detail: PDPO does not address automated decision-making or provide rights specific to AI-driven decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement through AITI; no express private right of action in the PDPO.

synthetic_media.detail: PDPO does not address synthetic media or AI-generated content.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is classified as sensitive personal data requiring explicit consent for processing.

training_data_transparency.detail: PDPO does not address AI training data practices.

content_labeling.detail: PDPO does not address labeling of AI-generated content.

anti_discrimination.detail: PDPO does not contain anti-discrimination provisions.

risk_classification.detail: PDPO does not establish a risk classification system for data processing or AI activities.

enforcement_model.detail: Enforcement through AITI with powers to issue enforcement notices, impose fines up to BND 100,000, and refer serious cases for criminal prosecution.

operative_dates: Enacted May 2021 (S 96/2021). Phase 1 effective January 1, 2022. Full implementation through 2024.

short_name: Australia Voluntary AI Safety Standard 2024
full_name: Australian Voluntary AI Safety Standard — 10 Mandatory Guardrails for Responsible AI
enforcement_body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
summary: Australia's Voluntary AI Safety Standard articulates ten guardrails for responsible AI — covering accountability, transparency, human oversight, risk assessment, security, testing, privacy, data quality, explainability, and fairness/non-discrimination — published as a voluntary precursor to a proposed mandatory regime for high-risk AI. Organizations adopting the standard receive guidance for compliance with existing consumer protection, privacy, and anti-discrimination law. As of May 2026, the mandatory regime had not yet been enacted.
notable: Intended as a voluntary bridge to mandatory regulation; the ten guardrails are expected to become binding for 'high-risk AI' under Australia's forthcoming mandatory AI governance regime, which will include third-party conformity assessment for the highest-risk applications.
key_obligations: Establish governance structures with clear accountability for AI systems throughout their lifecycle
Conduct structured risk assessments before deploying AI systems proportionate to potential impact
Implement human oversight and control mechanisms enabling review and override of AI decisions
Test AI systems before deployment and conduct ongoing evaluation including bias assessments
Comply with Privacy Act 1988 Australian Privacy Principles for AI systems processing personal data

impact_assessment.detail: Guardrail 4 recommends structured risk assessments proportionate to potential impact; Guardrail 7 recommends Privacy Impact Assessments for AI involving significant personal data processing. Both are voluntary.

prohibited_categories.detail: Standard does not prohibit specific AI applications; it recommends safeguards and risk assessment.

human_review_rights.detail: Guardrail 3 recommends human oversight for high-stakes AI decisions but does not create individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary standard; no direct enforcement mechanism. Existing consumer protection and privacy laws provide enforcement pathways.

synthetic_media.detail: Standard does not specifically address synthetic media or AI-generated content labeling.

biometric_data.detail: Standard does not specifically address biometric data; Guardrail 7 references Privacy Act compliance generally.

training_data_transparency.detail: Guardrail 8 recommends data quality documentation including data provenance and bias assessment in training data.

content_labeling.detail: Guardrail 2 recommends transparency about AI use in products and services but does not mandate content labeling.

anti_discrimination.detail: Guardrail 10 requires compliance with Australian anti-discrimination statutes (Racial Discrimination Act 1975, Sex Discrimination Act 1984, Age Discrimination Act 2004, Disability Discrimination Act 1992) and recommends bias testing.

risk_classification.detail: Standard does not establish a formal risk classification system; it anticipates high-risk AI categories will be defined under the forthcoming mandatory regime.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary standard; no direct enforcement. ACCC, OAIC, and Human Rights Commission retain enforcement authority under existing law. Standard adoption may receive regulatory credit in enforcement proceedings.

operative_dates: Published September 5, 2024. Voluntary; no mandatory effective date. Mandatory regime expected but not enacted as of May 2026.

short_name: ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021
full_name: Abu Dhabi Global Market Data Protection Regulations 2021
bill_number: ADGM Board of Directors Resolution No. 3 of 2021
max_penalty: Up to USD 28 million for serious violations
summary: The ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 establish a comprehensive GDPR-aligned data protection framework for entities operating in Abu Dhabi's international financial free zone. Enacted by the ADGM Board of Directors on 14 February 2021, with staggered compliance deadlines: new entities by August 2021, existing entities by February 2022. Key provisions include lawful basis requirements, full data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection), rights to contest automated decisions and obtain human intervention, mandatory DPIAs for high-risk processing, 72-hour breach notification, cross-border transfer mechanisms, and DPO requirements. Administrative penalties capped at USD 28 million; data subjects may also claim compensation for material and non-material damage through the ADGM Courts.
key_obligations: Process personal data only on a valid lawful basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests)
Conduct DPIAs before commencing high-risk processing including systematic automated profiling
Provide individuals with rights to contest automated decisions and obtain human intervention
Notify ADGM Registration Authority of data breaches within 72 hours
Appoint a Data Protection Officer for large-scale or sensitive data processing activities
Register with the ADGM Office of Data Protection and pay required annual fees
Implement data protection by design and by default in all processing systems
notable: Staggered implementation — new entities from August 2021, existing entities from February 2022. Data subjects have a civil right of action in ADGM Courts for material and non-material damages, mirroring GDPR Article 82.

short_name: APEC Cross-Border Privacy Rules System
summary: APEC's voluntary certification framework enabling free personal data flows between participating economies (US, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Canada, Mexico, Philippines, Chinese Taipei, Australia). Organizations certified against APEC Privacy Framework principles by accredited Accountability Agents can transfer data across participating economies. In 2022 the Global CBPR Forum was established to expand the system beyond APEC. Increasingly relevant for AI training data flows in Asia-Pacific.
key_obligations: Implement APEC Privacy Framework's nine principles to obtain CBPR certification
Submit to assessment by an APEC-accredited Accountability Agent
Maintain ongoing compliance monitored by Accountability Agent
Respond to consumer complaints through Accountability Agent mechanism
Renew certification periodically
full_name: APEC Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR) System

short_name: Australia National AI Strategy 2021
summary: Australia's AI Action Plan 2021 is a high-level national strategy organised around three pillars — getting AI foundations right (data, infrastructure, trust), growing Australia's AI capability (research, business adoption, international engagement), and using AI for the greater good (health, environment, regional communities). It reinforces Australia's voluntary AI Ethics Principles (2019) and commits the federal government to applying them in all AI procurement and development, while encouraging (but not requiring) private sector adoption. The Action Plan has been substantially superseded by the Voluntary AI Safety Standard (September 2024) and the forthcoming mandatory high-risk AI regime.
key_obligations: Government agencies must apply Australia's AI Ethics Principles in all AI procurement and development (voluntary/internal policy)
CSIRO Data61 to establish and operate the National AI Centre (NAIC) as national coordination hub
Digital Transformation Agency to coordinate whole-of-government AI adoption strategy
Government to release high-value public datasets for AI research through data.gov.au
DISER to invest in AI research through ARC and CSIRO and to support SME AI adoption through advisory programs
Australia to actively participate in OECD AI Policy Observatory and GPAI
full_name: Australia's AI Action Plan 2021 — National Artificial Intelligence Strategy

short_name: Bahrain PDPL 2018
max_penalty: Up to BHD 20,000 (~$53,000) and 1 year imprisonment
summary: Bahrain's PDPL was one of the first comprehensive data protection statutes in the GCC, establishing the Personal Data Protection Authority and a consent-based framework covering all organizations processing personal data in Bahrain or about Bahrain residents. Key provisions include sensitive data categories (health, genetic, biometric, racial, financial), data subject rights (access, correction, deletion, objection), cross-border transfer restrictions, mandatory breach notification, DPO requirements for large-scale or sensitive processing, and a licensing regime for high-risk processing activities.
key_obligations: Obtain consent or establish another lawful basis before processing personal data
Classify and apply heightened protections for sensitive data categories including biometric, health, and financial data
Respond to data subject access, correction, deletion, and objection requests within statutory timeframes
Notify PDPA and affected individuals of personal data breaches without undue delay
Obtain a PDPA license before commencing large-scale processing of sensitive personal data
full_name: Bahrain Personal Data Protection Law 2018 (Law No. 30 of 2018)

short_name: Canada Bill C-27 / AIDA
summary: Canada’s proposed federal AI governance statute, Part 3 of Bill C-27 (Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022). Would have created obligations for developers and deployers of ‘high-impact AI systems’ to assess and mitigate risks of harm and biased output, maintain records, and publish plain-language descriptions. A new Artificial Intelligence and Data Commissioner would have overseen compliance with powers to audit AI systems and impose administrative penalties. Prohibited processing personal data obtained unlawfully to train AI, deepfake intimate images, and deployment of AI systems known to cause serious harm. Also proposed GPAI-specific obligations (added in 2023 amendments) addressing general-purpose AI systems. Died January 6, 2025 when Parliament prorogued following PM Trudeau’s resignation announcement.
key_obligations: Assess whether AI system is a high-impact system and identify foreseeable risks of harm or biased output
Implement and document measures to mitigate identified risks of harm and biased output
Make available plain-language public description of high-impact AI system and its uses
Notify Minister of serious risks and cease operation if serious risk cannot be mitigated
Maintain records of risk assessments and mitigation measures for regulatory review
Developers of GPAI must maintain technical documentation and publish training data summaries (2023 amendments)
Prohibition on processing personal data obtained unlawfully to train AI systems
Prohibition on deploying AI systems known or recklessly likely to cause serious harm
Prohibition on generating non-consensual synthetic intimate images (deepfakes)
full_name: Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA) — Part 3 of Bill C-27, Canada

short_name: Canada Bill C-63 (Online Harms Act)
max_penalty: Up to CAD $10 million or 3% of global revenues for systemic violations.
summary: Bill C-63 (first reading February 26, 2024) proposed creating a new Online Harms Act establishing a Digital Safety Commission with powers to regulate online platforms. It imposed duties of care on platforms to mitigate harmful content (CSAM, non-consensual intimate images, hate speech, incitement to violence), required age-appropriate design, restricted algorithmic recommendation of harmful content, and created a Digital Safety Ombudsperson. The bill died when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025.
key_obligations: Regulated platforms must implement duty of care to protect users from harmful content
Platforms must not algorithmically recommend content that constitutes child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, or incitement to violence
Platforms must implement age verification for adult content
Annual digital safety plans and transparency reports required
Emergency removal orders for CSAM within 24 hours
full_name: Bill C-63 — Online Harms Act (Canada)

short_name: Ivory Coast Personal Data Protection Law 2013
max_penalty: Up to XOF 10,000,000 (~$17,000) and 5 years imprisonment
summary: Côte d'Ivoire's comprehensive personal data protection law designating ARTCI as the supervisory body for data protection in addition to its telecommunications regulatory role. Provides data protection principles, lawful processing bases, special category data protections, mandatory ARTCI declaration, data subject rights, cross-border transfer restrictions, and criminal penalties.
key_obligations: Declare processing activities to ARTCI before commencing
Obtain prior ARTCI authorization for sensitive or high-risk processing
Comply with data protection principles (proportionality, accuracy, purpose limitation)
Protect special category data with explicit consent or legal authority
Provide data subject rights (information, access, rectification, opposition)
Implement technical and organizational security measures
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
full_name: Côte d'Ivoire Law No. 2013-450 on the Protection of Personal Data

short_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260)
max_penalty: Framework document; enforcement through existing regulatory channels.
summary: China's National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity (SAC NTC260) released the AI Safety Governance Framework in September 2024. The framework establishes principles for AI safety governance, classifies AI safety risks into inherent and systemic categories, and provides guidance on risk identification, assessment, and mitigation across the AI lifecycle. It complements China's binding CAC regulations on generative AI and algorithmic recommendations.
key_obligations: AI developers and operators should implement AI safety governance aligned with the framework's principles
Classify AI risks into inherent risks (data, model, application) and systemic risks
Conduct safety assessments across the AI lifecycle
Implement technical and management controls for identified risks
full_name: China AI Safety Governance Framework (SAC NTC260, 2024)

short_name: Costa Rica Data Protection Law 2011
max_penalty: Up to CRC 172 million (~$340,000); criminal penalties; processing suspension
summary: Costa Rica's primary data protection law and Central America's most developed data protection framework. Establishes PRODHAB as a powerful independent agency. Provides ARCO rights, lawful processing bases, sensitive data categories, habeas data judicial remedy, mandatory database registration, cross-border transfer restrictions, and significant administrative fines up to CRC 172 million.
key_obligations: Register all personal data databases with PRODHAB
Implement lawful processing basis
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or legal authority
Provide data subject ARCO rights (access, rectification, cancellation, opposition)
Implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection or PRODHAB-approved safeguards
Cooperate with PRODHAB audits and investigations
full_name: Costa Rica Law No. 8968 — Protection of Personal Data

short_name: Dominican Republic Data Protection Law 2013
max_penalty: Fines and criminal penalties up to 2 years imprisonment
summary: Dominican Republic's primary data protection law covering personal data in public and private databases. INDOTEL serves as supervisory authority. Provides data subject ARCO rights, habeas data judicial remedy, lawful processing requirements, mandatory database registration, sensitive data protections, and criminal penalties up to 2 years imprisonment. Particular focus on credit bureau and financial data.
key_obligations: Register personal databases with INDOTEL
Obtain consent or other legal basis for processing
Protect sensitive data categories
Provide data subject rights (access, rectification, cancellation, opposition)
Implement appropriate security measures
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with equivalent protection
Comply with credit data retention time limits
full_name: Dominican Republic Law No. 172-13 on the Protection of Personal Data

short_name: Algeria Personal Data Protection Law 2018
max_penalty: Up to DZD 5,000,000 (~$37,000) and 5 years imprisonment for serious violations
summary: Algeria's comprehensive personal data protection law establishing the ANPDP as an independent supervisory authority. Provides lawful processing bases, extensive sensitive data categories (health, genetic, biometric, political, religious, criminal), data subject rights, mandatory registration and authorization requirements, cross-border transfer restrictions, and criminal penalties.
key_obligations: Declare standard processing activities to ANPDP or obtain prior authorization for high-risk processing
Implement lawful processing basis for all personal data processing
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or specific legal authority
Provide data subject rights (information, access, rectification, opposition, deletion)
Implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures
Notify ANPDP of significant personal data breaches
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection or ANPDP approval
full_name: Algeria Law No. 18-07 on the Protection of Personal Data

short_name: Ecuador LOPDP 2021
max_penalty: Up to $700,000 USD or 1% of annual revenue for serious violations
summary: Ecuador's first comprehensive data protection law with GDPR-inspired structure. Establishes the SNPDP as supervisory authority. Provides seven principles, ARCO+ rights (including portability and non-discrimination), automated decision-making notification and human review rights, DPO requirements, DPIA obligations, sensitive data categories, 72-hour breach notification, and significant administrative fines.
key_obligations: Implement lawful processing basis for all personal data processing
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or specific legal authority
Provide ARCO+ rights (access, rectification, cancellation, opposition, portability, non-discrimination)
Notify data subjects of automated decision-making and provide human review right
Appoint DPO for public bodies and high-risk processing
Conduct DPIAs for high-risk processing activities
Notify SNPDP of breaches within 72 hours
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequacy determination or approved safeguards
full_name: Ecuador Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP) 2021

short_name: EU AI Liability Directive (withdrawn)
max_penalty: Proposed civil liability regime; no administrative penalties. Withdrawn before enactment.
summary: The European Commission proposed the AI Liability Directive (COM/2022/496) in September 2022 as a companion to the AI Act, adapting civil liability rules to AI systems. It introduced a rebuttable presumption of causation for high-risk AI systems (shifting burden of proof to defendants) and a disclosure mechanism allowing claimants to request AI-related evidence from developers. The Commission withdrew the proposal in February 2025 following the AI Act's adoption, citing the AI Act's enforcement mechanisms and the Omnibus simplification package.
key_obligations: High-risk AI systems: rebuttable presumption of causal link between fault and damage
Developers and deployers must disclose relevant AI documentation to claimants upon court order
National courts to apply EU AI Act risk classification in liability proceedings
Claimants harmed by AI entitled to request evidence disclosure from AI operators
full_name: European Commission Proposal for an AI Liability Directive (COM/2022/496) — Withdrawn

short_name: EU Data Governance Act (DGA)
max_penalty: Penalties determined by Member States; DGA requires effective, proportionate, and dissuasive penalties but does not specify a maximum
summary: The Data Governance Act establishes EU-wide frameworks for re-using protected public sector data, operating trusted data intermediation services, and collecting voluntary data donations for general-interest purposes including AI research. Its data altruism mechanism enables individuals to lawfully contribute personal data (including health records and genomic data) to AI training datasets for public benefit, while the intermediation services framework prohibits data brokers from using pooled data to train their own AI models. The DGA provides the governance infrastructure underlying Common European Data Spaces in health, mobility, agriculture, and other sectors.
key_obligations: Art. 5: Public sector bodies must allow re-use of protected data via secure processing environments; conditions must be non-discriminatory and cost-based
Art. 11: Data intermediation service providers must notify national competent authority before operating
Art. 12: Data intermediaries must not use shared data for their own commercial purposes, including AI model training
Art. 12: Data intermediaries must be structurally separated from other commercial activities
Art. 20: Recognised data altruism organisations must be non-profit, publish annual activity reports, and use data only for declared general-interest purposes
Art. 25: Commission must adopt standardised European Data Altruism Consent Form compatible with GDPR
Art. 17: Data altruism organisations must register on national registers to obtain recognised status
full_name: EU Regulation (EU) 2022/868 — Data Governance Act (DGA)

short_name: EU Digital Services Act (DSA)
max_penalty: 6% of global annual worldwide turnover (VLOPs/VLOSEs); 1% for misleading information; temporary service ban for repeated infringements
summary: The Digital Services Act establishes a tiered regulatory framework for online intermediary services in the EU, imposing the heaviest obligations — including annual algorithmic audits, systemic risk assessments, and researcher data access — on Very Large Online Platforms and Very Large Online Search Engines with ≥45 million EU users. All online platforms using recommender systems must disclose their main parameters and offer at least one non-profiling recommendation option. The European Commission has direct enforcement jurisdiction over VLOPs/VLOSEs with penalties up to 6% of global turnover.
key_obligations: Art. 27: All online platforms using recommender systems must disclose main parameters in plain language and offer at least one non-profiling option
Art. 38: VLOPs/VLOSEs must make the non-profiling recommender option prominently available at the point of recommendation
Art. 34: VLOPs/VLOSEs must conduct at least annual systemic risk assessments covering algorithmic amplification effects
Art. 35: VLOPs/VLOSEs must implement proportionate risk mitigation measures addressing identified systemic risks
Art. 37: VLOPs/VLOSEs must submit to at least annual independent algorithmic audits and publish audit reports
Art. 40: VLOPs/VLOSEs must provide vetted researchers with access to data necessary for systemic risk research
Art. 26: All online platforms must label advertisements and disclose targeting parameters to recipients
Art. 39: VLOPs/VLOSEs must maintain a publicly searchable advertising repository
full_name: EU Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 — Digital Services Act (DSA)

short_name: G20 AI Principles (Osaka)
max_penalty: Non-binding principles; no penalty regime.
summary: The G20 Osaka Summit (June 2019) adopted AI principles as an annex to the Ministerial Statement on Trade and Digital Economy, mirroring the OECD AI Principles adopted weeks earlier. The G20 principles affirm trustworthy, human-centred AI across five pillars: inclusive growth, human-centred values, transparency, robustness/safety, and accountability. They represent the broadest political endorsement of AI governance principles to date, covering all major economies including the US, EU, China, India, and Brazil.
key_obligations: AI actors should commit to transparency and responsible disclosure
AI systems should be robust, secure and safe throughout their lifecycle
AI actors should be accountable for proper functioning of AI systems
Governments should invest in AI research and promote international cooperation
full_name: G20 AI Principles (Osaka, June 2019)

short_name: UK AI Regulation White Paper (2023)
summary: The UK Government's March 2023 White Paper sets out a deliberately non-statutory, sector-led approach to AI governance — explicitly diverging from the EU AI Act model — based on five cross-sector principles (safety, transparency, fairness, accountability, and contestability) to be implemented by existing UK sector regulators within their statutory mandates. Rather than creating a new AI regulator or binding obligations, the White Paper delegates implementation to bodies including the FCA, Ofcom, ICO, CMA, and MHRA. The February 2024 consultation response confirmed this architecture while introducing planned 'backstop' legislative powers for Ministers to direct regulators if they fail to implement the principles.
key_obligations: Principle 1 (Safety, Security, Robustness): Sector regulators should address AI system testing, monitoring, and secure failure modes
Principle 2 (Transparency and Explainability): Sector regulators should require appropriate transparency about AI functioning, proportionate to risk of harm
Principle 3 (Fairness): Sector regulators should ensure AI does not discriminate unlawfully under the Equality Act 2010
Principle 4 (Accountability and Governance): Sector regulators should require clear accountability lines for AI systems and their outcomes
Principle 5 (Contestability and Redress): Sector regulators should ensure affected individuals can contest AI decisions and seek redress
DSIT: Publish AI regulatory landscape monitoring and coordinate cross-sector regulatory consistency
Sector regulators: Report AI regulatory activities to DSIT; update guidance to address AI within existing statutory remit
full_name: AI Regulation: A Pro-Innovation Approach (UK Government White Paper, 2023)

short_name: Ghana Data Protection Act 2012
max_penalty: Up to GHS 60,000 (~$4,000) and 2 years imprisonment
summary: Ghana's primary data protection law and one of sub-Saharan Africa's earliest comprehensive data protection frameworks. Establishes the Data Protection Commission, mandates registration of data controllers and processors, enshrines eight data protection principles, provides data subject rights including access and correction, and protects sensitive data categories including health, financial, and biometric data.
key_obligations: Register all data controllers and processors with the DPC before processing
Comply with eight data protection principles
Implement appropriate security measures for personal data
Respond to data subject access and correction requests
Obtain explicit consent or legal basis before processing sensitive data
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
full_name: Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843)

short_name: India MeitY AI Advisory (2024)
summary: India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) issued this advisory requiring all intermediaries and platforms to ensure AI models, LLMs, and generative AI tools do not produce unlawful content, do not enable bias or discrimination or threaten electoral integrity, and that under-tested AI is labelled with fallibility warnings. It also requires deepfake/synthetic media to be embedded with permanent unique metadata for traceability. Compliance required with immediate effect.
key_obligations: AI/LLM outputs must not contain unlawful content under IT Rules 3(1)(b)
AI must not enable bias, discrimination or threaten electoral integrity
Under-tested AI models must be labelled with fallibility warnings; consent popup required
Synthetic/deepfake media must be embedded with permanent unique metadata identifying the source
full_name: India MeitY AI Advisory Note — Responsible Development and Deployment of AI (March 2024)

short_name: Bletchley Declaration 2023
summary: First international political declaration on frontier AI risks, signed by 28 countries including the US, UK, EU, China, and major economies. Acknowledges potentially catastrophic risks from frontier AI systems and commits signatories to international cooperation on AI safety including information sharing, research collaboration, and risk assessment. Non-binding but launched the AI Safety Summit series and catalyzed creation of national AI Safety Institutes.
key_obligations: Commit to international dialogue and cooperation on AI safety
Share information on AI safety evaluation methodologies
Collaborate on identifying and assessing frontier AI risks
Support development of internationally recognized safety guidelines
Participate in ongoing AI Safety Summit process
full_name: Bletchley Declaration on Frontier AI Safety (November 2023)

short_name: Paris AI Action Summit Statement 2025
summary: Third AI safety summit statement (Bletchley 2023 → Seoul 2024 → Paris 2025). Broader thematic scope than predecessors covering AI for public good (healthcare, climate, science), AI governance for developing countries, AI and the workplace, and open-source AI. Adopted by approximately 60 countries. Notable for US non-participation and strong inclusion of Global South perspectives.
key_obligations: Commit to harnessing AI for public good (healthcare, climate, science)
Support inclusive AI governance incorporating Global South perspectives
Ensure AI benefits are shared equitably across income levels and regions
Reaffirm Bletchley and Seoul commitments on frontier AI safety
Develop frameworks for worker protection in the context of AI adoption
Support international AI governance through UN and multilateral institutions
full_name: Paris AI Action Summit Statement — Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet (February 2025)

short_name: Seoul AI Safety Declarations 2024
summary: Two outputs from the AI Seoul Summit: government ministerial statement on AI safety frameworks and international governance, and voluntary Frontier AI Safety Commitments signed by major AI companies (Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, xAI, and others) on safety evaluations, dangerous capability thresholds, information sharing, and incident reporting. Formally established the international AI Safety Institute network.
key_obligations: Conduct pre-deployment safety evaluations for frontier AI models
Define and observe dangerous capability thresholds (red lines)
