Share safety-relevant information with governments and peer organizations
Report significant safety incidents to relevant national authorities
Participate in international AI Safety Institute network
Develop and strengthen national AI safety frameworks
Coordinate on safety evaluation methodologies internationally
full_name: Seoul AI Safety Declarations 2024 (Ministerial Statement and Company Commitments)

short_name: Jordan PDPL 2023
max_penalty: Fines up to JOD 1,000,000 (~$1.4M) and criminal penalties
summary: Jordan's first comprehensive data protection law establishes the Personal Data Protection Council as an independent supervisory authority and creates a consent-based framework covering all organizations processing data of Jordanians and residents. Key provisions include core processing principles, sensitive data categories (health, genetic, biometric, political, religious, criminal, financial), full data subject rights including portability, DPO requirements for large-scale or sensitive processing, mandatory breach notification, and cross-border transfer restrictions. Implementing regulations were still in development as of 2026.
key_obligations: Establish a valid lawful basis before processing personal data of Jordanians or residents
Apply heightened protections for sensitive data categories including biometric, health, financial, and criminal data
Respond to data subject access, correction, deletion, objection, and portability requests within regulatory timeframes
Notify PDPC and affected individuals of personal data breaches without undue delay
Appoint a DPO and register with PDPC for large-scale or sensitive data processing activities
full_name: Jordan Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023

short_name: NZ Algorithm Charter
max_penalty: Voluntary charter; no penalty regime. Signatories commit to annual reporting.
summary: The Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand, launched in July 2020, is a voluntary commitment by New Zealand government agencies to use algorithms transparently and accountably. Signatory agencies commit to: explaining how algorithms affect decisions, considering Māori data sovereignty (Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations), assessing and managing risks, engaging with affected communities, and maintaining human oversight. By the Year 1 Review (December 2021), 26 agencies had signed.
key_obligations: Signatory agencies must explain how algorithms affect decisions that affect people
Engage with people affected by algorithms before and during development
Consider impacts on Māori and Te Tiriti obligations
Maintain human oversight and ability to override algorithmic decisions
Annually report on charter compliance to Stats NZ
full_name: Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand (2020)

short_name: Oman PDPL 2022
max_penalty: Administrative fines up to OMR 500,000 (~$1.3M) and criminal penalties
summary: Oman's first comprehensive data protection law establishes a consent-based framework covering all organizations processing personal data in Oman or about Oman residents, administered by the Information Technology Authority. Key provisions include six core processing principles, sensitive data categories (health, genetic, biometric, racial, religious), data subject rights (access, correction, deletion, restriction, objection, consent withdrawal), DPO requirements for large-scale processing, mandatory breach notification, and cross-border transfer restrictions. Implementing regulations issued in 2023 provide procedural detail.
key_obligations: Establish a valid lawful basis before processing personal data
Apply heightened protections for sensitive data categories including biometric, genetic, health, and religious data
Respond to data subject access, correction, deletion, restriction, and objection requests within 30 days
Notify ITA and affected individuals of personal data breaches without undue delay
Appoint a DPO for large-scale processing of personal or sensitive data or systematic monitoring activities
full_name: Oman Personal Data Protection Law 2022 (Royal Decree No. 6/2022)

short_name: Panama Data Protection Law 2019
max_penalty: Up to USD 50,000 administrative fines; criminal penalties
summary: Panama's first comprehensive personal data protection law establishing APDATOS within AIG as the supervisory authority. Provides seven data protection principles, consent-based processing, sensitive data categories, ARCO data subject rights, mandatory database registration, cross-border transfer restrictions, security obligations, breach notification, and administrative fines up to USD 50,000.
key_obligations: Register personal databases with APDATOS before commencing processing
Implement seven data protection principles
Obtain consent or other lawful basis for processing
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or legal authority
Provide data subject ARCO rights
Implement appropriate security measures
Notify APDATOS and data subjects of significant breaches
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
full_name: Panama Law No. 81 on the Protection of Personal Data

short_name: Paraguay Data Protection Law 2020
max_penalty: Administrative fines up to PYG 500 million (~$67,000); criminal penalties
summary: Paraguay's primary data protection law establishing SENATIC as the supervisory authority. Provides data protection principles, lawful processing bases, sensitive data special categories (health, genetic, biometric, political, criminal), ARCO data subject rights, mandatory database registration, cross-border transfer restrictions, and administrative and criminal penalties.
key_obligations: Register personal databases with SENATIC before commencing processing
Comply with data protection principles
Implement lawful processing basis
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or legal authority
Provide ARCO rights (access, rectification, cancellation, opposition)
Implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
full_name: Paraguay Law No. 6534 — Personal Data Protection

short_name: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework (2020)
summary: Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework (Second Edition) is a detailed voluntary guide for private-sector organisations on responsible AI deployment, published by PDPC at the World Economic Forum in January 2020. Its most distinctive contribution is a risk-calibrated human oversight matrix — distinguishing human-in-the-loop, human-over-the-loop, and human-out-of-the-loop oversight models based on the probability and severity of harm — along with practical guidance on training data governance, algorithmic explainability, and customer transparency. Widely cited internationally and influential on ASEAN, OECD, and UK regulatory thinking.
key_obligations: Principle 1: Establish internal governance structures with clear accountability for AI systems at board/senior management level
Principle 2: Calibrate human oversight (human-in-loop / over-loop / out-of-loop) based on probability and severity of harm matrix
Principle 3: Ensure training data is representative, bias-tested, and documented; monitor for model drift
Principle 3: Provide explainability for AI decisions affecting individuals (technical and process-level)
Principle 4: Inform individuals when they are interacting with an AI system
Principle 4: Provide accessible mechanisms for individuals to raise concerns about AI-based decisions
Self-Assessment Guide: Complete 61-question self-assessment to identify governance gaps and prioritise improvements
full_name: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework, Second Edition (2020)

short_name: Senegal Personal Data Protection Law 2008
max_penalty: Up to XOF 10,000,000 (~$17,000) and 5 years imprisonment
summary: One of West Africa's earliest and most comprehensive personal data protection laws. Establishes the CDP as an independent supervisory authority and serves as an ECOWAS reference framework. Provides five data protection principles, mandatory CDP declaration or authorization, sensitive data categories, data subject rights (information, access, rectification, opposition), cross-border transfer restrictions, and criminal penalties.
key_obligations: Declare processing activities to CDP or obtain prior authorization for sensitive/high-risk processing
Comply with five data protection principles
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or legal authority
Provide data subject rights (information, access, rectification, opposition)
Implement technical and organizational security measures
Maintain data confidentiality among staff
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
full_name: Senegal Law No. 2008-12 on the Protection of Personal Data

short_name: Tanzania Personal Data Protection Act 2022
max_penalty: Up to TZS 50 million (~$19,000) or 5 years imprisonment
summary: Tanzania's first comprehensive personal data protection law establishing the Personal Data Protection Commission. Incorporates modern data protection concepts including nine principles, data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection), DPO requirements, DPIA obligations for high-risk processing, sensitive data categories, mandatory breach notification, and cross-border transfer rules.
key_obligations: Register with PDPC as data controller or processor
Comply with nine data protection principles
Appoint a DPO for public bodies and high-risk processing
Conduct DPIAs for high-risk processing activities
Provide data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection)
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or legal authority
Notify PDPC and affected individuals of significant breaches
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection or approved safeguards
full_name: Tanzania Personal Data Protection Act 2022

short_name: Uganda Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019
max_penalty: Up to UGX 250 million (~$67,000) or 10 years imprisonment for aggravated offenses
summary: Uganda's primary data protection law implementing the constitutional right to privacy under Article 27. Establishes the Personal Data Protection Office under NITA-U, enshrines six data protection principles, provides data subject rights including access, correction, deletion, and objection, protects sensitive data categories including biometric and health data, and mandates breach notification.
key_obligations: Register data collectors, processors, and controllers with PDPO
Comply with six data protection principles
Implement technical and organizational security measures
Respond to data subject access, correction, deletion, and objection requests
Obtain explicit consent or legal basis for processing sensitive data
Notify PDPO of significant personal data breaches
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
full_name: Uganda Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019

short_name: UN Global Digital Compact
max_penalty: Non-binding intergovernmental agreement; no penalty regime.
summary: The Global Digital Compact was adopted by the UN General Assembly on September 22, 2024 as part of the Summit of the Future. It establishes a framework for global digital cooperation covering AI governance, data flows, digital public infrastructure, and internet fragmentation. On AI, it calls for an international AI governance dialogue, supports the establishment of an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, and promotes human rights–based approaches to AI. It also endorses the establishment of a UN AI Advisory Body follow-up mechanism.
key_obligations: States to promote safe, secure and trustworthy AI systems
Establish Independent International Scientific Panel on AI
States to develop national AI strategies aligned with human rights
Promote digital inclusion and reduce digital divides
Support global data governance frameworks
full_name: United Nations Global Digital Compact (September 2024)

short_name: California SB 1047
max_penalty: Up to 10% of model training cost (non-willful); up to 30% of training cost (knowing/reckless) — vetoed, never enacted
summary: The most debated AI safety bill of 2024. Would have required California-based developers of frontier AI models (trained with ≥10²⁶ FLOPs or costing over $100M) to implement safety and security programs, conduct pre-deployment hazardous capability evaluations, maintain kill-switch capability, and submit to annual third-party audits. Also proposed a new Frontier Model Division within the California Department of Technology. Passed the California Legislature on August 28, 2024. Vetoed by Governor Newsom on September 29, 2024 as technically flawed and harmful to California AI innovation.
key_obligations: Implement written safety and security program before training any covered model
Conduct pre-deployment hazardous capability evaluations (CBRN, critical infrastructure, cyberweapons)
Maintain ability to fully shut down all covered models (kill switch)
Protect model weights against unauthorized access with NIST-standard cybersecurity
Submit to annual third-party audits by AG-certified auditors
Retain safety testing records for at least three years
Report critical safety incidents to new Frontier Model Division
full_name: California SB 1047 — Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act (vetoed)

short_name: DHS AI Critical Infrastructure Safety Guidelines
max_penalty: Guidance document; no penalty regime.
summary: Issued pursuant to the Biden AI Executive Order (EO 14110), DHS published this Roles and Responsibilities Framework assigning accountability across the AI supply chain for critical infrastructure sectors. It defines responsibilities for cloud and compute providers, AI developers, critical infrastructure owners/operators, and civil society. The framework addresses AI-specific risks to the 16 critical infrastructure sectors and provides sector-specific guidance.
key_obligations: Cloud and compute providers: implement baseline AI safety practices for infrastructure they provide
AI developers: design AI with safety-by-design principles and provide documentation to downstream deployers
Critical infrastructure owners/operators: conduct AI risk assessments before deployment
All actors: report AI-related safety incidents to CISA
full_name: DHS Guidelines for AI Safety and Security in Critical Infrastructure (April 2024)

short_name: EO 13960 (Trump Trustworthy AI EO)
max_penalty: None — Executive order; no penalty regime. Directed agency action only.
summary: EO 13960, signed by President Trump on December 3, 2020, established nine principles to guide all federal agencies in the design, development, acquisition, and use of artificial intelligence. The principles — lawful, purposeful and performance-driven, accurate and reliable, safe and secure, understandable, responsible and traceable, regularly monitored, transparent, and accountable — were intended to promote trustworthy AI across the federal government and foster public trust. Agencies were required to submit plans documenting how their existing AI use cases align with these principles. Implemented in conjunction with the AI in Government Act of 2020 and the NIST AI standards effort.
key_obligations: Federal agencies must design, develop, acquire, and use AI consistently with nine enumerated trustworthy AI principles
Agencies must designate officials responsible for AI governance and submit consistency plans to OMB within 60 days
Each agency must inventory AI use cases and document alignment with the nine principles
NIST to develop standards and guidelines for trustworthy AI consistent with the principles
Agencies must ensure AI applications are regularly tested and monitored against the nine principles
full_name: Executive Order 13960 — Promoting the Use of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in the Federal Government

short_name: NSPM-33 (R&D Security Policy)
max_penalty: Presidential memorandum; violations may result in loss of federal funding. No standalone criminal penalties.
summary: NSPM-33, issued January 14, 2021 (final days of Trump administration), establishes national security policy for federally-funded R&D. It addresses the risk of foreign governments — particularly China — accessing US research through talent recruitment programs, undisclosed affiliations, and research theft. Key requirements: disclosure of foreign funding/affiliations for all federally-funded researchers, standardized disclosure forms across agencies, export controls alignment, and agency-specific research security programs. The memo was implemented through NSPM-33 Implementation Guidance (January 2022) issued by the Biden OSTP.
key_obligations: Federally-funded researchers must disclose all foreign affiliations and funding sources
Federal agencies must standardize disclosure and certification requirements for research grants
Agencies must develop research security programs covering cybersecurity, export control, and foreign travel
Institutions receiving federal R&D funding must implement research security training
full_name: National Security Presidential Memorandum 33 (NSPM-33) — National Security Strategy for United States Government-Supported Research and Development

short_name: OMB M-24-10 (Federal AI Governance Memo)
max_penalty: None — OMB memorandum; non-compliance triggers agency reporting obligations and potential cessation of non-compliant AI use. No fines.
summary: OMB M-24-10, issued March 28, 2024 under the Biden administration, was the primary binding governance framework for federal agency use of AI. It required each CFO Act agency to designate a Chief AI Officer (CAIO) within 60 days, establish an AI governance board, maintain an annual public inventory of AI use cases, and develop enterprise AI strategies. The memo established mandatory minimum risk-management practices for 'rights-impacting AI' and 'safety-impacting AI' — requiring AI impact assessments, ongoing monitoring, and human oversight before such systems could be used. Agencies that could not comply by December 1, 2024 were required to cease using non-compliant systems. M-24-10 was rescinded and replaced by OMB M-25-21 on April 3, 2025, by the Trump administration.
key_obligations: Each CFO Act agency must designate a Chief AI Officer (CAIO) within 60 days
Agencies must establish an AI governance board including senior legal, privacy, IT, procurement, and mission officials
Agencies must maintain an annual public-facing inventory of AI use cases
Each agency must develop an enterprise AI strategy covering responsible AI adoption
Before using rights-impacting or safety-impacting AI, agencies must complete an AI impact assessment documenting purpose, expected benefits, risks, data quality, and mitigation measures
Agencies must conduct ongoing human monitoring of rights-impacting and safety-impacting AI post-deployment
Agencies must regularly evaluate risks and mitigate emerging harms from safety- and rights-impacting AI
Agencies unable to comply with minimum practices by December 1, 2024 must cease using the non-compliant AI system
Agencies must develop and publish compliance plans within 180 days, updated biennially
full_name: OMB Memorandum M-24-10: Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence

short_name: OMB M-25-21 (Federal AI Governance)
max_penalty: Administrative guidance; no penalty regime. Binding on federal agencies.
summary: OMB Memorandum M-25-21, issued by OMB Director Russell Vought, replaces the Biden-era M-24-10 and reframes federal AI governance around innovation acceleration while maintaining risk management. It retains the Chief AI Officer (CAIO) structure, requires agencies to designate high-impact AI use cases, mandates risk management for rights-and-safety-impacting AI, and emphasizes domestic AI leadership. Unlike M-24-10, it removes requirements for equity-focused AI impact assessments and deemphasizes civil rights considerations.
key_obligations: Each Executive Branch agency must designate a Chief AI Officer (CAIO)
Agencies must maintain AI use case inventories
High-impact AI uses (rights or safety affecting) require documented risk management
Agencies must report annually on AI use and governance progress to OMB
full_name: OMB Memorandum M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of Artificial Intelligence through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust

short_name: OSTP Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (2022)
max_penalty: None — Non-binding policy framework; no penalty regime.
summary: The OSTP Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, released on October 4, 2022, is a non-binding framework articulating five principles for the design, development, and deployment of automated systems in the United States: (1) safe and effective systems, (2) algorithmic discrimination protections, (3) data privacy, (4) notice and explanation, and (5) human alternatives, consideration, and fallback. Published by the Biden White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), the Blueprint is intended to guide both government and private sector actors and to inform future legislation and rulemaking. It does not carry the force of law and creates no enforceable rights.
key_obligations: Systems should be tested, assessed, and monitored for safety and effectiveness before and after deployment (non-binding)
Systems should be designed to prevent algorithmic discrimination based on protected characteristics
Data collection should be limited to what is necessary; users should have meaningful consent over data use
Users should be notified when automated systems make or inform decisions affecting them and receive plain-language explanations
Users should be able to opt out of automated systems and access a human alternative where reasonably practicable
full_name: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights — Making Automated Systems Work for the American People (OSTP, 2022)

short_name: Maryland SB 936 (High-Risk AI Consumer Protection)
summary: Maryland SB 936 (2025), with House companion HB 1331, would have required developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to use reasonable care to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination. Developers would have been required to document intended uses, limitations, and risks; deployers would have been required to implement risk management policies, conduct pre-deployment impact assessments, and notify consumers when high-risk AI is used in consequential decisions affecting them. The Attorney General would have enforced the act. Both bills died in committee during the 2025 regular session without reaching a floor vote. Note: sometimes cited in secondary sources under the bill numbers SB 1050/HB 1457, which do not correspond to AI legislation in the 2025 Maryland session.
key_obligations: Developers of high-risk AI must document intended uses, known limitations, and foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination
Deployers must implement written risk management policies before deploying high-risk AI
Deployers must conduct impact assessments prior to deployment of high-risk AI
Consumers must be notified when high-risk AI is used in consequential decisions affecting them
Consumers have the right to correct personal data and appeal adverse AI-driven decisions
Attorney General may enforce; no private right of action
full_name: Maryland SB 936 — Artificial Intelligence — Consumer Protections (failed)

short_name: Virginia SB 1090 (High-Risk AI Act)
summary: Virginia’s proposed comprehensive AI consumer protection statute, closely modeled on Colorado SB 24-205 (Colorado AI Act). Would have required developers and deployers of ‘high-risk AI’ systems used in consequential decisions (employment, housing, credit, healthcare, education, insurance) to conduct algorithmic impact assessments, notify consumers of AI use, provide human review rights, and use reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination. Passed both chambers of the Virginia General Assembly in early 2025. Vetoed by Governor Glenn Youngkin in April 2025 on grounds of regulatory burden and innovation concerns.
key_obligations: Deployers must use reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination in consequential decisions
Complete documented algorithmic impact assessment before deployment and annually thereafter
Notify consumers when high-risk AI is used in a consequential decision
Provide opportunity for human review and appeal of AI-assisted consequential decisions
Developers must provide deployers with documentation on intended uses, limitations, and performance data
Maintain impact assessment records for at least three years
full_name: Virginia SB 1090 — High-Risk Artificial Intelligence Developer and Deployer Act

short_name: Uruguay Automated Decision Decree 2020
max_penalty: Administrative penalties under Law 18.331 framework
summary: Uruguay's regulation on automated individual decision-making, requiring meaningful human intervention for decisions significantly affecting individuals based solely on automated processing. Provides rights to human review, explanation of algorithmic logic, and DPIAs for high-risk automated processing. One of Latin America's most advanced AI-specific data protection rules.
key_obligations: Provide meaningful human intervention for significant automated decisions upon request
Provide intelligible explanation of logic and criteria underlying automated decisions
Conduct DPIAs for high-risk automated decision-making systems
Inform data subjects when they are subject to automated decision-making
Prohibit automated decisions based solely on sensitive data categories unless exceptions apply
Maintain records of automated decision-making systems and their logic
Implement safeguards to prevent discriminatory or arbitrary outcomes
full_name: Uruguay Decree No. 64/020 — Automated Individual Decision-Making

short_name: Uruguay Data Protection Law 2008
max_penalty: Fines and criminal penalties; URCDP may order suspension of processing
summary: Uruguay's primary data protection law and the first outside Europe to receive EU adequacy recognition (2012). Establishes the URCDP as supervisory authority, provides seven data protection principles, ARCO rights (access, rectification, cancellation, opposition), habeas data judicial action, mandatory database registration, sensitive data categories, and cross-border transfer restrictions.
key_obligations: Register all personal data databases with URCDP
Comply with seven data protection principles
Implement lawful processing basis for all personal data processing
Protect sensitive data categories with explicit consent or legal authority
Provide data subject ARCO rights (access, rectification, cancellation, opposition)
Implement appropriate security measures
Restrict cross-border transfers to countries with adequate protection
full_name: Uruguay Law No. 18.331 — Protection of Personal Data and Habeas Data Action

short_name: Zimbabwe Cybersecurity and Data Protection Act 2021
max_penalty: Up to USD 15,000 fine or 10 years imprisonment for serious offenses
summary: Zimbabwe's combined cybersecurity and data protection framework in a single statute. Establishes POTRAZ as the data protection supervisory authority and the Cybersecurity Centre for operational cybersecurity functions. Provides eight data protection principles, data subject rights, sensitive data protections, breach notification obligations, critical infrastructure protection requirements, and cybercrime offenses.
key_obligations: Register data controllers with POTRAZ
Comply with eight data protection principles
Implement appropriate security measures
Provide data subject rights (access, rectification, objection, erasure)
Protect sensitive data categories including biometric data
Notify POTRAZ and data subjects of significant breaches
Comply with critical infrastructure cybersecurity standards
full_name: Zimbabwe Cybersecurity and Data Protection Act, 2021

short_name: Alabama HB 365 — AI Labor and Employment Study Act
full_name: Alabama House Bill 365 — Artificial Intelligence Labor and Employment Study
summary: Requires a study on the effects of artificial intelligence on labor and employment in Alabama. Examines AI impacts on workforce, education, and job training.
key_obligations: State agency must study effects of AI on labor and employment
Report findings to legislature on AI workforce impacts

short_name: Arizona HB 2175 — AI Prior Authorization (Health)
full_name: Arizona House Bill 2175 — Claims and Prior Authorization — AI Restrictions
summary: Restricts the use of AI systems in health insurance prior authorization decisions. Requires human oversight for AI-driven coverage determinations and gives patients recourse when AI systems deny claims.
key_obligations: AI prior authorization decisions require human review
Insurers must disclose when AI is used in coverage determinations
Patients have right to appeal AI-driven denials

short_name: Arizona HB 2342 — AI/Blockchain Governance
full_name: Arizona House Bill 2342 — Blockchain Technology and AI Oversight
summary: Establishes governance framework for government and private sector use of blockchain technology and AI systems in Arizona. Addresses oversight, interoperability, and accountability.
key_obligations: Government agencies must follow AI/blockchain governance standards
Oversight committee reviews technology implementations

short_name: Arizona HB 2678 — AI-Generated CSAM Prohibition
full_name: Arizona House Bill 2678 — Indistinguishable Visual Depiction — AI-Generated Child Exploitation Material
summary: Criminalizes the creation, distribution, and possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM). Expands the definition of prohibited visual depictions to include AI-generated images indistinguishable from real minors.
key_obligations: Prohibition on creating, distributing or possessing AI-generated CSAM
Criminal penalties for violations

short_name: Arkansas HB 1876 — Generative AI Training Data and Content Disclosure
full_name: Arkansas House Bill 1876 — Model Training and Content Generated by Generative AI
summary: Requires disclosure when content is generated by AI models and establishes transparency requirements for AI training data. Mandates labeling of AI-generated content for commercial use.
key_obligations: AI-generated commercial content must be labeled as such
Disclosure of training data sources for publicly deployed models
Prohibition on deceptive AI-generated content

short_name: Arkansas HB 1877 — AI-Generated CSAM Criminal Offenses
full_name: Arkansas House Bill 1877 — Criminal Offenses — AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Material
summary: Establishes criminal offenses for creating, distributing, or possessing AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Applies existing CSAM laws to synthetic and AI-generated depictions.
key_obligations: Creation or distribution of AI-generated CSAM is a criminal offense
Criminal penalties align with those for traditional CSAM

short_name: Arkansas HB 1958 — Government AI Policy Requirement
full_name: Arkansas House Bill 1958 — Public Entities Required to Create AI Use Policy
summary: Requires Arkansas state agencies and public entities to establish written policies governing the use of artificial intelligence. Policies must address accountability, transparency, and appropriate use limitations.
key_obligations: All state agencies must adopt written AI use policies
Policies must address prohibited uses, human oversight, and accountability
Annual reporting on AI policy compliance

short_name: Arkansas SB 612 — Social Media AI Private Right of Action
full_name: Arkansas Senate Bill 612 — Private Right of Action Against Social Media Platforms for AI Harms
summary: Establishes a private right of action for individuals harmed by AI systems deployed on social media platforms. Allows affected persons to sue platforms for AI-related harms including algorithmic manipulation and non-consensual AI-generated content.
key_obligations: Social media platforms liable for AI-caused harms
Private right of action for affected individuals
Platforms must respond to removal requests for harmful AI content

short_name: Colorado SB 288 — AI Intimate Digital Depictions
full_name: Colorado Senate Bill 288 — Intimate Digital Depictions — Criminal and Civil Actions
summary: Establishes criminal and civil liability for creating or distributing non-consensual AI-generated intimate images of identifiable individuals. Creates private right of action for victims.
key_obligations: Criminal penalties for creating or distributing non-consensual AI intimate images
Civil right of action for victims
Takedown obligations for platforms

short_name: Delaware HB 16 — Artificial Intelligence Commission
full_name: Delaware House Bill 16 — Establishment of Artificial Intelligence Commission
summary: Establishes an Artificial Intelligence Commission in Delaware to study, advise, and make recommendations on AI policy, regulation, and government use. Commission to report findings and recommend legislation.
key_obligations: AI Commission established to study AI risks and benefits
Commission produces annual reports and legislative recommendations

short_name: Hawaii SB 742 — Data Sharing and AI Governance Working Group
full_name: Hawaii Senate Bill 742 — Data Sharing and Governance Working Group
summary: Establishes a working group to study and recommend policies for data sharing and AI governance in Hawaii state government. Focuses on interoperability, privacy protections, and AI accountability.
key_obligations: Working group studies data sharing and AI governance
Recommendations to legislature on AI policies

short_name: Indiana SB 5 — AI Software Use in Government
full_name: Indiana Senate Bill 5 — Artificial Intelligence Software Use
summary: Regulates the use of artificial intelligence software by Indiana state agencies. Establishes requirements for procurement, transparency, accountability, and oversight of AI systems used in government operations.
key_obligations: State agencies must register AI systems used in operations
AI procurement must meet transparency and accountability standards
Annual review of government AI systems

short_name: Kansas SB 186 — AI Evidence in Criminal Proceedings
full_name: Kansas Senate Bill 186 — Sworn Testimony and Probable Cause — AI-Generated Evidence
summary: Establishes standards for the admissibility and handling of AI-generated evidence in Kansas criminal proceedings. Addresses authentication requirements for AI-generated images, recordings, and documents used in sworn testimony and probable cause determinations.
key_obligations: AI-generated evidence must be authenticated before admission
Disclosure required when AI-generated content is submitted in proceedings
Standards for challenging AI evidence

short_name: Louisiana HB 178 — AI in Civil Procedure
full_name: Louisiana House Bill 178 — Civil Procedure — Artificial Intelligence Use
summary: Addresses the use of AI in Louisiana civil legal proceedings, including authentication requirements for AI-generated evidence and disclosure obligations when AI tools are used in legal practice.
key_obligations: Disclosure when AI tools are used in court proceedings
Authentication standards for AI-generated evidence
Judicial oversight of AI-assisted legal processes

short_name: Maine HP 1303a — Non-Consensual AI Intimate Images
full_name: Maine House Paper 1303a — Threatened Unauthorized Dissemination of Private Intimate Images
summary: Criminalizes threatened or actual non-consensual dissemination of intimate images, including AI-generated deepfake images. Creates criminal penalties and civil remedies for victims of non-consensual intimate imagery.
key_obligations: Criminal prohibition on threatening to distribute or distributing non-consensual intimate images
Applies to AI-generated deepfakes of real individuals
Civil right of action for victims

short_name: Maryland SB 705 — DoIT AI Governance
full_name: Maryland Senate Bill 705 — Department of Information Technology — AI Governance Framework
summary: Directs Maryland's Department of Information Technology to develop and implement an AI governance framework for state agencies. Establishes standards for AI procurement, risk assessment, and accountability in government operations.
key_obligations: DoIT must develop AI governance framework
State agencies must adhere to AI standards
Risk assessment required for new AI deployments
Annual reporting on AI use

short_name: Maryland HB 956 — Workgroup on AI Implementation
full_name: Maryland House Bill 956 — Workgroup on Artificial Intelligence Implementation
summary: Establishes a workgroup to study the implementation of AI in private sector industries in Maryland. Examines economic impacts, workforce displacement risks, and best practices for responsible AI deployment.
key_obligations: Workgroup studies AI implementation in private sector
Report with recommendations submitted to legislature

short_name: Minnesota HF 2432 — AI in Public Safety
full_name: Minnesota House File 2432 — Public Safety — Artificial Intelligence Use
summary: Regulates the use of AI tools by Minnesota law enforcement and public safety agencies. Addresses facial recognition, predictive policing algorithms, and AI-generated evidence. Creates accountability requirements and prohibits certain AI uses in criminal proceedings.
key_obligations: Law enforcement must document and audit AI system use
Facial recognition restricted to specific circumstances
Prohibition on AI-generated CSAM
Human review required for AI-assisted criminal decisions

short_name: Montana HB 82 — AI-Generated CSAM
full_name: Montana House Bill 82 — Crimes Against Children — AI-Generated Sexual Exploitation Material
summary: Extends Montana's child sexual exploitation laws to cover AI-generated and synthetic images of minors. Criminalizes creation, distribution, and possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material with penalties equivalent to traditional CSAM.
key_obligations: AI-generated CSAM prohibited and criminal
Penalties equivalent to traditional CSAM
Law enforcement can prosecute AI-generated child exploitation material

short_name: Montana HB 178 — Government AI Use Policy
full_name: Montana House Bill 178 — Government Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems
summary: Establishes rules for Montana state agencies using AI systems in government operations. Requires disclosure to citizens when AI is used in government decisions affecting them, and mandates human oversight for consequential determinations.

summary: Creates criminal offenses related to deceptive and injurious media in the course of election campaigns, provides that it shall be unlawful for a person to purposely injure a candidate for office in the State by creating or causing to be created a deep fake and publishing, distributing, or causing to be published or distributed the deep fake a specified number of days before the date of the general election and on the date of the general election with the knowledge that the communication was a deep fake.

short_name: Arkansas H 1283 — Division of Elementary
full_name: Arkansas H 1283 — Division of Elementary
summary: Requires the division of elementary and secondary education to include digital media standards in kindergarten through grade twelve library media standards.

short_name: Arkansas H 1297 — Artificial Intelligence Algorithms
full_name: Arkansas H 1297 — Artificial Intelligence Algorithms
summary: Concerns artificial intelligence, algorithms, and other automated technologies, regulates certain practices of healthcare insurers.

short_name: Arkansas H 1518 — Offense of Creating Distributing Possessing or Viewing
full_name: Arkansas H 1518 — Offense of Creating Distributing Possessing or Viewing
summary: Creates the offense of creating, distributing, possessing, or viewing artificial intelligence-generated matter depicting sexually explicit conduct involving a child.

short_name: Arkansas H 1529 — Deepfake Visual Material of a Sexual Nature
full_name: Arkansas H 1529 — Deepfake Visual Material of a Sexual Nature
summary: Concerns deepfake visual material of a sexual nature, creates the criminal offense of unlawful creation and distribution of deepfake visual material, establishes a cause of action for unlawful creation of deepfake visual material, provides that engaging in sexual contact, sexual intercourse, deviate sexual activity, or sexually explicit conduct such that an ordinary person viewing the deepfake visual material would conclude that the depiction is of the identifiable person engaging in sexual contact.

short_name: Arkansas H 1726 — Arkansas Kids Online Safety Act
full_name: Arkansas H 1726 — Arkansas Kids Online Safety Act
summary: Creates the Arkansas Kids Online Safety Act, provides that a covered platform shall take reasonable measures in the design and operation of any product, service, or feature that the covered platform knows is used by minors to avoid any heightened risk of harm to minors caused by such product, service, or feature, including without limitation the mental health disorders, consistent with evidence-informed medical information.

short_name: Arkansas H 1816 — Healthcare Providers
full_name: Arkansas H 1816 — Healthcare Providers
summary: Prohibits healthcare providers and healthcare insurers from using artificial intelligence in the delivery of healthcare services or the generation of medical records unless certain requirements are met.

short_name: Arkansas H 1823 — Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Nonconsensual Edits
full_name: Arkansas H 1823 — Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Nonconsensual Edits
summary: Establishes the disrupt explicit forged images and nonconsensual edits act of 2025, clarifies the rights for an individual affected by nonconsensual activities involving intimate digital forgeries.

short_name: California S 300 — Companion Chatbots
full_name: California S 300 — Companion Chatbots
summary: Require a companion chatbot operator to take the above actions when it has constructive knowledge that a user is a minor. Requires an operator to prevent its companion chatbot from producing or facilitating the exchange of any sexually explicit material or proposing sexually explicit conduct.

short_name: California A 412 — Generative Artificial Intelligence: Training Data
full_name: California A 412 — Generative Artificial Intelligence: Training Data
summary: Relates to copyrighted materials. Requires a developer of a generative artificial intelligence model to document any covered materials that the developer knows were used by the developer to train the model. Requires the developer to make available a mechanism on the developer's website allowing a rights owner to submit a request for information. Authorizes a rights owner who complies with specified requirements for submitting a request that is not provided with information to bring a civil action.

short_name: California S 430 — Local Agencies: Automated Decision Systems
full_name: California S 430 — Local Agencies: Automated Decision Systems
summary: Imposes certain restrictions on the use of an automated decision system by a local agency to confer supportive services, permits, or licenses. Includes a prohibition on using an output from the system as the sole basis for an adverse eligibility or benefit determination affecting a natural person, except as specified. Requires the local agency to verify the accuracy of the system's outputs and to promote nondiscrimination in its use.

short_name: California S 574 — Generative Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California S 574 — Generative Artificial Intelligence
summary: Obligates an attorney who uses generative artificial intelligence to practice law to ensure that confidential personal identifying, or other nonpublic information, is not entered into a public generative artificial intelligence system. Requires an attorney to ensure that reasonable steps are taken to verify the accuracy of generative artificial intelligence material and to correct any erroneous or hallucinated output in any material used by the attorney.

short_name: California S 607 — California Institutes for Science and Innovation
full_name: California S 607 — California Institutes for Science and Innovation
summary: Provides that existing law authorizes the Regents of the University of California to establish 4 California Institutes for Science and Innovation at separate campuses of the University of California for specified purposes. Provides that existing law authorizes the concentration of each institute to include, among other concentrations, medicine, bioengineering, or space. Authorizes the concentration of an institute to include artificial intelligence.

short_name: California S 719 — Department of Technology: Inventory
full_name: California S 719 — Department of Technology: Inventory
summary: Provides that existing law, until January 1, 2029, requires the Department of Technology to annually submit to certain legislative committees a report regarding a specified required comprehensive inventory of all high-risk automated decision systems that have been, or are being, used, developed, or procured by a state agency. Extends that reporting requirement until January 1, 2032.

short_name: California S 813 — California AI Standards and Safety Commission
full_name: California S 813 — California AI Standards and Safety Commission
summary: Require the agency to establish the California AI Standards and Safety Commission and would provide for its membership. Requires the commission to take certain actions related to the safety of artificial intelligence, including maintaining formal liaison relationships with state agencies deploying or procuring artificial intelligence, providing artificial intelligence technical expertise and artificial intelligence risk assessment.

short_name: California S 867 — Toys: Companion Chatbots
full_name: California S 867 — Toys: Companion Chatbots
summary: Prohibits, until 1/1/2031, the manufacture, sale, exchange, possession with intent to sell or exchange, and exposition or offer for sale or exchange to a retailer a toy, as defined, that includes a companion chatbot, and would make violations of the bill subject to the same civil liability as violations of the provisions applicable to operators of companion chatbots in the above-described paragraph.

short_name: California S 903 — Mental Health Professionals: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California S 903 — Mental Health Professionals: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Regulates the use of artificial intelligence by licensed professionals providing psychotherapy services. Prohibits an individual, corporation, or entity from using artificial intelligence to record or transcribe psychotherapeutic communications or sessions or to triage or screen a person for the need for psychotherapy services unless the patient or their authorized representative is informed that artificial intelligence will be used and provides consent.

short_name: California S 916 — Civil Actions: Housing Development Projects
full_name: California S 916 — Civil Actions: Housing Development Projects
summary: Provides that existing law provides that in a civil action brought by a plaintiff to challenge a housing development project that meets or exceeds the requirements for low or moderate income housing, a defendant may seek an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish an undertaking as security for costs and damages. Provides that existing law authorizes the court to limit the amount of the undertaking or to decline that requirement under certain conditions. Applies provisions to a student housing development.

short_name: California S 928 — California State University: Faculty Employees
full_name: California S 928 — California State University: Faculty Employees
summary: Provides that existing law requires certain community college employees to be a person who meets specified minimum qualifications. Requires the instructor of record for a course of instruction to be a person who meets the rule provided by the Trustees of the California State University to serve as a faculty employee teaching credit instruction or noncredit instruction.

short_name: California S 947 — Employment: Automated Decision Systems
full_name: California S 947 — Employment: Automated Decision Systems
summary: Requires an employer that primarily relied upon an ADS to make a disciplinary, termination, or deactivation decision to provide the affected worker with a written postuse notice, as specified.

short_name: California S 951 — Employment: Technological Displacement: Notice
full_name: California S 951 — Employment: Technological Displacement: Notice
summary: Requires an employer to provide a written technology hiring disruption notice to the Employment Development Department and the local workforce investment board when it executes a technological cessation in hiring directly and primarily due to the adoption of artificial intelligence or other automating technology. Imposes various reporting requirements on the Employment Development Department.

short_name: California S 1000 — California AI Transparency Act
full_name: California S 1000 — California AI Transparency Act
summary: Provides that the California AI Transparency Act requires a covered provider to make available an AI detection tool at no cost to the user. Provides that existing law requires a covered provider to include a certain latent disclosure in AI generated image, video, or audio content, or content that is any combination thereof, created by the covered providers GenAI system. Requires a covered provider to include in the latent disclosure whether the content is generated or modified by artificial intelligence.

short_name: California S 1011 — Energy: Utility Infrastructure AI Safety
full_name: California S 1011 — Energy: Utility Infrastructure AI Safety
summary: Requires every public utility to furnish and maintain adequate, efficient, just, and reasonable service, instrumentalities, equipment, and facilities, as are necessary to promote the safety, health, comfort, and convenience of its customers, its employees, and the public. Requires the commission, on or before a specified date, to adopt standards for an electrical or gas corporation's use of artificial intelligence models, as provided.

short_name: California S 1015 — Crimes: Minors
full_name: California S 1015 — Crimes: Minors
summary: Makes any adult person who recruits, induces, coerces, or persuades a minor to commit an illegal act against another minor, or to solicit physical harm, sexual conduct, or images of an intimate body part, from another minor, or who utilizes a minor as a conduit of communication to facilitate any such acts guilty of a crime punishable either as a misdemeanor or a felony. Relates to images of an intimate body part that is produced by artificial intelligence and depicts the identity of another minor.

short_name: California S 1050 — False Advertising: Synthetic Digital Performers
full_name: California S 1050 — False Advertising: Synthetic Digital Performers
summary: Makes it an unlawful advertising practice for a person to create and cause to be published in an advertising medium an advertisement that includes a synthetic performer without a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the performer is synthetic. Prohibits an advertising medium from transmitting, distributing, displaying, airing, or otherwise making available an advertisement containing a synthetic performer if a court of competent jurisdiction has issued an order.

short_name: California S 1074 — Covered Provider: Goods and Services: Self Preferencing
full_name: California S 1074 — Covered Provider: Goods and Services: Self Preferencing
summary: Prohibits a covered provider from preferencing its own products, services, or lines of business over those of another business user, including manipulating the order of search results or rankings to favor the products or services of the covered provider. Prohibits a covered provider from restricting interoperability or data portability, including restricting a business user or consumer from obtaining a copy of their data in a useful and portable format. Relates to actions for civil or criminal penalties.

short_name: California S 1111 — Digital Replicas
full_name: California S 1111 — Digital Replicas
summary: Provides that existing law creates a civil cause of action against any person who knowingly uses the name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness of another person, without their consent, for specified purposes. Clarifies that a voice or likeness includes a digital replica. Clarifies that false impersonation includes the use of a digital replica with the intent to impersonate another.

short_name: California S 1119 — Companion Chatbots: Childrens Safety
full_name: California S 1119 — Companion Chatbots: Childrens Safety
summary: Requires an operator of a companion chatbot to do various things with respect to child safety and companion chatbots, including annually performing and documenting a comprehensive risk assessment to identify any child safety risk posed by the design, configuration, and operation of the companion chatbot that assesses, among other things, the likelihood of a covered harm occurring to users.

short_name: California S 1133 — Pupil Instruction: Preventative Health Instruction
full_name: California S 1133 — Pupil Instruction: Preventative Health Instruction
summary: Provides for the Ready to Learn, Ready for Health Act. Requires, when the Health Education Framework for California Public Schools is next revised on or after the specified date, the Instructional Quality Commission to consider including information on evidence based preventative health instruction, including information on nutrition, food literacy, sleep, movement, stress management, and digital balance in an integrated manner that discusses these key health factors and the interrelationship between them.

short_name: California S 1142 — Digital Dignity Act
full_name: California S 1142 — Digital Dignity Act
summary: Enacts the Digital Dignity Act. Provides that subject to specified liability a person who, by distributing content with actual knowledge that the content includes a digital replica, is found guilty of violating a criminal provision for which false impersonation of another is a required element or is found liable in a civil action arising from the use or portrayal through a digital replica.

short_name: California S 1146 — Advertisement Claims: Health Related Consumer Products
full_name: California S 1146 — Advertisement Claims: Health Related Consumer Products
summary: Requires, subject to specified exceptions, a person who creates or causes to be created an advertisement that includes the image, audio, or video of a digital replica or synthetic performer depicted as a health care provider that is generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence or other computer technology to promote the sale of a health related consumer product or service to include a clear and conspicuous disclosure that no human health care provider is depicted.

short_name: California S 1159 — Artificial Intelligence: Transparency and Governance
full_name: California S 1159 — Artificial Intelligence: Transparency and Governance
summary: Specifies that, for purposes of the State Public Records Act, the Bagley Keene Open Meeting Act, the Ralph M. Brown Act, the Political Reform Act of 1974, the Administrative Procedure Act, and the California Environmental Quality Act, the terms person, interested person, participant, member of the public, and any other similar terms under each act referring to those who may engage with governmental agencies, do not include artificial intelligence.

short_name: California A 1159 — Student Personal Information
full_name: California A 1159 — Student Personal Information
summary: Applies the provisions of the K-12 Pupil Online Personal Information Protection Act and the Early Learning Personal Information Protection Act to an operator of a website, online service, online application, or mobile application with actual knowledge that the site, service, or application is used for the applicable school purposes and was designed or marketed for those purposes. Enacts the Higher Education Student Information Protection Act. Authorizes a harmed student or pupil to bring a civil action.

short_name: California S 1181 — Central Valley School Safety Coordination Pilot Program
full_name: California S 1181 — Central Valley School Safety Coordination Pilot Program
summary: Requires the Office of Emergency Services, in consultation with the State Department of Education, to establish the Central Valley School Safety Coordination Pilot Program for the purpose of studying and evaluating improved communication pathways between local educational agencies and regional fusion centers regarding credible safety threats affecting school communities.

short_name: California S 1217 — Nonconsensual Intimate Image Clearinghouse
full_name: California S 1217 — Nonconsensual Intimate Image Clearinghouse
summary: Requires the Department of Justice to establish the Nonconsensual Intimate Image Clearinghouse to allow individuals who were exploited in the State to submit a request for the removal of nonconsensual intimate images from covered platforms. Requires the department to transmit verified identifiers of images to covered platforms and require those platforms to remove verified matches within 48 hours of receipt and to prevent the images from being uploaded again.

short_name: California S 1248 — State Agencies: Automated Decision Systems
full_name: California S 1248 — State Agencies: Automated Decision Systems
summary: Imposes certain restrictions on the use of an automated decision system by a state agency to confer services, defined as, among other things, the issuance of professional licenses and provision of public benefits.

short_name: California S 1276 — Crimes: Sexual Exploitation of a Child
full_name: California S 1276 — Crimes: Sexual Exploitation of a Child
summary: Makes a person guilty of a misdemeanor or a felony if the person downloads, streams, or accesses through electronic or digital media material that depicts a person under 18 years of age engaged in an act of sexual conduct, except as specified.

short_name: California A 1337 — Information Practices Act of 1977
full_name: California A 1337 — Information Practices Act of 1977
summary: Provides that the Information Practices Act of 1977 prescribes a set of requirements, prohibitions, and remedies applicable to agencies with regard to their collection, storage, and disclosure of personal information. Prohibits an agency from using records containing personal information for any purpose or purposes other than the purpose or purposes for which that personal information was collected, except as required or authorized by State law.

short_name: California A 1609 — Customer Service Chatbots
full_name: California A 1609 — Customer Service Chatbots
summary: Prohibits a large private business from representing that a customer service chatbot is a human. Requires the large private business to provide certain disclosures if a reasonable person interacting with the chatbot would be misled to believe they are interacting with a human. Requires a large private business to provide customers with human customer service support and communications within a specified number of minutes of requesting human customer service.

short_name: California A 1651 — State Bar of California: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 1651 — State Bar of California: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Requires the State Bar to disclose, on its internet website, the use of artificial intelligence generated content in developing or administering State Bar examinations. Requires the State Bar to disclose, on the cover page of study materials, the use of artificial intelligence generated content in examination study material it, among other things, publishes or endorses.

short_name: California A 1705 — Pornographic Internet Websites
full_name: California A 1705 — Pornographic Internet Websites
summary: Requires an operator of a pornographic internet website, among other things, to exercise ordinary care and reasonable diligence to ensure that each instance of sexually explicit content displayed on the operator's pornographic internet website does not include a depicted individual. Defines terms, including depicted person, for its purposes.

short_name: California A 1766 — Health Curriculum Framework: Human Trafficking
full_name: California A 1766 — Health Curriculum Framework: Human Trafficking
summary: Requires the Instructional Quality Commission, when the health curriculum framework is next revised on or after January 1, 2027, to consider providing for inclusion in that framework recommendations related to school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools providing annual, developmentally appropriate lessons for each grade served by the local educational agency about how to prevent human trafficking and how to prevent exploitation for labor and services.

short_name: California A 1792 — Pupil Instruction: Health Framework: Sexual Health
full_name: California A 1792 — Pupil Instruction: Health Framework: Sexual Health
summary: Requires the Instructional Quality Commission, during the next revision of the publication �Health Framework for California Public Schools,� to consider including, and recommending for adoption by the State Board of Education, specific content related to sexual health instruction to educate pupils about dating abuse and digital violence.

short_name: California A 1883 — Workplace Surveillance Tools
full_name: California A 1883 — Workplace Surveillance Tools
summary: Prohibits an employer from using a workplace surveillance tool on workers for various purposes. Includes preventing compliance with laws or regulations, inferring information about workers engaging in a protected activity, making inferences about an individual's emotional state or based on their gait, or collecting neural data. Prohibits an employer from using facial recognition technology, unless it is used strictly to open a locked device or grant access to locked or secure areas.

short_name: California A 1898 — Workplace Artificial Intelligence Tools
full_name: California A 1898 — Workplace Artificial Intelligence Tools
summary: Requires an employer to provide a written notice to a worker that a workplace artificial intelligence tool was used to assist the employer in making employment related decisions or to surveil workers in the workplace. Requires the notice to be given to a worker within a specified time and requires the notice to contain specified information, including the specific employment related decisions likely to be affected by the use of the workplace AI tool. Provides for civil actions for damages.

short_name: California A 1946 — Reporting Mechanism: Child Sexual Abuse Material
full_name: California A 1946 — Reporting Mechanism: Child Sexual Abuse Material
summary: Makes a social media company liable to a depicted individual, as defined, for actual and statutory damages, as provided. Imposes a civil penalty on a noncomplying company to be collected in a civil action by certain public attorneys, including the Attorney General. Establishes the Survivor Support Fund within the state treasury and makes moneys in the fund available, upon appropriation by the Legislature, for grants by the State Victim Compensation Board to community-based organizations.

short_name: California A 1979 — Health Care Services: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 1979 — Health Care Services: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Requires a health facility, clinic, physician's office, or office or a group practice to ensure that no clinical decision, is based solely on the output of a clinical decision support system, as defined, and that a licensed health care professional exercises independent professional judgment when reviewing and approving a clinical decision that is based on the output of a clinical decision support system.

short_name: California A 1988 — Companion Chatbots: Crisis Interruption Pauses
full_name: California A 1988 — Companion Chatbots: Crisis Interruption Pauses
summary: Provides for the Preventing AI User Self Endangerment (PAUSE) Act. Requires an operator of companion chatbots to adopt and make publicly available a policy governing its protocol for identifying and responding to credible crisis expressions and, for each companion chatbot an operator makes available to users in the State, implement a system for monitoring and detecting credible crisis expressions in user conversations with companion chatbots.

short_name: California A 2023 — Companion Chatbots: Childrens Safety
full_name: California A 2023 — Companion Chatbots: Childrens Safety
summary: Relates to artificial intelligence. Requires an operator of a companion chatbot to, on or before specified date to do various things with respect to child safety and companion chatbots, including annually perform and document a comprehensive risk assessment to identify any child safety risk, as defined, posed by the design, configuration, and operation of the companion chatbot that assesses, among other things, the likelihood of a covered harm, as defined, occurring to child users.

short_name: California A 2025 — Tenancy: Digitally Altered Images: Disclosure
full_name: California A 2025 — Tenancy: Digitally Altered Images: Disclosure
summary: Requires a person who includes a digitally altered image, as defined, in an advertisement or other promotional material for the rental of real property to include a disclosure, as specified.

short_name: California A 2027 — Worker Data: Prohibitions: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 2027 — Worker Data: Prohibitions: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Prohibits an employer from using a workers personal information to train an artificial intelligence system to replicate, automate, or replace a workers job, and prohibits an employer from selling, disclosing, or otherwise providing access to a workers personal information to a third party for the purpose of training an AI system to replicate, automate, or replace a job. Authorizes a worker who suffered a violation to bring a civil action for damages, injunctive relief, punitive damages, and attorneys fees.

short_name: California A 2071 — Pupil Instruction: Digital Wellness
full_name: California A 2071 — Pupil Instruction: Digital Wellness
summary: Requires the State Department of Education, on or before a specified date, to develop a plan to expand mental health instruction in State public schools. Requires the department, on or before a specified date, to develop a plan to expand digital wellness instruction in the state public schools, as provided.

short_name: California A 2148 — Elementary and secondary education
full_name: California A 2148 — Elementary and secondary education
summary: Establishes a system of public elementary and secondary education in this state. Requires school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools employ personnel to provide instruction to and services for pupils in kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, at school sites throughout the state. Defines, for purposes of the Education Code, both a public school employee and a contractor providing services in a public school to mean a natural person.

short_name: California A 2169 — Social Media Platforms: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 2169 — Social Media Platforms: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Enacts the Digital Choice Act. Requires a social media company or a person that makes an artificial intelligence model available to a third party for use, modification, copying, or combination with other software, defined as a deployer, to allow a consumer to request a copy of the consumer's personal information, contextual data, and social graph and would require the social media company or deployer to respond to that request within five business days.

short_name: California A 2212 — Postsecondary Education: Sexual Harassment
full_name: California A 2212 — Postsecondary Education: Sexual Harassment
summary: Requires, in order to receive State funds for student financial assistance, the governing board of a community college district, the Trustees of the State University, the Regents of the University of California, and the governing boards of independent postsecondary educational institutions to update their sexual harassment policies to include, among other things, a list of organizations to assist students and employees with the removal of digitized sexually explicit material from digital platforms.

short_name: California A 2245 — Lubricants Waste: Packaging: Producer Responsibility
full_name: California A 2245 — Lubricants Waste: Packaging: Producer Responsibility
summary: Creates a producer responsibility program for lubricants waste that is not covered by the Oil Recycling Enhancement Act and packaging associated with lubricant products. Requires a producer responsibility organization to provide a convenient collection and management system. Requires the charge be set at an amount that is adequate to cover CalRecycle's and DTSC's actual and reasonable costs of administering and enforcing the program.

short_name: California A 2291 — Pupil Safety: Nonconsensual Artificial Intimate Images
full_name: California A 2291 — Pupil Safety: Nonconsensual Artificial Intimate Images
summary: Requires the State Department of Education to conduct a study on nonconsensual artificial intimate images involving pupils in the specified grades. Requires the study to include, among other things, a summary of the resources for schools regarding nonconsensual artificial intimate images and the effects of nonconsensual artificial intimate images on pupils.

short_name: California A 2392 — Public Postsecondary Education: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 2392 — Public Postsecondary Education: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Requires the California Community Colleges and the California State University, and requests the University of California, before providing a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) system to students, faculty, or staff, to as specified, convene a joint working group to present recommendations for procurement standards and training, which the bill would require to be submitted on or before a specified date.

short_name: California A 2403 — Income Tax: Credits: Commercial Production
full_name: California A 2403 — Income Tax: Credits: Commercial Production
summary: Excludes any commercial that is created entirely by generative artificial intelligence, as specified, or that utilizes generative artificial intelligence, automated technologies, or autonomous vehicles in a manner that replaces or diminishes the job functions customarily performed by a human worker in the production. Requires any bill authorizing a new tax expenditure to contain, among other things, specific goals, purposes, and objectives that the tax expenditure will achieve.

short_name: California A 2412 — State Agencies or Departments: Public Communications
full_name: California A 2412 — State Agencies or Departments: Public Communications
summary: Provides that existing law requires a State agency or department that utilizes generative artificial intelligence to directly communicate with a person regarding government services and benefits to ensure that those communications include a disclaimer that indicates to the person that the communication was generated by GenAI. Requires that disclaimer when a State agency or department communicates with the public.

short_name: California A 2431 — Downcoding Medical Claims
full_name: California A 2431 — Downcoding Medical Claims
summary: Provides that existing law sets forth requirements by which a health care service plan or health insurer reimburses a provider for health care services. Requires a determination to downcode a claim, which is the unilateral alteration by a payer of the service or procedure code submitted on a claim resulting in a lower payment, to include a documented review of the clinical information supporting the billed service.

short_name: California A 2487 — Artificial Intelligence: Education and Workforce
full_name: California A 2487 — Artificial Intelligence: Education and Workforce
summary: Enacts the Artificial Intelligence Education and Workforce Development Act to accomplish specified goals, including, among others, empowering and supporting community college instructors in using and deploying artificial intelligence responsibly in administrative and classroom settings, and strengthening the States AI and technology workforce pipeline by upskilling and educating all workers so they can benefit from AI.

short_name: California A 2504 — Community Colleges: Artificial Intelligence: Pilot
full_name: California A 2504 — Community Colleges: Artificial Intelligence: Pilot
summary: Relates to the Chancellor of the California Community Colleges. Requires the chancellors office to implement the Future of Creative Industries Pilot Program and to select up to a specified number of community college districts to participate in the pilot program. Requires the chancellors office to submit a report to the Legislature evaluating the effectiveness of the pilot program.

short_name: California A 2545 — Report: Labor Force Impact: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 2545 — Report: Labor Force Impact: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Establishes the State Artificial Intelligence Worker Impact Data Assessment Project and establishes the State Artificial Intelligence Worker Impact Data Assessment Project Advisory Panel in the Employment Development Department. Requires the EDD, in consultation with the advisory panel, to perform an assessment of data sources and collection methods regarding the use and impact of advanced artificial intelligence systems on the labor force. Requires the advisory panel to submit a report to the Legislature.

short_name: California A 2575 — Health Care Services: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 2575 — Health Care Services: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Requires a health facility, clinic, physician's office, or office of a group practice that uses or deploys a clinical decision support system, as defined, for patient care to provide written notice of required information to any licensed health care professional or other person using a clinical decision support system or viewing outputs from a clinical decision support system.

short_name: California A 2582 — Crimes: Prostitution
full_name: California A 2582 — Crimes: Prostitution
summary: Requires a person who commits prostitution with intent to receive compensation, money, or anything of value from another person to, for a first or second violation of those provisions, be offered a diversion program pursuant to specified provisions.

short_name: California A 2583 — Small Business Advocate: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 2583 — Small Business Advocate: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Enacts the AI for Main Street Act, which would require the Small Business Advocate to provide assistance to small businesses in evaluating artificial intelligence concerning operations, including by providing information, guidance, and training, developing training materials, and conducting outreach.

short_name: California A 2653 — State Contracts: Report: Modern Foundation Models
full_name: California A 2653 — State Contracts: Report: Modern Foundation Models
summary: Requires the Department of Industrial Relations, in consultation with the Department of Technology, to convene a Foundation Model Labor and Procurement Working Group consisting of 9 members, assess labor practices underlying the development of modern foundation models and associated artificial intelligence systems and develop recommendations regarding whether and how the state should incorporate labor standards into procurement decisions for foundation models and associated artificial intelligence systems.

short_name: California A 2656 — Public Employees: Notice: Artificial Intelligence
full_name: California A 2656 — Public Employees: Notice: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Relates to the deployment of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools by the State. Requires certain State and local public employers to provide written notice to a recognized employee organization at least a specified number of days before taking an action to develop, purchase, implement, or utilize GenAI to perform a service that is within the scope of work of the job classification represented by the recognized employee organization.

short_name: California A 2713 — California AI Transparency Act: System Provenance Data
full_name: California A 2713 — California AI Transparency Act: System Provenance Data
summary: Provides that the State AI Transparency Act requires a large online platform to detect whether any provenance data that is compliant with widely adopted specifications adopted by an established standards-setting body is embedded into or attached to content distributed on the large online platform. Requires a large online platform to detect any system provenance data that is embedded into, attached to, or associated with content.

short_name: California S 7 — Employment: Automated Decision Systems
full_name: California S 7 — Employment: Automated Decision Systems
summary: Requires an employer to provide a written notice that an automated decision system, for the purpose of making employment-related decisions, not including hiring, is in use at the workplace to all workers that will foreseeably be directly affected by the ADS. Requires an employer to notify a job applicant that the employer utilizes an ADS in hiring decisions, if the employer will use the ADS in making decisions for that position. Prohibits an employer from using an ADS that does certain functions.

short_name: California S 11 — Artificial Intelligence Technology
full_name: California S 11 — Artificial Intelligence Technology
summary: Defines various terms related to artificial intelligence and digital replication and clarifies that false impersonation includes the use of a digital replica with the intent to impersonate another for purposes of these and other criminal provisions. Requires a specified warning to be hyperlinked on any page or screen where the consumer may input a prompt to the technology and included in the terms and conditions for use of the technology.

short_name: California S 47 — February 2025 Bar Exam: Audit
full_name: California S 47 — February 2025 Bar Exam: Audit
summary: Relates to the State Bar Act. Requires the State Auditor to conduct an audit of the specified bar exam and to submit the audit as soon as possible to the Board of Trustees of the State Bar, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and to the Assembly and Senate Committees on Judiciary. Requires the State Bar to provide the California State Auditor with the funding necessary to cover the costs of the audit.

short_name: California S 52 — Housing Rental Terms: Algorithmic Devices
full_name: California S 52 — Housing Rental Terms: Algorithmic Devices
