full_name: Wisconsin S 400 — State and Local Government Electronic Device Use
summary: Concerns use restrictions on state and local government electronic devices.

short_name: Wisconsin A 415 — Use Restrictions on Electronic Devices
full_name: Wisconsin A 415 — Use Restrictions on Electronic Devices
summary: Concerns use restrictions on state and local government electronic devices.

short_name: Wyoming H 91 — Ban on Government Social Scoring With AI
full_name: Wyoming H 91 — Ban on Government Social Scoring With AI
summary: Relates to administration of the government, prohibits government entities from using artificial intelligence to calculate and assign social scores, prohibits government entities from using artificial intelligence to identify persons using biometric data or gathering of images, provides exceptions, provides definitions, provides for an effective date.

short_name: Wyoming D 149 — Misleading Synthetic Media
full_name: Wyoming D 149 — Misleading Synthetic Media
summary: Relates to consumer protection, prohibits the dissemination of synthetic media as specified, provides definitions, provides remedies, provides penalties, provides for an effective date.

short_name: California AB 2655 (Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act)
full_name: Defending Democracy from Deepfake Deception Act of 2024
max_penalty: Injunctive relief; civil damages
summary: Requires large online platforms to label AI-generated content depicting political candidates or measures within 120 days of an election. Prohibits platforms from distributing materially deceptive AI-generated images or audio of candidates that did not actually make the depicted statements. Platforms must add disclosure labels and may be ordered to remove unlabeled deepfakes.
notable: Platform-facing law; pairs with AB 2839 (individual liability) for a two-track California election deepfake regime.
legal_citation: Cal. Elec. Code §§ 20012–20013 (as added); AB 2655, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Large platforms must label AI-generated election content within 72 hours of being notified
Platforms must maintain mechanisms for candidates and campaigns to report unlabeled deepfakes
Applies within 120 days before an election

short_name: California SB 1120 (Health Insurance AI Utilization Review)
full_name: Physicians Make Decisions Act
enforcement_body: California Department of Managed Health Care
max_penalty: Administrative penalties; license actions
summary: Prohibits health insurers and managed care plans from using AI or algorithms as the sole basis for denying, delaying, or modifying health care coverage decisions. Requires that any coverage determination made or assisted by AI must be reviewed and approved by a licensed California physician or appropriate health care provider. Applies to utilization review processes.
notable: First California law directly restricting AI in health insurance coverage decisions; part of a national trend of state healthcare AI bills.
legal_citation: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1367.01 (as amended); Cal. Ins. Code § 10123.135 (as added); SB 1120, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: AI-assisted coverage decisions must be reviewed and signed off by a licensed physician
Insurers must document AI involvement in utilization review decisions
Patients retain rights to appeal AI-influenced denials through standard grievance procedures

short_name: California AB 2839 (Election Deepfakes — Individual Liability)
full_name: Elections: Deceptive AI Content
max_penalty: Actual damages; statutory damages up to $25,000 per violation; injunctive relief
summary: Prohibits distributing materially deceptive AI-generated images, audio, or video depicting candidates for office or election officials within 120 days of an election without a clear disclosure. Creates a private right of action for candidates, election officials, and the Attorney General. Enacted as urgency statute, effective immediately on signing.
notable: Urgency statute; companion to AB 2655 (platform obligations). Individual-level liability for election deepfakes.
legal_citation: Cal. Elec. Code §§ 20010–20011 (as added); AB 2839, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Must include clear disclosure when distributing AI-generated election content
Prohibition on materially deceptive deepfakes of candidates within 120-day election window
Candidates and AG may seek injunctions and damages

short_name: California AB 2355 (Political Ad AI Disclosure)
full_name: Political Advertisements: Artificial Intelligence Disclosures
max_penalty: Administrative fines; civil penalties
summary: Requires political advertisements that include AI-generated content to include a clear and conspicuous disclosure stating the content was created or substantially altered using AI. Applies to paid political advertisements in any medium. Enforced by the California Fair Political Practices Commission.
notable: Extends California's existing political ad disclosure regime to cover AI-generated content specifically.
legal_citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 84504.3 (as added); AB 2355, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Political ads using AI-generated content must include conspicuous disclosure
Applies to any paid political communication in any medium
FPPC to adopt implementing regulations

short_name: California AB 1831 (AI-Generated CSAM)
full_name: Child Sexual Abuse Material: Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: Felony; imprisonment up to 8 years
summary: Expands California's child sexual abuse material (CSAM) laws to expressly cover AI-generated, computer-generated, or otherwise digitally created depictions of minors engaged in sexual conduct. Makes it a felony to possess, distribute, or produce such material regardless of whether any real child is depicted.
notable: Closes the AI-generated CSAM loophole in California law; part of a wave of similar state laws in 2024.
legal_citation: Cal. Penal Code § 311 et seq. (as amended); AB 1831, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Prohibition on possessing, producing, or distributing AI-generated CSAM
No requirement of a real minor victim for prosecution

short_name: California SB 926 (AI Nonconsensual Intimate Imagery)
full_name: Artificial Intelligence: Intimate Images
max_penalty: Misdemeanor or felony; civil damages
summary: Expands California's nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) law to cover AI-generated or digitally altered intimate images of real, identifiable persons. Creates both criminal liability (misdemeanor/felony depending on intent) and a private civil right of action for victims. Addresses sextortion using AI-generated imagery.
notable: Extends existing revenge porn law to cover synthetic deepfakes of real people. Companion to SB 981 (platform reporting obligations).
legal_citation: Cal. Penal Code § 647(j)(4) (as amended); Cal. Civ. Code § 1708.87 (as amended); SB 926, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Prohibits distributing AI-generated intimate images of identifiable real persons without consent
Criminal and civil liability for perpetrators
Victims may seek injunctive relief and actual damages

short_name: California SB 981 (Deepfake Intimate Image Reporting — Platforms)
full_name: Social Media Platforms: Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content
max_penalty: Civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
summary: Requires large social media platforms to implement a mechanism allowing users to report sexually explicit AI-generated or digitally altered content depicting real people without their consent. Platforms must provide an easily accessible reporting tool and take action on valid reports. Complements SB 926 by imposing platform-level obligations.
notable: Platform-side obligation for AI NCII; pairs with SB 926 (individual liability). Early example of platform duty-to-act requirements for AI-generated harmful content.
legal_citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22949.30 (as added); SB 981, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Large social media platforms must provide user-accessible reporting tool for AI-generated sexually explicit content
Platforms must act on valid reports within a reasonable timeframe
Platform must publish an annual transparency report on NCII reports received and actions taken

short_name: Japan AI Utilization Guidelines (2025)
full_name: Guidelines on the Utilization of Artificial Intelligence (Article 13 Guidelines)
enforcement_body: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications
max_penalty: Administrative guidance; sector-specific enforcement via existing laws
summary: Statutory guidelines issued by the government pursuant to Article 13 of Japan's AI Promotion Act (2025). Establish operational standards for responsible AI development and utilization across sectors, covering transparency, accountability, safety evaluation, and human oversight. Provide sector-specific guidance for high-risk AI applications in healthcare, finance, and transportation. Issued by the AI Strategy Headquarters on December 19, 2025.
notable: First statutory AI utilization guidelines issued under Japan's AI Promotion Act; operationalize the Act's principles with sector-specific detail.
legal_citation: Guidelines on AI Utilization under Art. 13 of Act No. 14 of 2025 (Japan); promulgated December 19, 2025.
key_obligations: AI developers must implement safety evaluation processes aligned with government guidelines
Deployers must document AI system purpose, risks, and oversight mechanisms
Transparency obligations for AI interactions in consumer-facing applications
Sector ministries to issue supplementary guidance for high-risk domains

short_name: Japan Basic AI Plan (2025)
full_name: Basic Plan on the Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies
summary: Cabinet-approved Basic Plan issued pursuant to Article 18 of Japan's AI Promotion Act (2025). Sets out the government's multi-year strategic priorities for AI research, development, and deployment. Specifies measurable targets for AI investment, talent development, international cooperation, and AI safety. Binding on all government ministries, which must align their sectoral AI policies and budgets with the Plan. Approved by the AI Strategy Headquarters on December 23, 2025.
notable: The core planning instrument under Japan's AI Promotion Act; binds all ministries and establishes the national AI investment roadmap.
legal_citation: Basic Plan under Art. 18 of Act No. 14 of 2025 (Japan); Cabinet approval December 23, 2025.
key_obligations: All government ministries must align sectoral AI policies and budgets with the Basic Plan
Annual progress reports to the Cabinet on Plan implementation
AI Strategy Headquarters to coordinate cross-ministry AI initiatives
International AI governance engagement obligations tied to G7/OECD commitments

short_name: Australia National AI Plan 2025
full_name: Australia's National Artificial Intelligence Plan 2025
enforcement_body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
summary: Australia's whole-of-government AI strategy through 2030, superseding the 2021 National AI Strategy. Establishes the government's AI investment priorities, safety and governance framework, and international engagement positions. Commits to mandatory safeguards for high-risk AI applications in regulated sectors, builds on the 2024 Voluntary AI Safety Standard, and establishes a National AI Centre as the coordination body. Endorsed by the Albanese government December 2, 2025.
notable: Supersedes au-au-naistrategy-2021; signals shift from voluntary to mandatory high-risk AI obligations in Australia.
legal_citation: Australia's National AI Plan 2025, released December 2, 2025 by the Department of Industry, Science and Resources.
key_obligations: Government agencies must apply mandatory AI safety standards for high-risk AI procurement
Mandatory reporting for high-risk AI incidents in regulated sectors
All Commonwealth entities to publish AI transparency statements by 2026
Establish mandatory high-risk AI regime with statutory basis by 2027

short_name: Singapore Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
full_name: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI Systems
summary: Singapore's first dedicated governance framework for agentic AI systems — AI that can autonomously plan, execute multi-step tasks, and interact with other AI agents or external systems. Published by IMDA and the AI Verify Foundation in January 2026. Addresses unique risks of agentic AI including unpredictable behavior, cascading failures in multi-agent pipelines, and reduced human oversight. Provides a five-layer accountability model covering principal hierarchy, agent transparency, human control mechanisms, and incident response.
notable: First major national governance framework specifically targeting agentic AI. Builds on Singapore's 2020 MAIGF and positions Singapore as the global reference for agentic AI governance.
legal_citation: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI Systems, IMDA / AI Verify Foundation, January 2026.
key_obligations: Organizations deploying agentic AI must establish a principal hierarchy with clear human override mechanisms
Agentic AI systems must maintain action logs sufficient for post-hoc accountability
Human review required for high-stakes agentic decisions (financial, legal, medical)
Multi-agent pipelines must designate a responsible entity for overall system behavior

short_name: Spain Royal Decree 729/2023 (AESIA)
full_name: Real Decreto 729/2023 por el que se crea la Agencia Española de Supervisión de la Inteligencia Artificial
enforcement_body: AESIA (Agencia Española de Supervisión de la Inteligencia Artificial)
summary: Royal Decree establishing the Agencia Española de Supervisión de la Inteligencia Artificial (AESIA) as Spain's national AI supervisory authority. AESIA is responsible for supervising the application of the EU AI Act in Spain, conducting market surveillance, handling complaints, and representing Spain in EU AI governance bodies. Spain was the first EU member state to establish a dedicated national AI supervisory authority. Located in A Coruña (Galicia). AESIA is separate from the AI regulatory sandbox (established by RD 817/2023).
notable: Spain was the first EU country to designate its EU AI Act national competent authority, ahead of the Act's full application. AESIA became operational in late 2023.
legal_citation: Real Decreto 729/2023, de 22 de julio (BOE núm. 175, 24 julio 2023).
topics: EU AI Act national authority Spain
key_obligations: AESIA to serve as Spain's national competent authority and market surveillance authority for EU AI Act
AESIA to establish national AI registry and complaint handling mechanisms
AESIA to represent Spain at EU AI Board
Budget and staffing under Ministry of Economic Affairs and Digital Transformation

short_name: DIFC Laws Amendment Law No. 1 of 2025 (Data Protection Amendments)
full_name: DIFC Laws Amendment Law, DIFC Law No. 1 of 2025
max_penalty: USD 100,000 per violation
preemption_notes: DIFC is a separate free zone with its own legal system; these regulations apply only within the DIFC.
summary: Omnibus amendment law amending four DIFC laws. Part 2 amends the Data Protection Law 2020: clarifies territorial scope, strengthens data sharing safeguards (validity, proportionality, minimisation), restructures liability provisions, and adds an explicit private right of action for data subjects (new Article 64A). Also adjusts DPIA fine from $50 to $20,000 and data sharing fine from $50 to $10,000. Parts 3–5 amend the Law of Security 2024, Insolvency Law 2019, and Employment Law 2019.
notable: Extends DIFC's world-leading autonomous systems regulation with sector-specific AI governance requirements. DIFC continues to position itself as the most comprehensive AI regulatory jurisdiction in the Gulf.
legal_citation: DIFC Law No. 1 of 2025
key_obligations: AI systems processing personal data must meet ethicality, fairness, transparency, security, and accountability design principles
High-risk AI systems require third-party audit and certification before deployment
Data controllers must maintain an AI system register
Automated decisions with significant effects on individuals require human review upon request

short_name: Rwanda National AI Policy 2023
full_name: Rwanda National Artificial Intelligence Policy
summary: Rwanda's first national AI policy, approved by the Cabinet on April 20, 2023, making Rwanda the first African country to adopt a national AI policy. Establishes Rwanda's vision for AI-driven economic transformation and public service delivery across agriculture, health, education, and justice. Focuses on responsible AI development, data governance, AI talent development, and international AI cooperation. The policy commits Rwanda to human-centric AI aligned with African Union principles.
notable: First African country to adopt a formal national AI policy; a landmark for the continent.
legal_citation: Rwanda National Artificial Intelligence Policy, Cabinet approval April 20, 2023.
key_obligations: Government to establish AI governance coordination mechanism
Public sector to adopt responsible AI procurement standards
Investment in national AI talent and research capacity
Data governance framework to support AI development

short_name: Kenya National AI Strategy 2025–2030
full_name: Kenya National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2030
enforcement_body: Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy
summary: Kenya's five-year national AI strategy, formally launched March 27, 2025, positioning Kenya as East Africa's regional AI hub. Organized around seven pillars: AI infrastructure and data, talent development, research and innovation, ethical AI governance, public sector adoption, private sector transformation, and international partnerships. Commits Kenya to establishing an AI governance framework and a Centre of Excellence in AI by 2027. Includes specific targets for AI adoption in healthcare, agriculture, and financial services.
notable: Kenya positions itself as Africa's regional AI leader, particularly for the East Africa corridor. The Strategy was developed with UNESCO and World Bank support.
legal_citation: Kenya National AI Strategy 2025–2030, Ministry of ICT, March 27, 2025.
key_obligations: Government to establish AI governance framework by 2026
Public sector to publish AI deployment guidelines
Investment in national AI research infrastructure and data centres
Centre of Excellence in AI to be established by 2027

short_name: Nigeria National AI Strategy (NAIS) 2024
full_name: Nigeria National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024–2029
enforcement_body: Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy
summary: Nigeria's five-year national AI strategy, launched August 2024 by the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy. Establishes Nigeria's vision to become Africa's largest AI economy by leveraging its population of over 220 million and growing tech sector. Organized around five pillars: AI education and skills, AI-powered public services, AI innovation ecosystem, responsible AI governance, and international AI collaboration. Nigeria's National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (NCAIR) under NITDA leads implementation.
notable: Nigeria has Africa's largest economy and population; this strategy positions it as the continental AI superpower. Implementation is anchored in the NDPA 2023 data governance framework.
legal_citation: Nigeria National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024–2029, NITDA/NCAIR, August 2024.
key_obligations: NCAIR to publish national AI standards and guidelines by 2025
Federal agencies to conduct AI readiness assessments
Investment in AI education programs and STEM curriculum integration
Annual AI governance progress reports to the President

short_name: South Africa National AI Policy Framework 2024
full_name: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
enforcement_body: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies (DCDT)
summary: South Africa's National AI Policy Framework, published by the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies (DCDT) in August 2024. Establishes six pillars for responsible AI development: inclusive innovation, human-centred AI, responsible governance, data sovereignty, AI skills and education, and economic transformation. Introduces a risk-based approach to AI oversight aligned with international standards. The Framework preceded the formal draft National AI Policy published in April 2026 (which opened for public consultation). Applies to both public and private sector AI adoption.
notable: South Africa's first formal AI policy document; signals commitment to risk-based governance before formal legislation. Led to the April 2026 draft AI Policy published for consultation.
legal_citation: South Africa National AI Policy Framework, DCDT, August 2024.
key_obligations: Government to develop sector-specific AI guidelines building on the framework
Risk-based assessment of AI applications across sectors
Data governance alignment with POPIA requirements
Annual review of framework against international developments

short_name: Zimbabwe National AI Strategy 2026–2030
full_name: Zimbabwe National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026–2030
enforcement_body: Ministry of Information Communication Technology, Postal and Courier Services
Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe (POTRAZ)
summary: Zimbabwe's first national AI strategy, launched by President Mnangagwa on March 13, 2026. Establishes Zimbabwe's vision for AI-driven inclusive digital transformation through 2030. Organized around four pillars: AI infrastructure and connectivity, AI skills and human capital, ethical and responsible AI governance, and AI-powered economic sectors (agriculture, mining, tourism, financial services). Cabinet-approved national instrument with implementation overseen by POTRAZ.
notable: Most recent African national AI strategy as of its launch; emphasizes Zimbabwe's natural resource sectors as AI adoption targets.
legal_citation: Zimbabwe National AI Strategy 2026–2030, Cabinet approval / launch March 13, 2026.
key_obligations: Government agencies to adopt AI policies aligned with the strategy by 2027
Establishment of National AI Governance Council
Investment in AI connectivity infrastructure in rural and peri-urban areas
Sector ministries to develop AI action plans within 12 months of strategy launch

short_name: Qatar Central Bank AI Guideline 2024
full_name: Qatar Central Bank Artificial Intelligence Guideline for Financial Institutions
max_penalty: License revocation; regulatory sanctions; prior QCB approval withdrawal
summary: Binding AI guideline issued by the Qatar Central Bank on September 4, 2024, mandatory for all QCB-licensed financial institutions. Requires licensed entities to develop an AI strategy, conduct AI risk assessments, implement human oversight protocols, and establish AI governance committees at board level. High-risk AI systems (credit scoring, fraud detection, customer authentication) require explicit QCB pre-approval before deployment. Sets minimum standards for AI model documentation, validation, and performance monitoring in the financial sector.
notable: One of the first binding sector-specific AI regulations in the Gulf region. Pre-approval requirement for high-risk financial AI is unusually stringent by regional standards.
legal_citation: Qatar Central Bank AI Guideline, issued pursuant to QCB Governor's Decision, September 4, 2024.
topics: financial sector AI governance Middle East
key_obligations: Licensed financial institutions must develop a board-approved AI strategy
AI risk assessment required before deploying any AI system
High-risk AI systems require explicit pre-approval from QCB
Human oversight protocols must be in place for all AI-assisted decisions
Annual reporting to QCB on AI system performance and incidents

short_name: Saudi Arabia SDAIA AI Adoption Framework 2024
full_name: Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework: Maturity Model and Risk Classification
max_penalty: Non-compliance with SDAIA guidance may trigger sector-specific regulatory action
summary: Saudi Arabia's SDAIA AI Adoption Framework, published September 2024, establishes a maturity model and risk-based classification system for AI adoption across government and the private sector. Introduces a four-tier risk classification (low, limited, high, unacceptable) aligned with OECD and EU AI Act principles. Binding for all government entities and referenced as best practice for private sector. Specifies mandatory conformity assessments, transparency requirements, and human oversight obligations for high-risk AI. Accompanied by SDAIA's Generative AI Guideline for public and private use.
notable: Positions Saudi Arabia as having one of the most structured AI governance frameworks in the GCC. Complements Saudi Vision 2030's AI investment priorities.
legal_citation: SDAIA AI Adoption Framework: Maturity Model and Risk Classification, SDAIA / NCAI, September 2024.
key_obligations: Government entities must conduct AI maturity assessments and classify AI systems by risk tier
High-risk AI systems require conformity assessment before government deployment
Mandatory human oversight mechanisms for Tier 3 (high-risk) AI applications
AI transparency disclosures required for all citizen-facing government AI systems

short_name: UAE AI Charter 2024
full_name: UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
enforcement_body: UAE Office of AI (under Ministry of State for AI)
UAE Government Data and AI Authority (GDAIA)
summary: A 12-principle ethical charter issued by the UAE federal government on July 30, 2024, establishing values and principles for responsible AI development and use across the UAE. Covers human dignity, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, sustainability, and international cooperation. Non-binding but issued with Cabinet-level endorsement; functions as the national AI ethical compass guiding sector regulation. Distinct from the DIFC and ADGM jurisdictional frameworks.
notable: UAE is one of the few countries with a dedicated Minister of State for AI; this charter reflects the government's proactive AI positioning.
legal_citation: UAE Charter for the Development and Use of AI, UAE Federal Government, July 30, 2024.
key_obligations: Government entities to align AI deployments with the 12 charter principles
GDAIA to publish sector guidance implementing charter principles
Annual reporting on AI governance alignment

short_name: Colombia CONPES 4144 — National AI Policy
full_name: CONPES 4144: Política Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial 2024–2030
enforcement_body: Ministerio de Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación (MINCIENCIAS)
Ministerio de Tecnologías de la Información y las Comunicaciones (MINTIC)
summary: Colombia's National AI Policy 2024–2030, adopted by the National Council of Economic and Social Policy (CONPES) on February 14, 2025. Allocates COP 479 billion (~USD 117 million) over six years for AI investment. Establishes three axes: responsible and inclusive AI development, AI adoption for economic transformation, and AI governance. CONPES documents carry binding planning force for government entities and define mandatory investment commitments. Includes risk-based AI governance aligned with OECD AI Principles. Colombia's most comprehensive AI policy instrument to date.
notable: CONPES documents are Colombia's primary binding public policy instrument; this is the operative national AI policy with mandatory budget commitments.
legal_citation: CONPES 4144: Política Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial, DNP, February 14, 2025.
key_obligations: Government entities must align AI programs with CONPES 4144 goals and investment framework
MINCIENCIAS and MINTIC to establish AI governance standards by 2026
Annual investment tracking and reporting against CONPES commitments
Responsible AI principles to be embedded in public sector AI procurement

short_name: Argentina AAIP Resolution 161/2023 (AI Transparency Program)
full_name: Resolución 161/2023: Programa de Transparencia y Protección de Datos Personales en el uso de IA
enforcement_body: Agencia de Acceso a la Información Pública (AAIP)
max_penalty: Administrative sanctions under Law 25.326 (PDPA) — up to ARS 3 million
summary: Binding administrative resolution issued by Argentina's data protection authority (AAIP) on September 4, 2023, creating a 'Program for Transparency and Personal Data Protection in the Use of AI'. Establishes Argentina's first formal AI governance framework under the 2000 Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA, Law 25.326). Requires entities processing personal data with AI to register AI systems, conduct data protection impact assessments, disclose AI use to affected individuals, and participate in the national AI observatory. Creates an AI Advisory Council and transparency certification mechanism.
notable: Argentina's first binding AI-specific instrument; issued under existing data protection authority rather than requiring new legislation. A notable regulatory approach for Latin America.
legal_citation: Resolución AAIP 161/2023, September 4, 2023 (Boletín Oficial de la República Argentina).
key_obligations: Entities using AI to process personal data must register AI systems with AAIP
Mandatory data protection impact assessments for high-risk AI applications
Disclosure to individuals when AI is used in decisions affecting their rights
Participation in AAIP's AI observatory and transparency certification program

short_name: Israel — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225)
full_name: Israel Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)
preemption_notes: Not yet ratified as of May 2026; signature is binding on Israel under international law not to act against the Convention's object and purpose, but domestic implementation awaits ratification.
summary: Israel signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI, Human Rights, Democracy, and the Rule of Law (CETS 225) on September 5, 2024, becoming one of the first non-European countries to sign. As a signatory, Israel commits to implementing the Convention's principles — human rights safeguards, democratic oversight, and rule of law requirements for AI — upon ratification. The Convention entered into force in 2025 after receiving the required five ratifications. Israel was among the first Middle Eastern countries to sign an international AI governance treaty.
notable: First Middle Eastern country to sign CETS 225. Signals Israel's alignment with European AI governance standards despite not being an EU member.
legal_citation: Signature by Israel of CETS 225, Council of Europe, Vilnius, September 5, 2024.
key_obligations: Signatory obligation not to act against the Convention's object and purpose prior to ratification
Upon ratification: implement human rights impact assessments for AI systems
Upon ratification: establish national oversight mechanism for high-risk AI

short_name: Uruguay — Signature of CoE AI Convention (CETS 225)
full_name: Uruguay Signature of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI and Human Rights (CETS 225)
preemption_notes: Not yet ratified as of May 2026; signature is binding on Uruguay under international law not to act against the Convention's object and purpose, but domestic implementation awaits ratification.
summary: Uruguay signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI, Human Rights, Democracy, and the Rule of Law (CETS 225) on September 5, 2024, becoming the first Latin American country to sign an international AI governance treaty. Uruguay's signature reflects its strong data protection tradition (home to one of Latin America's most respected data protection frameworks and the Unidad Reguladora y de Control de Datos Personales, URCDP). As a signatory, Uruguay commits to implementing the Convention's human rights, democratic oversight, and rule of law requirements for AI upon ratification.
notable: First Latin American country to sign CETS 225 — a significant milestone in the Convention's global reach beyond Europe.
legal_citation: Signature by Uruguay of CETS 225, Council of Europe, Vilnius, September 5, 2024.
key_obligations: Signatory obligation not to act against the Convention's object and purpose prior to ratification
Upon ratification: implement human rights impact assessments for AI systems
Upon ratification: establish national oversight mechanism for high-risk AI

short_name: Puerto Rico HJR 68 — AI Study for Anti-Corruption (PRITS)
full_name: Puerto Rico House Joint Resolution 68 — R. C. de la C. 68
summary: Orders PRITS to conduct a comprehensive study on the feasibility and benefits of using AI to optimize government auditing, fraud detection, risk mitigation, and expenditure oversight; requires 180-day report to the Governor, Legislature, and oversight agencies.

short_name: Puerto Rico SR 133 — Senate Investigation of Electoral Technology
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Resolution 133 — R. del S. 133
summary: Orders the Senate Committee on Science, Technology and Artificial Intelligence to conduct a comprehensive investigation into the technological capabilities of Puerto Rico's State Elections Commission (CEE), including cybersecurity, database management, and strategic technology planning for future elections; requires 180-day report.

short_name: OMB M-25-22 (AI Acquisition)
full_name: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government
max_penalty: None — OMB policy memorandum; no penalty regime.
preemption_notes: OMB policy memorandum; applies only to federal agency procurement
summary: OMB guidance directing federal agencies on responsible AI acquisition. Rescinds Biden-era M-24-18. Establishes requirements across the AI acquisition lifecycle — from requirements identification through contract closeout — focused on three themes: competitive AI marketplace, performance tracking and risk management, and cross-functional engagement. Requires agency policy updates within 270 days and full compliance within 180 days.
notable: Rescinds and replaces OMB M-24-18 (Biden-era AI acquisition guidance). Adds "buy American AI" policy per EO 14179. Permanently prohibits use of non-public agency data to train commercial AI models absent explicit agency consent.
legal_citation: OMB Memorandum M-25-22 (Apr. 3, 2025)
key_obligations: Agencies must update acquisition policies within 270 days to comply with this memorandum
Contracts must permanently prohibit vendors from using non-public agency data to train commercial AI models
Agencies must disclose high-impact AI use cases in solicitations
Contracts must include ongoing testing, monitoring, and vendor lock-in protections
GSA must develop AI procurement guides (100 days) and shared repository (200 days)

impact_assessment.detail: Agencies must identify high-impact AI use cases per M-25-21 and disclose them in solicitations; vendors must provide documentation to support AI Impact Assessments.

training_data_transparency.detail: Contracts must permanently prohibit vendors from using non-public agency data or outputs to train publicly or commercially available AI algorithms, absent explicit agency consent.

vendor_lock_in.detail: Agencies must include vendor lock-in protections in solicitations and contracts, including data/model portability, knowledge transfer requirements, and pricing transparency.

enforcement_model.detail: OMB policy memorandum; enforced through agency compliance requirements and OMB oversight. No penalty regime.

operative_dates: Issued April 3, 2025. Applies to contracts from solicitations issued 180 days after issuance (approx. October 1, 2025). Agency policy updates required within 270 days.

short_name: OMB M-26-04 (Unbiased AI)
full_name: Increasing Public Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Unbiased AI Principles
max_penalty: None — OMB policy memorandum; contract termination for default available for noncompliance.
preemption_notes: OMB policy memorandum; applies only to federal agency LLM procurement
summary: OMB guidance implementing EO 14319 (Preventing Woke AI) by requiring federal agencies to ensure procured LLMs comply with two Unbiased AI Principles: truth-seeking and ideological neutrality. Requires contractual transparency documentation from vendors (acceptable use policies, model cards, feedback mechanisms) and agency policy updates by March 11, 2026. Sunsets two years after issuance.
notable: Implements Trump EO 14319 Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government. Requires vendors to disclose any training or development outside the US and any modifications made to comply with non-US government regulations. Contract termination for default is available enforcement mechanism.
legal_citation: OMB Memorandum M-26-04 (Dec. 11, 2025)
key_obligations: New LLM procurement contracts must include Unbiased AI Principles compliance requirements
Existing LLM contracts should be modified to include Unbiased AI Principles requirements at latest before option exercise
Agency policies must be updated by March 11, 2026, including user reporting processes for principle violations
Vendors must provide minimum transparency documentation: acceptable use policy, model/system/data cards, end user resources, feedback mechanism
Agencies must request disclosure of any training outside the US or modifications to comply with foreign government regulations

training_data_transparency.detail: Agencies must request model cards, system cards, and data cards from vendors. Enhanced transparency may require disclosure of pre- and post-training activities, bias evaluation results, and any foreign training or foreign-government-compliance modifications.

enforcement_model.detail: Agencies should make Unbiased AI Principles requirements material to contract eligibility and payment, enabling termination for default if vendor refuses corrective action. Sunsets December 11, 2027 unless extended.

anti_discrimination.detail: Focuses on preventing ideological bias and political manipulation in LLM outputs rather than traditional protected-class anti-discrimination. Requires models to be neutral, nonpartisan tools.

operative_dates: Issued December 11, 2025. New contracts: immediately. Agency policy updates: by March 11, 2026. Sunsets December 11, 2027.

short_name: NIS2 Directive
full_name: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (NIS2)
max_penalty: €10M or 2% global annual turnover (essential entities); €7M or 1.4% (important entities)
preemption_notes: Directive sets minimum requirements; member states may impose stricter national measures
summary: The NIS2 Directive significantly expands the scope of the original NIS Directive (2016/1148), establishing cybersecurity risk-management and incident-reporting obligations for essential and important entities across 18 sectors including energy, transport, banking, health, digital infrastructure, and ICT service management. Entities must implement risk-proportionate technical and organisational cybersecurity measures covering supply chain security, vulnerability handling, cryptography, access control, and multi-factor authentication. Incident reporting follows a three-stage timeline: an early warning within 24 hours, a formal notification within 72 hours, and a final report within one month. Entities that are substantially dependent on network and information systems face management-body accountability requirements. National supervisory authorities may impose fines up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover for essential entities and €7 million or 1.4% for important entities. Member states must designate national competent authorities and establish CSIRTs. Repeals and replaces the original NIS Directive.
notable: Transposition deadline was 17 October 2024; several EU member states missed the deadline. Companion to the EU AI Act for cybersecurity of AI systems. Covers AI infrastructure providers as digital infrastructure entities.
legal_citation: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022, O.J. L 333/80 (27 Dec 2022)
key_obligations: Essential and important entities must implement risk-proportionate cybersecurity measures (Art. 21)
24-hour early warning, 72-hour incident notification, 1-month final report to national CSIRT/authority
Supply chain security assessments required including ICT suppliers
Management bodies must approve and supervise cybersecurity risk-management measures
Member states must designate national competent authorities and CSIRTs by Oct 17, 2024
Entities must register with national competent authorities
Cross-border cooperation via EU-CyCLONe network for large-scale incident response

impact_assessment.detail: Entities must conduct and maintain cybersecurity risk assessments; management bodies must oversee implementation. No AI-specific impact assessment required but risk management applies to AI-integrated systems.

prohibited_categories.detail: Cybersecurity directive; does not prohibit specific AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action; enforcement through national competent authorities.

risk_classification.detail: Two-tier classification: essential entities (Annex I — energy, transport, banking, health, digital infrastructure, etc.) subject to stricter supervision and higher fines; important entities (Annex II) subject to lighter supervision.

enforcement_model.detail: National competent authorities conduct ex ante supervision (essential) or ex post supervision (important); fines up to €10M or 2% global turnover for essential, €7M or 1.4% for important entities.

operative_dates: Published OJ 27 Dec 2022; entered into force 16 Jan 2023; transposition deadline 17 Oct 2024; applicable from 18 Oct 2024.

short_name: UK ICO ADM Detailed Guidance
full_name: ICO Detailed Guidance on Automated Decision-Making Including Profiling (UK GDPR)
max_penalty: £17.5M or 4% global annual turnover (underlying UK GDPR)
preemption_notes: Interpretive guidance issued under UK GDPR; underlying UK GDPR binding on all UK organisations processing personal data
summary: Detailed interpretive guidance from the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) on the automated decision-making (ADM) provisions of the UK GDPR (Articles 22A-22D), last updated March 2026. Covers when ADM provisions apply (significant decision + solely automated + no meaningful human involvement), lawful bases for ADM (consent, contract, public task, legitimate interests — but not recognised legitimate interest), special category data restrictions, required safeguards (right to information about decisions, right to make representations, right to human intervention, right to contest), transparency obligations, and DPIA requirements. Explicitly addresses AI and machine learning systems in context of profiling and ADM. The guidance will inform a forthcoming statutory code of practice on AI and ADM. Currently being updated to reflect the Data (Use and Access) Act.
notable: Reflects post-Brexit UK GDPR ADM regime, which diverges from EU GDPR Article 22 by introducing Articles 22A-22D with expanded scope. Explicitly addresses AI and ML throughout. A forthcoming statutory AI and ADM Code of Practice will build on this guidance.
legal_citation: ICO Guidance under UK GDPR Articles 22A-22D (Data Protection Act 2018)
key_obligations: Identify whether ADM provisions apply: significant decision + solely automated + no meaningful human involvement
Establish and document a lawful basis for ADM processing (consent, contract, public task, or legitimate interests)
ADM using special category data requires one of three article 22B conditions: explicit consent, contract, or required/authorised by law
Implement four mandatory safeguards: provide decision information, enable representations, enable human intervention, enable contestation
Respond to rights requests without undue delay and within one month
Conduct DPIA for systematic and extensive ADM based on profiling with significant effects
Provide age-appropriate transparency when processing children's data for ADM

impact_assessment.detail: DPIA mandatory for systematic and extensive ADM based on profiling that produces legal or similarly significant effects; ICO recommends a DPIA for all ADM given high-risk likelihood.

prohibited_categories.detail: UK GDPR does not prohibit specific AI applications; restricts conditions under which ADM using special category data may be carried out.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 22C mandates right to obtain human intervention in any ADM that produces significant decisions; human review must be meaningful — not tokenistic — with discretion to alter the outcome.

private_right_of_action.detail: Underlying UK GDPR Art. 82 provides individual right to compensation for material or non-material damage; ICO can also take enforcement action.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is special category; ADM using biometric data requires one of the three article 22B conditions plus an article 9 condition.

anti_discrimination.detail: Guidance extensively addresses bias and discrimination risks in ADM; DPIA must consider discriminatory effects; legitimate interests balancing test must account for bias risks.

risk_classification.detail: No risk tier system; ADM provisions apply based on three-factor test (significant decision, solely automated, no meaningful human involvement).

enforcement_model.detail: ICO enforces UK GDPR; fines up to £17.5M or 4% global turnover; individuals also have right to compensation under Art. 82.

operative_dates: Guidance ongoing; last updated 31 March 2026; consultation on Data (Use and Access) Act updates ongoing.

short_name: Bahrain General Policy for Use of AI
full_name: General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence (iGA, Kingdom of Bahrain)
enforcement_body: Ministerial Committee for Information and Communication Technology (MCICT)
preemption_notes: Government policy applying to Bahraini government entities; non-binding on private sector
summary: Approved by the Ministerial Committee for ICT on 20 May 2025, this policy establishes a comprehensive framework governing how Bahraini government entities adopt and use artificial intelligence. Built around four pillars — (1) compliance with existing laws and policies (including the PDPL, cybercrime law, cloud computing decree, and GCC AI Ethics Guideline); (2) responsible adoption and use of AI technologies; (3) awareness and education for government employees; and (4) local and international cooperation — the policy sets out eleven foundational AI principles including human decision-making primacy, safety, fairness, transparency, accountability, and intellectual property protection. All government entities must coordinate AI adoption with the iGA, follow iGA-issued standards, and conduct regular audits. The policy explicitly assigns accountability for AI outcomes to responsible humans, not machines.
notable: Incorporates the GCC AI Ethics Guideline by reference and explicitly grounds AI governance in Islamic Sharia values alongside human rights principles. Companion to the Bahrain AI Regulation Law (2024) which governs private sector and binding prohibitions.
legal_citation: General Policy for the Use of Artificial Intelligence, Version 1.0, approved by MCICT 20 May 2025 (iGA, Kingdom of Bahrain)
key_obligations: All government entities must comply with AI policy and coordinate AI adoption with iGA
Government entities must follow iGA-issued standards for launching AI initiatives
Regular audits required to ensure AI use aligns with best practices
Human accountability for AI outcomes — negative effects attributed to responsible individuals, not machines
Entities must provide employee training on AI technologies
Compliance required with PDPL, cybercrime law, state documents law, cloud computing decree, and GCC AI Ethics Guideline

impact_assessment.detail: No formal impact assessment requirement; audits and reviews required for ongoing AI use.

prohibited_categories.detail: Binding prohibitions on specific AI uses are addressed in the separate Bahrain AI Regulation Law (2024), not this policy.

human_review_rights.detail: Policy requires human supervision at all stages of AI use; final decisions in important matters must remain under human control. No individual right to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Government policy only; no private right of action created.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed directly; covered by the PDPL referenced in Section 6.1.2.1.

anti_discrimination.detail: Principle 3 requires AI to be fair and non-discriminatory based on race, religion, gender, or other non-objective factors; no enforcement mechanism specified.

risk_classification.detail: No risk tier system; policy applies uniformly to all government AI adoption.

enforcement_model.detail: iGA supervises implementation; ICTGC handles exemption requests; no penalties specified in this policy document.

operative_dates: Approved and effective 20 May 2025.

short_name: GCC AI Ethics Guideline
full_name: Guiding Document on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Use in the Member States of the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf
preemption_notes: Non-binding guideline; member states encouraged to enact or amend national legislation consistent with the principles
summary: Published by the GCC General Secretariat in November 2023 and explicitly grounded in the UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation (2021), this non-binding guiding document establishes a shared ethical framework for AI development and use across all six GCC member states (Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE). It sets out four foundational values — respect for human dignity and autonomy; respect for Islamic Sharia, constitutions, and Gulf cohesion; environmental protection and sustainability; and promotion of peaceful use for citizens' welfare — alongside seven principles: (1) decisions are for humans; (2) safety and prevention of harm; (3) justice, equity, and non-discrimination; (4) privacy and data protection; (5) transparency and explainability; (6) responsibility, accountability, and awareness; (7) integrity and non-falsification. Each principle includes concrete recommendations covering human oversight activation, fallback plans, dataset auditing, traceability, explainability, legal accountability legislation, and awareness promotion. Member states are directed to use the document when developing new AI-related legislation, strategies, and policies.
notable: First regional AI ethics framework for the Arab/Gulf world. Explicitly integrates Islamic Sharia as a foundational value alongside human rights — a unique feature among regional AI frameworks globally. Adopted by Bahrain as part of its national AI policy (iGA General Policy, 2025) and introduced as a GCC-wide initiative at the Global AI Summit 2024 in Riyadh.
legal_citation: Guiding Document on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence Use in the Member States of the GCC, Version 1.0, November 2023 (GCC General Secretariat)
key_obligations: Member states should activate human oversight mechanisms for AI systems
Fundamental rights impact assessment recommended before AI system development where risks exist
AI systems must inform users they are interacting with AI; option for human interaction must be available
Datasets must be audited for unintended bias before training and operation
Member states should develop legislation ensuring legal accountability for AI system performance
Data access protocols must be established; personal data access restricted to qualified personnel
Member states should develop reporting mechanisms for AI system outputs and protect whistleblowers
Document to be referenced when developing national AI legislation, strategies, and digital transformation policies

impact_assessment.detail: Fundamental rights impact assessment recommended before AI development where rights risks exist; must assess harm level for all societal groups.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI applications specified; document is principles-based.

human_review_rights.detail: Principle 1 states users have the right not to be subjected to a decision based solely on automated processing with legal or significant effects; option for human interaction must be available.

private_right_of_action.detail: Non-binding guideline; no private right of action. Member states encouraged to develop accountability legislation.

biometric_data.detail: Privacy principle requires data governance frameworks consistent with national data protection laws; use of profiling data (age, gender, religion) for discrimination prohibited.

training_data_transparency.detail: Traceability principle requires documentation of datasets and processes; datasets should be audited and documented at every step (planning, training, testing, deployment).

content_labeling.detail: Transparency principle requires informing users they are interacting with an AI system; AI systems must be identifiable as such.

anti_discrimination.detail: Principle 3 requires equitable access and non-discrimination; dataset auditing recommended; no binding enforcement mechanism.

risk_classification.detail: No risk tier system; document applies uniform principles across all AI applications.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding guidance; no enforcement mechanism. Member states encouraged to develop legislation and oversight processes consistent with the principles.

operative_dates: Published November 2023; non-binding; member states to implement through national legislation and policy.

short_name: China AI Content Labeling Measures
full_name: Measures for Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content (State Information Office Tongzi [2025] No. 2)
enforcement_body: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT)
State Administration of Radio and Television (SART)
preemption_notes: National regulation; enforcement under existing laws including Cybersecurity Law and parent regulations
summary: Promulgated jointly by the CAC, MIIT, Ministry of Public Security, and SART on March 7, 2025 and effective September 1, 2025, these Measures operationalize content labeling obligations for AI-generated synthetic content (text, images, audio, video, virtual scenes) across the Chinese internet ecosystem. Service providers generating synthetic content must apply explicit labels (visible text, sound, or image notifications) in specified positions for each content type. They must also embed implicit labels (metadata including provider name/code and content reference number) in file headers; digital watermarks are encouraged. Distribution platforms must verify metadata for implicit labels and add conspicuous notices when AI content is detected, asserted by users, or suspected. Users who publish AI-generated content must proactively declare it; malicious deletion, alteration, or concealment of labels is prohibited. App stores must check labeling compliance when reviewing AI service apps. Service providers may omit explicit labels at user request only after informing users of their obligations and retaining logs for at least 6 months.
notable: Part of China's layered AI content governance stack, building on the 2022 Deep Synthesis Provisions and 2023 Generative AI Measures. Introduces a two-track labeling system (explicit + implicit/metadata) applicable to all AI-generated content modalities. Effective September 1, 2025 — same date as several other CAC AI regulations.
legal_citation: Measures for Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content, State Information Office Tongzi [2025] No. 2, promulgated 7 March 2025, effective 1 September 2025
key_obligations: Explicit labels required on all AI-generated text, audio, images, video, and virtual scenes at specified positions
Implicit labels (metadata: provider name/code, content reference number) required in file headers of all synthetic content
Digital watermarks encouraged as additional implicit labeling method
Distribution platforms must verify metadata, detect AI content, and add platform-level notices
App stores must check labeling compliance before approving AI service applications
Users must proactively declare AI-generated content when publishing; platform labeling tools must be used
Malicious deletion, alteration, fabrication, or concealment of labels prohibited
Logs must be retained for at least 6 months when explicit labels omitted at user request
Label information must be shared during algorithm filing and safety assessment procedures

impact_assessment.detail: No impact assessment requirement; labeling obligations are procedural/technical.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed; this regulation governs labeling, not prohibition of content categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement by regulatory departments; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: All AI-generated synthetic content requires both explicit (user-visible) and implicit (metadata) labels; digital watermarks encouraged; malicious removal prohibited.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed in this regulation; biometric data addressed in parent Deep Synthesis Provisions.

content_labeling.detail: Dual-track mandatory labeling: explicit (visible notifications) + implicit (file metadata); specific format requirements vary by content type (text, audio, image, video, virtual scene).

risk_classification.detail: No risk tier system; labeling obligations apply uniformly to all AI-generated synthetic content.

enforcement_model.detail: Multi-regulator enforcement (CAC, MIIT, MPS, SART) under existing laws including Cybersecurity Law and parent AI regulations; specific penalties determined by applicable parent instruments.

operative_dates: Promulgated 7 March 2025; effective 1 September 2025.

short_name: RBI FREE-AI Committee Report
full_name: Report of the Committee on Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence (FREE-AI), Reserve Bank of India
preemption_notes: Non-binding committee report; recommendations directed at RBI, other FSRs, and regulated entities. No preemption effect.
summary: Published in August 2025, this report by the RBI-constituted FREE-AI (Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence) Committee sets out a comprehensive framework for responsible AI adoption in the Indian financial sector. After conducting two RBI surveys and extensive stakeholder consultations, the Committee formulated 7 foundational Sutras (Trust is the Foundation; People First; Innovation over Restraint; Fairness and Equity; Accountability; Understandable by Design; Safety, Resilience and Sustainability), 6 strategic Pillars (Infrastructure, Policy, Capacity for innovation enablement; Governance, Protection, Assurance for risk mitigation), and 26 Recommendations. Highlights include: establishment of an AI innovation sandbox and shared financial sector data infrastructure; development of indigenous Indian financial sector AI models; board-approved AI policies required of all regulated entities; product approval processes expanded to cover AI risk evaluation; mandatory AI disclosures in annual reports; risk-based AI audit framework with independent third-party audits for high-risk use cases; AI incident reporting framework; accommodative liability framework for REs that follow required safety mechanisms; and creation of a permanent multi-stakeholder AI Standing Committee under the RBI.
notable: First comprehensive AI governance framework from the RBI. Introduces the "7 Sutras" as India's financial sector AI principles. Recommends a ₹5,000 crore (approx. M) public fund for AI data and compute infrastructure. Explicitly addresses agentic/autonomous AI governance (Rec 16). Non-binding but likely precursor to binding RBI Master Directions on AI.
legal_citation: Report of the Committee on Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence (FREE-AI), Reserve Bank of India, August 2025
key_obligations: Regulated entities (REs) should establish board-approved AI policies covering governance, accountability, risk appetite, and consumer protection (Rec 14)
REs must implement robust AI model lifecycle governance frameworks and strong governance for autonomous AI systems (Rec 16)
REs must include AI in product approval processes with AI-specific risk evaluations (Rec 17)
REs should include AI-related disclosures in annual reports and websites (Rec 25)
REs must implement risk-based AI audit framework; independent third-party audits required for high-risk use cases (Rec 24)
REs must maintain a comprehensive AI inventory updated at least half-yearly (Rec 23)
REs must establish structured red teaming processes for AI lifecycle proportionate to risk level (Rec 20)
REs must augment Business Continuity Plans to cover AI model performance degradation (Rec 21)
RBI recommended to establish AI innovation sandbox and shared financial sector data infrastructure (Recs 1, 2)
RBI recommended to establish a permanent multi-stakeholder AI Standing Committee (Rec 9)
AI incident reporting framework to be established by financial sector regulators (Rec 22)

impact_assessment.detail: Recommendation 17 requires AI-specific risk evaluations as part of institutional product approval processes for all AI-enabled products and solutions.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI applications specified. Framework is principles-based and recommendation-driven.

human_review_rights.detail: Sutra 2 (People First) and Recommendation 18 (consumer protection) require transparency and accessible recourse mechanisms, but no formal individual right to human review of AI decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Non-binding guidance; no private right of action. Consumer grievances addressed through existing RE consumer protection frameworks.

biometric_data.detail: Not directly addressed; covered by India DPDP Act (2023) referenced throughout the report.

training_data_transparency.detail: Recommendation 15 requires data lifecycle governance frameworks; Recommendation 24 includes data inputs in AI audit scope.

content_labeling.detail: Recommendation 18 requires consumers to be made aware when they are dealing with AI; Recommendation 25 requires AI-related disclosures by REs in annual reports and websites.

anti_discrimination.detail: Sutra 4 (Fairness and Equity) requires AI to promote fairness and reduce systemic bias. Recommendation 26 (AI Compliance Toolkit) includes fairness validation. No binding enforcement mechanism.

risk_classification.detail: Recommendation 24 establishes a risk-based AI audit framework with proportionate requirements; high-risk use cases require independent third-party audits. Recommendation 20 requires red teaming frequency proportionate to risk level.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding committee report; recommendations require RBI to issue formal circulars/master directions for binding effect. Graded liability framework recommended in Rec 8 with accommodative supervisory stance for first-time/good-faith breaches.

operative_dates: Published August 2025; non-binding recommendations require follow-on RBI circulars or master directions to become binding on regulated entities.

short_name: Bahrain Proposed AI Regulation Law
full_name: Proposed Law on Regulating Artificial Intelligence Technologies and Their Uses (Kingdom of Bahrain, Shura Council)
max_penalty: BD 20,000 + imprisonment (manipulation offenses); BD 40,000 for legal persons
preemption_notes: Proposed national law; not yet enacted. Would apply to all persons resident in or operating from Bahrain.
summary: Submitted to the Bahrain Shura Council on 28 February 2024 by five members (Ref. 16 Q F6 D2), this 38-article proposed law would create the first binding AI regulatory framework in Bahrain, covering all persons residing in or operating from the Kingdom. It establishes: a licensing regime for commercial AI development and sale; an AI Unit within a designated Ministry for oversight, licensing, and enforcement; design requirements mandating human supervisability and non-discrimination; prohibitions on dangerous robots, deepfakes, and exclusive AI decision-making over life or freedom; civil liability for programmers and robot owners; and a tiered criminal penalty structure reaching imprisonment plus BD 20,000 (≈,000) for deepfake manipulation offenses. The explanatory memo explicitly cites inspiration from the EU AI Act and the Arab Guiding Law on AI, while emphasizing cultural and religious values. Entry into force would be six months after Gazette publication, with Executive Regulations due within three months. The proposal was cleared as legally admissible by the Shura Council Legal Advisors Authority.
notable: First proposed binding AI law in Bahrain, intended to complement the non-binding General AI Policy (iGA, 2025). Explicitly draws on the EU AI Act and Arab AI Guiding Law. Notable provisions: Art. 12 bars exclusive AI decisions over life/freedom/bodily integrity; Art. 8 requires patient consent for AI in surgery; Art. 33 allows dissolution of legal persons as penalty for recidivism. High-risk program classification tables delegated to Executive Regulations (Art. 36).
legal_citation: Proposed Law on Regulating Artificial Intelligence Technologies and Their Uses, Ref. 16 Q F6 D2, submitted to the Bahrain Shura Council 28 February 2024
key_obligations: Commercial AI programming, processing, development, or sale requires a license from the AI Unit (Art. 18)
AI systems must be designed to allow human supervision and control; bias must be corrected by modifying algorithms or retraining (Art. 6)
Prohibited: compositing personal images; manipulating official speeches; manipulating audio/visual content without consent; manipulating personal/health data (Art. 9)
Prohibited: exclusive AI decision-making over a person's life, freedom, or bodily integrity (Art. 12)
Prohibited: total reliance on AI for individual decisions requiring selection, evaluation, and harmonization (Art. 13)
Patient prior consent required when AI is used in surgical operations (Art. 8)
Developers, programmers, and users must report incidents, violations, and breaches to the AI Unit (Art. 16)
Dangerous robots or intelligent machines whose paths cannot be controlled are prohibited (Art. 10)
Developers must train employees dealing with AI systems (Art. 7)
Council of Ministers must develop national AI strategy covering education, health, investment, and IP protection (Art. 4)

impact_assessment.detail: No formal impact assessment requirement. High-risk classification tables delegated to Executive Regulations (Art. 36).

prohibited_categories.detail: Art. 9 prohibits deepfakes, image manipulation, manipulation of official speeches, and manipulation of personal/health data. Art. 10 prohibits dangerous robots. Art. 12 prohibits exclusive AI decisions over life/freedom/bodily integrity. Art. 14 prohibits AI for sedition, terrorism, deception, and manipulation.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 12 prohibits decisions on life, freedom, or bodily integrity based exclusively on AI. Art. 13 prohibits total reliance on AI for individual selection/evaluation decisions. No explicit right to request human review, but exclusive AI decision-making is banned in high-stakes contexts.

private_right_of_action.detail: Chapter 5 (Arts. 21-22) grants harmed persons a right to demand compensation from programmers, processors, or developers. Robot owners liable for damage unless caused by external force.

synthetic_media.detail: Art. 9 prohibits compositing personal images affecting reputation and manipulating audio/visual/textual content without consent. Art. 28 makes intentional manipulation with intent to harm a criminal offense: imprisonment + BD 5,000–20,000 fine.

biometric_data.detail: Not specifically addressed; covered by the Personal Data Protection Law (Law 30/2018) referenced in the preamble.

training_data_transparency.detail: Not addressed directly. Art. 6 requires bias correction through algorithm modification or data retraining, but no disclosure obligation.

content_labeling.detail: No AI-generated content labeling requirement. Manipulation and deception prohibited under Arts. 9 and 14.

anti_discrimination.detail: Art. 6(3) requires AI to be free from bias or discrimination; where bias arises, developers must modify algorithms or retrain using cleaner data. Art. 25(2) makes designing discriminatory systems a criminal offense (fine up to BD 2,000).

risk_classification.detail: Art. 36 requires Executive Regulations to set tables classifying high-risk programs, processes, and systems. No classification scheme in the law itself.

enforcement_model.detail: AI Unit may issue warnings, withdraw licenses, and impose daily fines up to BD 200/day (cap BD 10,000) (Art. 23). Criminal penalties range from BD 1,000 fine to imprisonment + BD 20,000 (Art. 28). Legal persons face double fines; recidivists may face dissolution (Art. 33).

operative_dates: Submitted to Shura Council 28 February 2024. Not yet enacted. If enacted, would enter into force six months after Gazette publication.

short_name: Singapore PDPC AI Guidelines 2024
full_name: Advisory Guidelines on the Use of Personal Data in AI Recommendation and Decision Systems (PDPC, Singapore)
preemption_notes: Advisory guidelines interpreting PDPA obligations; non-binding but represent PDPC's authoritative view on compliance. Enforcement through underlying PDPA.
summary: Published by the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) in March 2024, these advisory guidelines interpret how Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) obligations apply specifically to AI recommendation and decision systems that process personal data. They address the full lifecycle of personal data in AI: purpose limitation and consent for using personal data to train or operate AI systems; data accuracy requirements for training datasets; transparency obligations when personal data is used to generate recommendations or decisions affecting individuals; and accountability mechanisms including documentation and human review. As advisory guidelines, they do not create new legal obligations but represent PDPC's authoritative interpretation of PDPA requirements in the AI context, and non-compliance with their guidance may be taken into account in enforcement proceedings.
notable: TEXT NOT VERIFIED — source website was unavailable at time of record creation. Provisions and summary based on secondary sources; record should be updated when full text is retrieved. Builds on Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework (2020) and the 2021 PDPA amendments which introduced data portability and strengthened accountability obligations.
legal_citation: Advisory Guidelines on the Use of Personal Data in AI Recommendation and Decision Systems, Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore, March 2024
key_obligations: NOTE: Key obligations not fully verified — source text unavailable at time of record creation
Personal data used to train AI systems must be collected and used in accordance with PDPA purpose limitation and consent requirements
Organisations must ensure personal data used in AI training datasets is accurate and relevant
Individuals must be informed when their personal data is used in AI recommendation or decision systems affecting them
Mechanisms must be available for individuals to raise concerns about AI-based decisions made using their personal data
Organisations must maintain accountability for AI systems processing personal data, including documentation of data sources and model governance

impact_assessment.detail: No formal DPIA/AIIA requirement specified; accountability and documentation obligations under PDPA apply. Record not verified from source.

prohibited_categories.detail: Advisory guidelines focus on data protection compliance, not categorical prohibitions on AI use cases. Record not verified from source.

human_review_rights.detail: Guidelines address accountability and mechanisms for individuals to raise concerns; extent of formal human review right not verified from source.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement through PDPC under PDPA; no new private right of action created by advisory guidelines.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed. Guidelines focus on personal data use in recommendation/decision AI.

biometric_data.detail: Not specifically addressed in these guidelines; biometric data covered by PDPA as personal data. Record not verified from source.

training_data_transparency.detail: Expected to address data accuracy and documentation for training data; specifics not verified from source.

anti_discrimination.detail: Expected to address accuracy and bias in AI systems; specifics not verified from source.

risk_classification.detail: No risk tier system. Guidelines apply to AI recommendation and decision systems generally.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding advisory guidelines; enforcement is through underlying PDPA by PDPC. PDPA penalties apply to the data protection violations the guidelines interpret.

operative_dates: Published March 2024. Advisory guidelines with immediate effect as PDPC's authoritative PDPA interpretation.

short_name: ASEAN Expanded Guide on AI Governance — Generative AI
full_name: Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics: Generative AI (2025)
preemption_notes: Voluntary guide; explicitly states it does not replace or change any member state's legal obligations.
summary: Published in 2025 and developed collaboratively by all ten ASEAN Member States, this Expanded Guide supplements the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2024) with GenAI-specific policy considerations. It organises recommendations across nine ecosystem dimensions: (1) Accountability — shared responsibility frameworks across the GenAI value chain, aligned with the G7 Hiroshima Process Code of Conduct; (2) Data — facilitating data sharing for ASEAN-relevant LLMs in regional languages (referencing PhoGPT, ThaiLLM, and SEA-LION as models), and common personal data governance; (3) Trusted Development and Deployment — guidelines for GenAI development/deployment and common disclosure elements analogous to ingredient labels; (4) Incident Reporting — tiered incident reporting aligned with OECD AI incident taxonomy; (5) Testing and Assurance — regionally applicable benchmarks and testing tools including Project Moonshot; (6) Security — vulnerability detection, security-by-design guidelines, referencing Singapore CSA guidance; (7) Content Provenance — support for digital watermarking and C2PA cryptographic provenance standards to address deepfakes; (8) Safety and Alignment R&D — coordination among ASEAN-region AI Safety Institutes; (9) AI for Public Good — regional GenAI use case compendium and digital literacy promotion. All recommendations are explicitly voluntary.
notable: Explicitly scoped to policymakers, not private actors; recommendations direct ASEAN-level cooperation, not national mandates. Highlights SEA-LION (AI Singapore), PhoGPT (VinAI Vietnam), and ThaiLLM as regional language model initiatives. Section 2.2 addresses frontier risks including CBRNE misuse, agentic AI misalignment, and environmental impact of AI compute. References the Accenture Responsible AI programme (750,000 employees trained) as ASEAN-wide private sector example.
legal_citation: Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics: Generative AI, ASEAN, 2025

ASEAN to facilitate collation of open ASEAN-language datasets and regional data sharing (Sec. 3.2)
ASEAN to establish guidelines for GenAI development and deployment with common disclosure elements (Sec. 3.3)
ASEAN to create common terminology and tiered framework for AI incident reporting (Sec. 3.4)
ASEAN to develop regionally applicable GenAI evaluation benchmarks and testing tools (Sec. 3.5)
ASEAN to coordinate vulnerability detection and security knowledge-sharing; establish security-by-design guidelines (Sec. 3.6)
ASEAN to support development of content provenance technologies and build regional knowledge repository (Sec. 3.7)
ASEAN to create platform for AI Safety Institute cooperation among member states (Sec. 3.8)
ASEAN to publish regional GenAI use case compendium and promote digital literacy (Sec. 3.9)
All recommendations voluntary — guide explicitly does not replace member state legal obligations

impact_assessment.detail: No formal impact assessment requirement. Risk assessment best practices referenced under Trusted Development and Deployment (Sec. 3.3). Formal requirements left to member states.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary guide; no prohibited AI applications defined. CBRNE and deepfake misuse risks flagged under frontier risks but no prohibition recommended at ASEAN level.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed in this GenAI-specific supplement. Human oversight covered in parent ASEAN AI Guide (2024).

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary framework; no enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: Section 3.7 recommends adoption of content provenance technologies including digital watermarking and C2PA cryptographic metadata. Deepfakes identified as a primary risk (Sec. 2.1). Recommendations are for ASEAN cooperation, not binding on private actors.

biometric_data.detail: Not specifically addressed. Privacy and data governance principles apply generally.

training_data_transparency.detail: Section 3.3 recommends transparency around safety best practices akin to ingredient labels. Section 1.3 recommends data traceability and transparency about training data sources within commercial bounds.

content_labeling.detail: Transparency principle (Sec. 1.3) requires users to be aware they are interacting with GenAI. Section 3.7 recommends content provenance labeling and support for watermarking technologies.

anti_discrimination.detail: Fairness and Equity principle (Sec. 1.3) requires safeguards against bias; references BOLD and RealToxicityPrompts as evaluation metrics. No binding anti-discrimination mandate.

risk_classification.detail: No risk tier system. Risk-proportionate approach recommended under Testing and Assurance and Incident Reporting but no formal classification framework defined.

enforcement_model.detail: Explicitly voluntary. Conclusion states recommendations apply on a voluntary basis and the guide does not replace any member state's legal obligations.

operative_dates: Published 2025; voluntary; member states implement at their own discretion.
