summary: Developed jointly by the Ethiopian Government, Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, and the AI for Good Foundation (drafted December 2020, formally adopted 2024), this National AI Policy sets out a development-oriented AI strategy for Ethiopia. Rather than a regulatory framework, it is a sector-by-sector investment and deployment roadmap, identifying where AI can drive Ethiopia's economic transformation. Core infrastructure priorities include: a national high-bandwidth fibre network (Terabit capacity, ~US$20-100M), 100 community technology centres, and a national computing grid co-located with the GERD hydroelectric project. Sector applications span healthcare (AI-guided triage, telehealth, electronic medical records, robotic surgery pilots), education (AI-assisted flexible learning pathways, national lab network at universities), eGovernment (identity-linked cashless payments, AI-optimised benefits targeting, digitised licensing), agriculture (six-stage modernisation from cooperative formation to precision farming), financial inclusion (alternative credit scoring for unbanked populations), mobility (automated vehicles for rural/difficult terrain), and national defence. The data ethics section explicitly rejects heavy GDPR-style regulation in favour of lighter principles-based data rights, and recommends risk-adjusted evaluation of government AI systems against non-automated benchmarks rather than categorical prohibitions.
notable: Drafted December 2020 — predates most African national AI strategies. Explicitly development-first rather than regulation-first: positions AI as enabler of Ethiopia's SDG progress rather than subject of regulatory control. Notable caution about textiles/manufacturing automation displacing jobs (recommends against large capital investment without contractual lock-in). Calls for AI monitoring of communications for counter-terrorism and national security but explicitly does not recommend AI tools within a criminal liability framework. Co-authored by AI for Good Foundation CEO James Hodson, who co-authored the Babina et al. AI/employment study cited in the document.
legal_citation: National Artificial Intelligence Policy, Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia (draft December 2020; jointly developed with Tony Blair Institute for Global Change and AI for Good Foundation)
key_obligations: Government to build national fibre-backed communications infrastructure with Terabit connectivity among regional hubs
Government to establish 100 regional fibre hubs with attached Community Technology Centres
Government to invest in National Computing Grid co-located with GERD hydroelectric project
AI systems in government or regulated contexts subject to risk-adjusted evaluation against non-automated benchmark costs of failure
Government AI systems to be reconstructed and re-evaluated regularly based on rate of change in predicted context

Six data ethics principles: individual right to access personal data, right to description of uses, timely responses, right to contest unlawful use, demonstration of non-discriminatory processing of protected categories, ISO/IEC 27001 compliance for sensitive data
Government to launch national telehealth system leveraging AI voice/language processing
Government to develop national EMR system with AI-driven alerts and anonymised public health aggregation
Universal biometric identity registration for all residents linked to eGovernment, education, healthcare, and finance

impact_assessment.detail: Policy recommends risk-adjusted evaluation for all critical government AI applications: real-world validation cases annotated with cost-of-failure metrics, compared against non-automated process errors. Not a formal statutory requirement.

prohibited_categories.detail: Policy is development-oriented; no prohibited AI use cases specified. Recommends against AI tools in criminal liability frameworks for hate speech/disinformation.

human_review_rights.detail: No formal individual right to human review. Policy recommends human-benchmarked AI evaluation in government contexts but does not create individual rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Non-binding policy framework; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action. Data ethics section recommends ombudsman and escalation process for data rights violations.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric identity registration recommended as universal infrastructure; no specific data protection framework for biometric data beyond general data ethics principles.

training_data_transparency.detail: Data ethics principles require organisations to describe uses of personal data on request; no specific training data transparency obligation.

anti_discrimination.detail: Policy recommends consistent treatment of protected categories in AI decision-making and notes market forces should self-correct bias in unregulated contexts. No formal anti-discrimination mandate for AI.

risk_classification.detail: Government and regulated contexts require risk-adjusted evaluation with cost-of-failure weighting. Unregulated/commercial contexts governed by general legal and ethical frameworks, not AI-specific regulation.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding policy recommendation document. AI and Robotics Centre of Excellence (ASTU) to harmonise regulatory framework. Explicitly rejects heavy GDPR-style regulation as unsuited to Ethiopia's development priorities.

operative_dates: Drafted December 2020; formally adopted 2024. Non-binding policy framework.

title: Egypt National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030 (Second Edition)
summary: Egypt's second national AI strategy (2025–2030), issued by the National Council for Artificial Intelligence. Builds on the first edition (2021) in response to the emergence of generative AI and large language models. Structured around six pillars — Governance, Technology, Data, ICT and AI Infrastructure, Ecosystem, and Talent — with 21 initiatives and 89 KPIs. Strategic goals include growing AI professionals to 30,000, establishing 250+ AI companies, reaching 7.7% ICT contribution to GDP, doubling AI publications to 6,000/year, and creating a national AI fund of $430–860M. Includes development of a national Arabic foundation LLM and finalization of an Egyptian AI law. Egypt ranked #52 on the Tortoise Global AI Index 2024 with a target of #20 by 2030.

title: Republic of Ghana National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2035

summary: Ghana's national AI strategy for 2025-2035, issued by the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations. Vision: 'Ghana 2035: The AI-Powered Society.' Structured around eight pillars: AI Education, Youth Employment, Digital Infrastructure, Data Governance, AI Community Ecosystem, Sector AI Adoption, Applied AI Research, and Public Sector AI. Key institutions to be created: Responsible AI Authority (RAI Authority, Year 1), National AI Fund (5 billion cedis 2025-2030, scaling to 15 billion 2030-2035), NLP Centre of Excellence, National Deep Science Institute, and a government LLM (GhanaChat). Targets include 1 million AI-ready youth by 2033, 10 AI unicorns by 2035, a private Ghanaian AGI lab competing globally, and a 500 billion cedi contribution to GDP by 2035. Fully aligned with the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (adopted by Ghana in 2021). Developed with support from GIZ FAIR Forward, British High Commission FCDO, KNUST, and MinoHealth AI Labs.

title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania
issuing_body: Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MICIT)
summary: Tanzania's first national AI guidelines, issued by the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology as Draft Version One (Version 2.0, June 2024). Provides guidance for all stakeholders — public and private — on the ethical and secure development, deployment, and adoption of AI. Structured around eight AI principles (Valid and Reliable, Safe, Managed Bias, Resilient, Transparency, Accountability, Explainable and Interpretable, Privacy-Enhanced), a recommended AI Code of Ethics, ten AI Guidelines, and six implementation proposals covering: human agency and control, technical reliability and security, privacy and data management, transparency/explainability/traceability, diversity and non-discrimination, and risk management and accountability. Explicitly states that Tanzania has no specific AI legislation yet, but notes that AI misuse can lead to penalties under the Data Protection Act of 2022. A formal AI legal framework is described as being in development.

summary: A three-article UAE federal decree law authorising the Cabinet to grant interim licenses for innovative AI and future-technology projects where no existing legislation applies. The Cabinet may set conditions and procedures for such projects and may temporarily exempt them from federal legislation to the extent required for implementation. The stated purpose is to enable piloting of projects while preparing future legislation to regulate them — a formal regulatory sandbox mechanism at the federal level.

title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
issuing_body: Office of the Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence (Omar Sultan Al Olama)
summary: The UAE's inaugural national AI strategy, published in 2018 under the newly created Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence. Vision: to make the UAE one of the leading nations in AI by 2031, aligned with UAE Centennial 2071. Structured around eight strategic objectives: building an AI destination brand (UAI), deploying AI in five priority sectors (energy, logistics, tourism, healthcare, cybersecurity), developing an AI ecosystem, AI-driven government services, talent development, world-class research, data infrastructure, and AI governance. Projects potential AI contribution of AED 335 billion in increased economic output (26% increase) and AED 353 billion GDP contribution by 2030 (13.6% of GDP). Introduces the 'UAI Seal of Approval' certification for ethical AI companies. The UAE AI and Blockchain Council oversees implementation across all emirates. Includes a proposal to co-create with France an 'IPCC for Artificial Intelligence' intergovernmental body.

short_name: AI and Data Governance White Paper (Moldova)
full_name: White Paper on Strategic Direction for Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance Policy (Republic of Moldova, Ministry of Economic Development and Digitisation)
enforcement_body: Ministry of Economic Development and Digitisation of the Republic of Moldova
summary: Moldova's Ministry of Economic Development and Digitisation published the country's first AI policy framework document on October 2, 2024—a White Paper on Strategic Direction for Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance Policy. The paper emphasizes ethical, inclusive, and sustainable AI development aligned with European standards, and complements Moldova's September 2024 signing of the Council of Europe AI Convention (CETS 225). As a non-binding framework, it signals Moldova's intent to align AI governance with EU norms ahead of its EU accession process.
notable: Moldova's first AI policy framework document; published alongside Moldova's signing of the Council of Europe AI Convention (CETS 225).
legal_citation: White Paper on Strategic Direction for Artificial Intelligence and Data Governance Policy (Republic of Moldova, October 2, 2024)
key_obligations: Establish strategic direction for AI and data governance policy
Align AI development with ethical and European standards
Promote inclusive and sustainable AI development

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed in non-binding white paper.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Not addressed.

anti_discrimination.detail: White paper emphasizes ethical and inclusive AI development principles.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding policy framework document.

short_name: Interagency AVM Quality Control Final Rule
full_name: Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models — 12 CFR Parts 34, 164, 225, 323, 722, 1026
enforcement_body: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
max_penalty: Per applicable banking statute — civil money penalties vary by agency
preemption_notes: Joint interagency rule under federal banking and consumer finance statutes; preempts conflicting state requirements for federally regulated entities.
summary: Six federal financial regulators jointly finalized quality control standards requiring mortgage originators and secondary market issuers to adopt policies ensuring automated valuation models (AVMs) produce credible, accurate estimates free from discriminatory bias. Covered entities must implement nondiscrimination controls, data integrity checks, conflict-of-interest safeguards, and random sample testing. The rule implements Section 1473 of the Dodd-Frank Act and is the first binding federal mandate specifically governing AI/ML-based property valuation.
notable: First binding federal rule specifically targeting AI/ML models in mortgage lending; mandates nondiscrimination quality controls for algorithmic appraisal tools.
key_obligations: Adopt written quality control policies for all AVMs used in loan origination and secondary market transactions
Implement controls to ensure nondiscrimination and compliance with applicable fair lending laws
Maintain data integrity and security protections for AVM inputs and outputs
Establish conflict-of-interest safeguards for AVM selection and use
Conduct random sample testing to validate AVM accuracy and quality

impact_assessment.detail: Requires covered institutions to implement ongoing quality control policies including testing and validation of AVM outputs before and during use.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not prohibit specific AVM uses; focuses on quality control and nondiscrimination standards.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual right to human review of AVM outputs; compliance obligations fall on institutions.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action under this rule; enforcement by the six participating agencies.

synthetic_media.detail: Mortgage valuation context only; does not address synthetic media.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure requirement; focus is on output quality and nondiscrimination.

anti_discrimination.detail: Requires explicit quality control policies designed to ensure nondiscrimination in AVM outputs; must comply with ECOA, FHA, and other applicable fair lending laws.

risk_classification.detail: No tiered risk classification; all covered AVMs subject to the same quality control requirements.

enforcement_model.detail: Enforced by six federal banking regulators through their existing examination and enforcement authorities; civil money penalties under applicable banking statutes.

short_name: HHS Section 1557 Nondiscrimination Rule — AI Provisions
full_name: Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities — AI Patient Care Decision Support Provisions, 45 CFR Part 92
max_penalty: Per ACA § 1557 — compensatory damages; injunctive relief; loss of federal funding
preemption_notes: Federal civil rights rule applicable to all health programs receiving federal financial assistance; does not preempt stronger state protections.
summary: The HHS Office for Civil Rights updated the Section 1557 nondiscrimination rule to explicitly address AI and algorithmic tools used in patient care decisions. Covered health entities must take reasonable steps to identify and mitigate discrimination risks in patient care decision support tools — including AI/ML clinical algorithms, prior authorization tools, and risk scoring systems — used to make or support decisions about patient care. The AI-specific provisions became effective May 2025; some other portions of the rule remain under litigation.
notable: First federal healthcare nondiscrimination rule to explicitly require covered entities to audit clinical AI tools for discriminatory bias; AI provisions operative separately from enjoined gender identity provisions.
key_obligations: Identify discrimination risks in patient care decision support tools including AI and ML systems
Take reasonable steps to mitigate identified discrimination risks
Ensure AI-based prior authorization and risk scoring tools comply with civil rights requirements
Covered entities remain responsible for third-party AI tools used in patient care

impact_assessment.detail: Requires covered entities to proactively identify discrimination risks in patient care decision support tools before and during use.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not categorically prohibit AI tools; requires risk identification and mitigation.

human_review_rights.detail: No explicit right to human review of AI-assisted clinical decisions; focuses on institutional obligations.

private_right_of_action.detail: Section 1557 provides private right of action; compensatory damages and injunctive relief available; HHS OCR administrative enforcement also available.

synthetic_media.detail: Healthcare context only; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions beyond existing HIPAA framework.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure requirement; focus is on nondiscriminatory outcomes.

anti_discrimination.detail: Explicitly requires covered health entities to identify and mitigate discrimination risks in AI/ML clinical tools; applies existing Section 1557 protected categories to algorithmic tools.

risk_classification.detail: No tiered risk classification; all covered AI patient care tools subject to nondiscrimination requirements.

enforcement_model.detail: HHS OCR administrative enforcement; private right of action under Section 1557; loss of federal funding as ultimate sanction.

short_name: FDA PCCP Final Guidance for AI-Enabled Device Software
full_name: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions (FDA Final Guidance)
enforcement_body: FDA Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH)
preemption_notes: Non-binding guidance; operationally required for FDA 510(k)/PMA clearance of AI-enabled medical devices.
summary: FDA's final guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) allows AI-enabled medical device makers to pre-specify the types of model updates and modifications that can be implemented after initial clearance without requiring a new 510(k) or PMA submission. The guidance expands the PCCP framework from ML-only to all AI-enabled device software functions and requires manufacturers to describe anticipated algorithm changes, performance objectives, and methodology for validating updates. This streamlines the regulatory pathway for continuously learning AI medical devices.
notable: Enables continuously learning AI medical devices to update algorithms post-clearance without new FDA submissions, providing a major regulatory pathway innovation for adaptive AI diagnostics.
legal_citation: FDA Final Guidance (Dec. 3, 2024); 21 U.S.C. 360 (FDCA); 89 Fed. Reg. 96,040 (Dec. 4, 2024)
key_obligations: Include PCCP in marketing submission describing planned AI/ML algorithm modifications
Specify performance objectives for each planned modification type
Describe validation methodology and testing protocols for post-clearance updates
Implement modifications only within pre-specified PCCP parameters without new FDA submission

impact_assessment.detail: Requires detailed performance objectives and validation methodology in pre-market PCCP submission; updates must be validated against pre-specified criteria.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not prohibit AI device categories; defines the pathway for approved device modification.

human_review_rights.detail: No patient rights provisions; focuses on manufacturer obligations in the regulatory pathway.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private right of action; FDA enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: Medical device context only; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions beyond existing medical device framework.

training_data_transparency.detail: No public training data disclosure; validation methodology must be documented in the PCCP.

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination provisions; performance metrics may include subgroup analysis.

risk_classification.detail: PCCP applicability differs by device risk class (Class I/II/III); PMA devices face higher scrutiny for planned modifications.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding guidance; enforcement through existing FDA medical device authorities including recall, warning letters, and civil penalties.

short_name: OMB M-24-18 — Responsible AI Acquisition Memo
full_name: Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government (OMB Memorandum M-24-18)
preemption_notes: Applies to federal agencies only; no effect on state or private sector.
summary: OMB Memorandum M-24-18 directed federal agencies on responsible AI acquisition principles under the Biden administration, establishing guidance on AI vendor due diligence, contractual safeguards for government AI purchases, and responsible AI principles that agencies must incorporate into procurement. The memo operationalized the AI acquisition aspects of EO 14110 for the federal contracting process. It was rescinded and superseded by OMB M-25-22 in April 2025.
notable: Rescinded by OMB M-25-22 in April 2025; replaced by Trump administration AI acquisition framework emphasizing innovation and reduced regulatory burden.
legal_citation: OMB Memorandum M-24-18 (Sept. 24, 2024)
key_obligations: Agencies must apply responsible AI acquisition principles in AI procurements
AI vendor due diligence requirements for significant AI acquisitions
Contractual safeguards required in federal AI contracts
Agencies must designate AI acquisition points of contact

impact_assessment.detail: Required agencies to assess AI risks before procurement; directed vendor due diligence on safety and reliability.

prohibited_categories.detail: Did not prohibit specific AI procurement categories; focused on responsible acquisition principles.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions; focused on agency obligations in procurement.

private_right_of_action.detail: Agency directive only; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Procurement focus; did not specifically address synthetic media.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure requirements; vendor due diligence broadly defined.

anti_discrimination.detail: Responsible AI principles included equity considerations but no specific anti-discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: No formal risk classification framework; risk-based acquisition approach.

enforcement_model.detail: OMB oversight of federal agencies; no external enforcement mechanism.

short_name: EO 14141 — Biden AI Infrastructure EO
full_name: Executive Order 14141 — Advancing United States Leadership in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure
enforcement_body: Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP)
preemption_notes: Executive order directing federal agency action; revoked by EO 14318.
summary: Signed in the final days of the Biden administration, EO 14141 directed DOE and DOD to identify and make available federal land sites for AI data center leasing, required clean energy coupling for federal AI infrastructure, and tasked OSTP with coordinating a national AI infrastructure strategy. The order aimed to accelerate domestic AI compute capacity while tying data center development to clean energy commitments. It was revoked by President Trump's EO 14318 on July 23, 2025.
notable: Issued on January 14, 2025 — six days before end of Biden administration. Revoked by EO 14318 on July 23, 2025, which removed the clean energy requirements and streamlined federal land permitting.
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,141, 90 Fed. Reg. 6,789 (Jan. 17, 2025)
key_obligations: DOE and DOD to identify federal sites suitable for AI data center development
AI data centers on federal land must be coupled with clean energy sources
OSTP to coordinate national AI infrastructure strategy
Streamlined leasing pathways for federal AI infrastructure sites

impact_assessment.detail: Infrastructure focus; no AI system impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Infrastructure order; does not address AI application categories.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Executive order; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Infrastructure focus; does not address synthetic media.

enforcement_model.detail: Executive order; no external enforcement; revoked before most directives were implemented.

short_name: EO 14316 — Preventing Woke AI in Federal Government
full_name: Executive Order 14319 — Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government
enforcement_body: Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP)
preemption_notes: Executive order directing federal AI procurement policy; no effect on state or private sector procurement.
summary: EO 14316 directs OMB to issue procurement guidance within 120 days requiring federal agencies to acquire AI systems that produce ideologically neutral outputs and avoid politically-biased responses. Federal agencies are directed not to procure AI systems that incorporate DEI frameworks, engage in viewpoint discrimination, or promote particular political perspectives. The order requires agencies to evaluate AI systems for ideological neutrality before procurement.
notable: Part of a trilogy of July 23, 2025 Trump AI executive orders alongside EO 14317 (AI exports) and EO 14318 (data center permitting).
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,316, 90 Fed. Reg. — (July 28, 2025)
key_obligations: OMB to issue AI procurement guidance within 120 days prioritizing ideologically neutral AI systems
Federal agencies to evaluate AI systems for political bias before procurement
Agencies to avoid procuring AI systems incorporating DEI frameworks
OSTP to develop standards for assessing AI ideological neutrality

impact_assessment.detail: No formal impact assessment requirement; agencies must evaluate ideological neutrality rather than safety or civil rights impacts.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not prohibit AI categories; restricts procurement based on ideological characteristics.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Executive order; no private right of action.

anti_discrimination.detail: Order targets ideological neutrality rather than protected-class discrimination; effectively reverses DEI-oriented AI procurement policies.

enforcement_model.detail: OMB oversight of federal agency compliance; no external enforcement mechanism.

short_name: EO 14317 — Promoting Export of American AI Technology Stack
full_name: Executive Order 14320 — Promoting the Export of the American AI Technology Stack
enforcement_body: Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP)
preemption_notes: Executive order directing federal trade and export policy; no preemption effect.
summary: EO 14317 establishes an American AI Exports Program through Commerce, State, and OSTP to promote US AI software, hardware, semiconductor, and cloud infrastructure exports globally. The order removes Biden-era AI chip export restrictions and directs agencies to identify trade barriers to US AI technology exports in foreign markets. It frames US AI exports as a national security and economic competitiveness priority and directs diplomatic efforts to open foreign markets.
notable: Reverses the Biden administration's AI diffusion export control framework; part of the July 23, 2025 trilogy of Trump AI executive orders.
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,317, 90 Fed. Reg. — (July 28, 2025)
key_obligations: Commerce and State to establish American AI Exports Program
Identify and reduce foreign trade barriers to US AI technology exports
Remove Biden-era AI chip export restrictions
OSTP to coordinate US AI export promotion strategy
Diplomatic missions to support US AI market access globally

impact_assessment.detail: Trade and export focus; no AI system impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Removes export restrictions rather than imposing new prohibitions.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Executive order; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Export policy focus; does not address synthetic media.

enforcement_model.detail: Executive order; implementation through Commerce/State/OSTP; no external enforcement mechanism.

short_name: EO 14318 — Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure
full_name: Executive Order 14318 — Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure
enforcement_body: Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP)
preemption_notes: Executive order directing federal land and permitting policy; may affect state environmental review timelines for projects on federal land.
summary: EO 14318 revokes Biden's EO 14141 and establishes an expedited federal permitting process for AI data center construction on federal land, removing the clean energy coupling requirement from Biden's order. The order directs DOE to identify priority federal sites for data center development, establishes a fast-track environmental review process, and directs agencies to eliminate regulatory bottlenecks impeding data center construction. It aims to dramatically accelerate domestic AI compute infrastructure build-out.
notable: Revokes EO 14141 (Biden AI infrastructure order); removes mandatory clean energy requirements; part of the July 23, 2025 trilogy of Trump AI executive orders.
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,318, 90 Fed. Reg. — (July 28, 2025)
key_obligations: DOE to identify priority federal sites for AI data center development
Establish fast-track environmental review for data center projects on federal land
Agencies to eliminate regulatory bottlenecks for data center permitting
CEQ to streamline NEPA review timelines for AI infrastructure projects

synthetic_media.detail: Infrastructure focus; does not address synthetic media.

short_name: NIST AI 100-4 — Reducing Risks from Synthetic Content
full_name: NIST AI 100-4: Reducing Risks Posed by Synthetic Content — An Overview of Technical Approaches to Digital Content Transparency
enforcement_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
preemption_notes: Voluntary guidance; no preemptive effect.
summary: NIST AI 100-4 provides technical guidance on approaches to mitigate risks from AI-generated synthetic content including deepfakes, synthetic audio, and AI-generated text. Produced pursuant to EO 14110 Section 4(i), the publication surveys watermarking approaches, content provenance tracking, cryptographic methods, and deepfake detection technologies. It is intended as foundational technical guidance for organizations implementing digital content transparency and provenance systems.
notable: Foundational NIST technical guidance on synthetic content risk mitigation; produced by the NIST AI Safety Institute (AISI) pursuant to Biden's EO 14110.
legal_citation: NIST AI 100-4 (Nov. 20, 2024); produced pursuant to EO 14110 § 4(i)
key_obligations: Voluntary technical guidance on watermarking and provenance tracking for AI-generated content
Surveys deepfake detection approaches and their limitations
Provides cryptographic content authentication methods overview
Identifies research gaps in synthetic content detection

impact_assessment.detail: Technical guidance document; no mandatory impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Non-binding guidance; does not prohibit synthetic content categories.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions; technical focus.

private_right_of_action.detail: Non-binding guidance; no enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: Core focus of document; surveys watermarking, provenance tracking, and deepfake detection approaches as voluntary technical measures.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions beyond deepfake facial synthesis discussion.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; technical focus on content outputs.

content_labeling.detail: Surveys content provenance and labeling technical approaches including C2PA standard and watermarking; voluntary recommendations only.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework; technical overview of mitigation approaches.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary guidance; no enforcement mechanism.

short_name: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 — Adversarial Machine Learning
full_name: NIST AI 100-2 E2025: Adversarial Machine Learning — A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (2025 Edition)
enforcement_body: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
preemption_notes: Voluntary guidance; no preemptive effect.
summary: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 is the updated 2025 edition of NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy, expanded to cover both predictive AI and generative AI attack and mitigation taxonomies. The publication classifies attack types — including evasion, poisoning, privacy attacks (including membership inference and model inversion), and misuse attacks — and corresponding mitigations for each. It is widely referenced in federal AI security contexts and provides the standard terminology for AI adversarial robustness discussions.
notable: The definitive US government taxonomy for AI/ML security attacks and mitigations; widely referenced in federal agency AI security requirements and procurement.
key_obligations: Voluntary taxonomy of adversarial ML attack types for predictive and generative AI
Standard terminology for evasion, poisoning, privacy, and misuse attacks
Mitigation strategies for each attack category
Extended coverage to generative AI-specific attack vectors from 2024 edition

impact_assessment.detail: Technical guidance document; no mandatory assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Non-binding guidance; does not prohibit AI categories.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions; technical focus.

private_right_of_action.detail: Non-binding guidance; no enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: Security focus on adversarial attacks; does not specifically address synthetic media regulation.

training_data_transparency.detail: Addresses data poisoning as an attack vector but no disclosure requirements.

risk_classification.detail: Provides taxonomy of attack severity and likelihood; voluntary risk-informed framework for AI security evaluation.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary guidance; no enforcement mechanism.

short_name: Puerto Rico H.B. 824 — Cybersecurity Act AI Amendment
full_name: Puerto Rico H.B. 824 — Amendment to Act 40-2024 (Cybersecurity Act) to Include Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity Education
summary: Amends Act 40-2024 (Cybersecurity Act of the Government of Puerto Rico) to expressly incorporate artificial intelligence as a topic in the virtual cybersecurity education program and continuing education course administered by PRITS. PRITS must include AI in the continuing education course on cybersecurity

short_name: Puerto Rico H.B. 968 — Ethical Use of AI in Educational Institutions
full_name: Puerto Rico H.B. 968 — Act on the Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Institutions of Puerto Rico
enforcement_body: Department of Education; Department of State
summary: Requires the Department of Education and all private educational institutions to establish and implement policies on the ethical use of AI. Policies must address safety, autonomy, privacy, transparency, diversity/inclusion, and accountability. Private institutions must file policies with the Department of State. Annual training required for students and staff. 180-day compliance window after enactment. PRITS provides technical guidance.

Private educational institutions must promulgate similar AI ethics policies
Private institutions must file policies with the Department of State
Policies must cover safety, autonomy, privacy, transparency, diversity, and accountability

short_name: Puerto Rico S.R. 485 — Amendment to SR 133 (Electoral Technology Investigation)
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Resolution 485 — Amendment to S.R. 133 Extending Reporting Deadline for Electoral Technology Investigation

short_name: Puerto Rico H.B. 978 — Cyber Privacy Protection for Children (AI Amendment)
full_name: Puerto Rico House Bill 978 — Amendment to the Cyber Privacy Protection Act for Children and Youth (Act 185-2024) adding digital duty of care, AI content protections, and economic rights for minor content creators

Platforms must conduct impact assessments before introducing new features

Prohibition on using minors' data for advertising

short_name: Puerto Rico H.B. 1099 — Rules of Evidence (AI Authentication)

Courts must rule on admissibility of AI-challenged evidence pursuant to Rule 109

short_name: Puerto Rico H.B. 1238 — AI Deception of Authorities (Penal Code)
full_name: Puerto Rico House Bill 1238 — Addition of Article 268A to Penal Code criminalizing use of artificial intelligence to produce deceptive content intended to deceive law enforcement or government officials

Misdemeanor base offense; felony (3 years) if the underlying act would constitute a felony.

full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Bill 769 — Puerto Rico Artificial Intelligence Development and Innovation Institute Act: creating a public-interest non-profit AI institute, AI development fund, and amending incentive code to promote AI research, commercialization, and talent development

short_name: Puerto Rico S 705 — AI in Sports (Vetoed)

short_name: Puerto Rico S 760 — AI-Generated Revenge Pornography (Criminal)
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Bill 760 — Amendment to Act 21-2021 (Puerto Rico Pornographic Revenge Act) to criminalize disclosure of AI-generated or AI-altered explicit intimate material without consent
max_penalty: 8 years imprisonment (aggravated circumstances); 3 years fixed term base felony
summary: Amends the Puerto Rico Pornographic Revenge Act (Act 21-2021) to explicitly cover intimate or sexual material produced by AI — including deepfakes. Criminalizes the unauthorized disclosure of real or AI-fabricated explicit material; felony (3 years) for dissemination, misdemeanor for threats; 8 years for extortion. Aligns with federal Take It Down Act (Public Law 119-12, 2025).
key_obligations: Prohibition on disseminating AI-generated intimate content without consent
Felony (3-year fixed term) for dissemination; misdemeanor for threats of dissemination
8-year imprisonment for extortion using AI-generated intimate content
10-year statute of limitations

short_name: Puerto Rico S 820 — Media and Information Literacy Act
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Bill 820 — Media and Information Literacy Act of Puerto Rico: requiring public school curriculum to include critical media literacy, AI literacy, and disinformation resistance competencies
summary: Creates the Media and Information Literacy Act of Puerto Rico, requiring the Department of Education to integrate media and digital literacy competencies into all K-12 subjects, with emphasis on identifying AI-generated content and deepfakes, understanding algorithmic bias, critical source evaluation, and responsible digital citizenship. Teachers must be trained; annual report to Legislature required.
key_obligations: DEPR must integrate media/AI literacy into all K-12 curriculum within 2 academic years
Teachers must receive continuous training in media/digital literacy
Annual report to Legislative Assembly on implementation progress
Regulations to be adopted within 180 days of enactment

short_name: Puerto Rico S 870 — Comprehensive Criminal AI Misuse Law
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Bill 870 — Amendment to Penal Code (Act 146-2012) creating a new Title VII on Crimes Related to the Malicious Use of Artificial Intelligence: deepfakes, cyberbullying, fraud, cybercrime, discrimination, privacy violations, disinformation, and market manipulation
max_penalty: 8 years imprisonment (felony); $15,000 per privacy violation
summary: Adds comprehensive criminal framework for malicious AI use to the Puerto Rico Penal Code. Creates new Title VII with Articles 310-317 covering: unauthorized commercial use of AI-generated image/voice without consent (felony); AI cyberbullying; AI fraud; AI cyberattacks; AI discrimination; AI privacy violations; AI disinformation affecting elections/health; and AI market manipulation. Also establishes AI use as a general aggravating circumstance (25% penalty increase, Article 64(k)).
key_obligations: Prohibition on unauthorized commercial use of AI-generated likeness/voice (felony, 3-6 years)
Prohibition on AI-powered cyberbullying (misdemeanor; felony for minors/severe harm)
AI used in fraud aggravates penalties by one degree
AI disinformation affecting elections/public safety is felony (1 year fixed)
AI use as aggravating circumstance adds 25% to any criminal penalty

short_name: Puerto Rico S 1226 — AI Transparency in Insurance Claims
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Bill 1226 — Act of Transparency and Supervision in the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Insurance Claims: amending the Insurance Code to require human review of all adverse insurance determinations and mandate disclosure of AI use
max_penalty: $25,000 per violation
summary: Creates new Chapter 55 of the Puerto Rico Insurance Code requiring that no adverse insurance determination (denial, reduction, or limitation of claim) be made exclusively by automated systems, algorithms, or AI; mandates qualified human professional review of all adverse determinations within 15 days; requires disclosure of AI participation in claim communications; establishes private right of action for consumers; creates presumption of arbitrariness when human review cannot be demonstrated; and authorizes Insurance Commissioner to impose fines of $5,000-$25,000 per violation.
key_obligations: No adverse claim determination may be based exclusively on AI/automated systems
Qualified human professional must independently review and approve all adverse determinations
Human review must be provided within 15 days of request
Detailed records of human review and AI participation must be maintained
Denial communications must state AI was not the sole decision-maker
Insurers must document AI use in internal manuals

short_name: Puerto Rico S.J.R. 16 — AI Monitoring App for Public Auctions
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Joint Resolution 16 — Ordering PRITS to create and implement an AI-based application for monitoring public auction processes for transparency and fraud prevention
summary: Orders PRITS to develop and implement an AI-based application for real-time monitoring of public auction processes in Puerto Rico, capable of detecting suspicious patterns, generating automatic alerts on irregularities, and providing accessible reports to oversight entities. Development plan due to Legislature within 90 days; quarterly implementation reports during first year.
key_obligations: PRITS must develop AI monitoring application for public auctions
Application must include real-time monitoring, pattern detection, and automatic alerts
Development plan due to Legislative Assembly within 90 days
Quarterly progress reports during first year of implementation

short_name: Puerto Rico S.J.R. 86 — AI-Supported Precision Medicine Feasibility Study
full_name: Puerto Rico Senate Joint Resolution 86 — Ordering Department of Health, in coordination with ASEM, UPR, and accredited medical schools, to investigate feasibility of an AI-supported Precision Medicine Program in Puerto Rico
summary: Orders the Puerto Rico Department of Health, in coordination with ASEM, the Science and Technology Trust, UPR Medical Sciences Campus, and accredited medical schools, to conduct a feasibility study on establishing a Precision Medicine Program supported by AI. Study must cover current use cases in oncology/chronic diseases/pharmacogenetics, infrastructure needs, human resources, legal/regulatory challenges around data protection, cost estimates, and equitable access strategies. Report due to Legislature within 270 days.
key_obligations: Department of Health must conduct AI precision medicine feasibility study
Study must cover use cases, infrastructure, regulatory challenges, and equity
PRITS serves as technical advisor on government system interoperability aspects
Report due to Legislative Assembly within 270 days
